(That tear must be mended; you should take a needle and darn it at once, as I taught you, or else tomorrow... khe! tomorrow... khe-khe-khe!.. it will tear worse!” she cried, straining herself)... “Then Prince Shchegolskoy, a gentleman of the bedchamber, had just come from Petersburg... he danced the mazurka with me and wanted to come the very next day to propose; but I thanked him myself in flattering terms and said that my heart had long belonged to another. That other was your father, Polya; Papa was terribly angry... Is the water ready? Well, give me the little shirt; and the stockings?.. Lida,” she turned to her little daughter, “you must sleep like that tonight, without your shirt; somehow... and put your stockings out beside it... I’ll wash them at the same time... Why doesn’t that ragamuffin come home, the drunkard! He has worn his shirt like a dishcloth, torn it all to pieces... I’d do it all at once, so as not to be tormented two nights running! Lord! Khe-khe-khe-khe! Again! What is it?” she cried, looking at the crowd in the passage and at the people pushing their way into her room with some burden. “What is it? What are they carrying? Lord!”
“Where shall we put him?” asked the policeman, looking round, when they had already dragged the bloodstained, unconscious Marmeladov into the room.
“On the sofa! Put him right on the sofa, with his head here,” Raskolnikov pointed.
“Run over in the street! Drunk!” someone shouted from the passage.
Katerina Ivanovna stood there quite pale, breathing with difficulty. The children were frightened. Little Lidochka screamed, rushed to Polenka, clung to her and trembled all over.
When he had laid Marmeladov down, Raskolnikov rushed to Katerina Ivanovna:

“For God’s sake, calm yourself, don’t be frightened!” he said, rattling it off. “He was crossing the street, a carriage ran him down; don’t worry, he’ll come to, I had him carried here... I was here before, remember... He’ll come to, I’ll pay!”
“He’s done it now!” Katerina Ivanovna cried in despair, and rushed to her husband.

Raskolnikov soon noticed that this woman was not one of those who faint at once. In an instant a pillow was under the unhappy man’s head, which no one had yet thought of; Katerina Ivanovna began to undress him, to examine him; she bustled about and did not lose her head, forgetting about herself, biting her trembling lips and stifling the cries that were ready to burst from her breast.
Meanwhile Raskolnikov persuaded someone to run for a doctor. A doctor, it turned out, lived next door but one.

“I have sent for a doctor,” he kept telling Katerina Ivanovna. “Don’t worry, I’ll pay. Isn’t there any water?.. And give me a napkin, a towel, something, quickly; we don’t know yet how badly he is hurt... He is hurt, not killed, you may be sure... We’ll see what the doctor says!”

Katerina Ivanovna rushed to the window; there, on a broken-down chair in the corner, stood a big earthenware basin of water, ready for the night washing of the children’s and her husband’s linen. This night washing was done by Katerina Ivanovna herself, with her own hands, at least twice a week and sometimes more often, for they had come to such a point that there was almost no change of linen left at all, and each member of the family had only one of everything; and Katerina Ivanovna could not bear dirt, and would rather torment herself at night, beyond her strength, when everyone was asleep, so as to dry the wet linen by morning on a line stretched across the room and give them clean things, than see dirt in the house. She seized the basin to carry it as Raskolnikov asked, but almost fell with the weight. But he had already found a towel, wetted it with water, and begun to wash Marmeladov’s blood-covered face. Katerina Ivanovna stood right there, painfully drawing breath and holding her chest with her hands. She needed help herself. Raskolnikov began to understand that perhaps he had done badly in persuading them to carry the injured man here. The policeman too stood there in perplexity.

“Polya!” cried Katerina Ivanovna. “Run to Sonya, quickly. If you don’t find her at home, never mind, say that Father has been run over by horses and that she must come here at once... as soon as she gets back. Quickly, Polya! Here, cover yourself with the shawl!”

“Wun as fast as you can!” the boy suddenly shouted from his chair, and having said it, sank back into his former silent, upright sitting on the chair, with eyes wide open, heels forward and toes apart.

Meanwhile the room had filled so that there was no room for an apple to fall. The police left, except one, who stayed for the time being and tried to drive the people who had gathered from the stairs back onto the stairs. On the other hand, almost all Madame Lippewechsel’s lodgers poured out of the inner rooms; at first they only crowded in the doorway, but then they surged in a crowd into the room itself. Katerina Ivanovna flew into a frenzy.

“You might at least let him die in peace!” she shouted at the whole crowd. “What a show you have found! With cigarettes! Khe-khe-khe! Why not come in with your hats on!.. And there is one in his hat... Get out! At least have some respect for the dying!”

The coughing choked her, but the scolding did its work. Katerina Ivanovna was evidently even a little feared; the lodgers, one after another, squeezed back to the door with that strange inner sense of satisfaction which is always to be noticed, even in those nearest to us, when sudden misfortune strikes a neighbour, and from which not a single person, without exception, is free, in spite of even the most sincere feeling of pity and sympathy.
From behind the door, however, voices could be heard about the hospital, and that there was no point in disturbing people here for nothing.

“No point in dying, is there!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, and she was about to rush and open the door to burst upon them with a whole thunderstorm, but in the doorway she ran into Madame Lippewechsel herself, who had only just heard of the misfortune and had come running to put things in order. She was an extremely quarrelsome and muddle-headed German woman.
“Ach, mein Gott!” she clasped her hands. “Your husband drunk horse trample. To hospital vith him! I am ze landlady!”

“Amalia Ludwigovna! I beg you to remember what you are saying,” Katerina Ivanovna began haughtily (she always spoke to her landlady in a haughty tone, so that she should ‘remember her place’, and even now she could not deny herself this pleasure). “Amalia Ludwigovna...”
“I told you vonce and for all zat you never dare call me Amal Ludwigovna; I am Amal-Ivan!”

“You are not Amal-Ivan but Amalia Ludwigovna, and since I am not one of your vile flatterers, like Mr Lebezyatnikov, who is laughing now behind the door” (behind the door there was indeed laughter and a shout: “They’re at it!”), “I shall always call you Amalia Ludwigovna, though I absolutely cannot understand why you dislike that name. You can see for yourself what has happened to Semyon Zakharovich; he is dying. I beg you to shut this door at once and let no one in here. Let him at least die in peace! Otherwise, I assure you, your conduct will be known tomorrow to the Governor-General himself. The Prince knew me when I was a girl, and remembers Semyon Zakharovich very well, and did him many favours. Everyone knows that Semyon Zakharovich had many friends and patrons, whom he himself gave up out of noble pride, feeling his unhappy weakness; but now” (she pointed to Raskolnikov) “a generous young man is helping us, who has means and connections, and whom Semyon Zakharovich knew as a child, and you may be sure, Amalia Ludwigovna...”

All this was uttered in an extraordinary patter, faster and faster, but coughing suddenly broke off Katerina Ivanovna’s eloquence. At that moment the dying man came to himself and groaned, and she ran to him. The injured man opened his eyes and, still not recognising or understanding, began to stare at Raskolnikov, who was standing over him. He was breathing heavily, deeply and slowly; blood had oozed out at the corners of his lips; sweat stood out on his forehead. Not recognising Raskolnikov, he began to look around uneasily. Katerina Ivanovna looked at him with a sad but stern gaze, and tears flowed from her eyes.
“My God! His whole chest is crushed! The blood, the blood!” she said in despair. “We must take all his outer clothes off! Turn a little, Semyon Zakharovich, if you can,” she cried to him.
Marmeladov recognised her.
“A priest!” he said in a hoarse voice.
Katerina Ivanovna went to the window, leaned her forehead against the window frame, and exclaimed in despair:
“Oh, accursed life!”
“A priest!” the dying man said again after a minute’s silence.

“They’ve gone for one!” Katerina Ivanovna shouted at him; he obeyed the shout and fell silent. With a timid, anguished look he sought her with his eyes; she came back to him again and stood at the head of the sofa. He grew a little calmer, but not for long. Soon his eyes rested on little Lidochka (his favourite), who was trembling in the corner as if in a fit and looking at him with her astonished, childishly intent eyes.
“Ah... ah...” he pointed at her uneasily. He wanted to say something.
“What now?” cried Katerina Ivanovna.
“Barefoot! Barefoot!” he muttered, pointing with a crazed look at the little girl’s bare feet.
“Be quie-e-et!” Katerina Ivanovna cried irritably. “You know yourself why she’s barefoot!”
“Thank God, the doctor!” cried Raskolnikov, relieved.

The doctor came in, a neat little old man, a German, looking about him with a distrustful air; he went up to the injured man, took his pulse, carefully felt his head and, with Katerina Ivanovna’s help, unfastened the whole blood-soaked shirt and bared the man’s chest. The whole chest was mangled, crushed and torn; several ribs on the right side were broken. On the left side, right over the heart, was an ominous, large, yellowish-black mark, a cruel blow from a hoof. The doctor frowned. The policeman told him that the man had been caught in the wheel and dragged, turning round and round, about thirty paces along the roadway.
“It’s surprising that he came to at all,” the doctor whispered softly to Raskolnikov.
“What do you say?” he asked.
“He will die in a moment.”
“Is there really no hope?”

“Not the slightest! He is at his last breath... Besides, his head is very dangerously hurt... Hm. Perhaps I could bleed him... but... it will be useless. In five or ten minutes he will certainly die.”
“Then bleed him, better!”
“Very well... But I warn you, it will be completely useless.”

At that moment more steps were heard, the crowd in the passage parted, and on the threshold appeared a priest with the sacrament, a grey-haired little old man. A policeman had gone for him, still from the street. The doctor at once gave up his place to him and exchanged a significant look with him. Raskolnikov begged the doctor to wait a little at least. He shrugged his shoulders and stayed.

Everyone stepped back. The confession lasted a very short time. The dying man hardly understood anything well; he could only utter broken, indistinct sounds. Katerina Ivanovna took Lidochka, lifted the boy from his chair and, going into the corner by the stove, knelt down and made the children kneel in front of her. The little girl only trembled; but the boy, kneeling on his bare little knees, raised his little hand in measured movements, crossed himself fully and bowed to the ground, knocking his forehead on the floor, which apparently gave him special pleasure. Katerina Ivanovna bit her lips and held back her tears; she too was praying, now and then straightening the child’s little shirt, and she managed to throw over the girl’s too bare shoulders a scarf which she took from the chest of drawers without getting up from her knees and while still praying. Meanwhile the doors from the inner rooms began to be opened again by the curious. In the passage, the onlookers, lodgers from the whole staircase, crowded closer and closer, not, however, stepping over the threshold of the room. A single candle end lit the whole scene.

At that moment Polenka, who had run for her sister, pushed her way quickly through the crowd from the passage. She came in, hardly able to breathe from running fast, took off her shawl, looked for her mother, went up to her and said: “She’s coming! I met her in the street!” Her mother pulled her down onto her knees and put her beside her. From the crowd, soundlessly and timidly, a girl pushed her way forward, and her sudden appearance in that room, among poverty, rags, death and despair, was strange. She too was in rags; her finery was cheap, but decked out in the street fashion, according to the taste and rules that have grown up in their own special world, with a bright and shameful purpose standing out. Sonya stopped in the passage right by the threshold, but did not cross the threshold, and looked like someone lost, seeming not to be aware of anything, having forgotten both her silk dress, bought fourth-hand, coloured and improper here, with its very long and ridiculous train, and her immense crinoline, which blocked the whole door, and her light-coloured boots, and the parasol, useless at night, which she had brought with her, and the ridiculous round straw hat with a bright flame-coloured feather. From under this hat, worn tilted to one side like a boy’s, there peeped out a thin, pale, frightened little face with its mouth open and eyes fixed with horror. Sonya was small, about eighteen, thin, but a rather pretty blonde, with remarkable blue eyes. She stared at the bed, at the priest; she too was breathless from walking fast. At last the whispering, some words in the crowd, probably reached her. She lowered her eyes, took a step over the threshold, and stood in the room, but again right in the doorway.

The confession and communion were over. Katerina Ivanovna went up to her husband’s bed again. The priest stepped back, and as he left he turned to say a few words of farewell and comfort to Katerina Ivanovna.
“And where am I to put these ones?” she interrupted sharply and irritably, pointing to the little ones.
“God is merciful; hope for the help of the Most High,” the priest began.
“Eh-eh! He is merciful, but not to us!”
“That is a sin, a sin, madam,” the priest remarked, shaking his head.
“And isn’t this a sin?” cried Katerina Ivanovna, pointing to the dying man.
“Perhaps those who were the involuntary cause will agree to compensate you, at least for the loss of income...”

“You don’t understand me!” Katerina Ivanovna cried irritably, waving her hand. “And compensate for what? He crawled under the horses himself, drunk! What income? He brought us no income, only torment. Why, the drunkard drank everything away. He robbed us and carried it to the tavern; he wasted their lives and mine in the tavern! And thank God he is dying! It’s less loss!”
“You should forgive in the hour of death; this is a sin, madam, such feelings are a great sin!”

Katerina Ivanovna was busy about the injured man; she gave him something to drink, wiped the sweat and blood from his head, straightened his pillows, and talked with the priest, now and then managing to turn to him in between. But now she suddenly fell on him almost in a frenzy.

“Eh, Father! Words and nothing but words! Forgive! If he had come home drunk today, if he hadn’t been run over, with only the one shirt on him, all worn out and in rags, he would have flopped down to snore, and I would have been splashing in water till dawn, washing his rags and the children’s, and then I would have dried them outside the window, and then, as soon as it was light, I would have sat down to darn them: that is my night!.. So why talk about forgiveness here! I have forgiven him as it is!”

A deep, terrible cough broke off her words. She coughed into her handkerchief and thrust it out for the priest to see, painfully holding her chest with her other hand. The handkerchief was all covered in blood...
The priest bowed his head and said nothing.

Marmeladov was in his last agony; he did not take his eyes off the face of Katerina Ivanovna, who was bending over him again. He kept wanting to tell her something; he even began, moving his tongue with an effort and pronouncing the words indistinctly, but Katerina Ivanovna, understanding that he wanted to ask her forgiveness, at once shouted at him imperiously:
“Be quie-e-et! There’s no need!.. I know what you want to say!..” And the injured man fell silent; but at that very moment his wandering gaze fell on the door, and he saw Sonya...
Until then he had not noticed her: she was standing in the corner, in the shadow.
“Who is that? Who is that?” he said suddenly in a hoarse, gasping voice, all in alarm, pointing with his eyes in horror at the door where his daughter was standing, and struggling to raise himself.
“Lie down! Lie dow-n!” Katerina Ivanovna began to shout.

But with an unnatural effort he managed to prop himself on his arm. He looked wildly and fixedly at his daughter for some time, as if not recognising her. And indeed he had never once seen her in such clothes. Suddenly he recognised her, humbled, crushed, dressed up and ashamed, meekly waiting her turn to say goodbye to her dying father. Infinite suffering showed in his face.

“Sonya! Daughter! Forgive me!” he cried, and tried to stretch out his hand to her; but losing his support, he slipped and crashed from the sofa, face down on the floor; they rushed to lift him and laid him down, but he was already passing. Sonya gave a faint cry, ran to him, put her arms round him, and froze like that in this embrace. He died in her arms.
“He has got what he wanted!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, seeing her husband’s body. “Well, what am I to do now! What am I to bury him with! And what, what am I to feed them with tomorrow?”
Raskolnikov went up to Katerina Ivanovna.

“Katerina Ivanovna,” he began, “last week your late husband told me his whole life and all the circumstances... Be assured that he spoke of you with rapturous respect. From that evening, when I learned how devoted he was to you all, and how he especially respected and loved you, Katerina Ivanovna, in spite of his unhappy weakness, from that evening we became friends... Allow me now... to do something towards paying my debt to my late friend. Here... twenty roubles, I think; and if this can be of help to you, then... I... in a word, I will come round, I will certainly come round... perhaps I will come round tomorrow... Goodbye!”

And he went quickly out of the room, pushing his way as fast as he could through the crowd to the stairs; but in the crowd he suddenly ran into Nikodim Fomich, who had heard of the accident and wished to give orders in person. They had not seen each other since the scene at the office, but Nikodim Fomich recognised him at once.
“Ah, it’s you?” he asked him.

“He is dead,” answered Raskolnikov. “The doctor came, the priest came, everything is in order. Don’t trouble the poor woman too much; she is consumptive as it is. Cheer her up, if you can in any way... You are a kind man, I know...” he added with a smile, looking him straight in the eyes.
“But how you have got yourself soaked in blood,” remarked Nikodim Fomich, noticing by the light of the lantern several fresh stains on Raskolnikov’s waistcoat.
“Yes, I am soaked... I am all over blood!” Raskolnikov said with a peculiar look; then he smiled, nodded, and went down the stairs.

He went down quietly, unhurriedly, all in a fever and, without being aware of it, full of a single, new, immense sensation of full and mighty life that had suddenly flooded in on him. This sensation might be like that of a man condemned to death who is suddenly and unexpectedly told that he is pardoned. Halfway down the stairs the priest, returning home, overtook him; Raskolnikov silently let him go ahead, exchanging a wordless bow with him. But as he was going down the last steps, he suddenly heard hurried footsteps behind him. Someone was catching up with him. It was Polenka; she was running after him and calling: “Listen! Listen!”

He turned round to her. She ran down the last flight and stopped right in front of him, one step above him. A dim light came in from the courtyard. Raskolnikov made out the thin but sweet little face of the girl, smiling at him and looking at him cheerfully, like a child. She had run after him with a message, which she evidently liked very much herself.
“Listen, what is your name?.. And another thing: where do you live?” she asked hurriedly, in a breathless little voice.
He put both hands on her shoulders and looked at her with a kind of happiness. It was so pleasant for him to look at her; he did not know why himself.
“And who sent you?”
“Sister Sonya sent me,” answered the girl, smiling still more cheerfully.
“I knew it was Sister Sonya who sent you.”
“Mama sent me too. When Sister Sonya started sending me, Mama came up too and said: ‘Run quickly, Polenka!’”
“Do you love Sister Sonya?”
“I love her more than anyone!” Polenka said with a peculiar firmness, and her smile suddenly became more serious.
“And will you love me?”

Instead of an answer he saw the little girl’s face coming closer to him, and her plump little lips naively held out to kiss him. Suddenly her arms, thin as matchsticks, hugged him tight, tight, her head bent onto his shoulder, and the little girl began to cry softly, pressing her face to him more and more tightly.

“I’m sorry for Papa!” she said a minute later, raising her tear-stained little face and wiping away the tears with her hands. “Such misfortunes keep happening now,” she added unexpectedly, with that especially solid air that children try hard to put on when they suddenly want to talk like “grown-ups”.
“And did your papa love you?”

“He loved Lidochka more than all of us,” she went on very seriously and without smiling, now exactly as grown-ups talk, “he loved her because she’s little, and also because she’s ill, and he always brought her presents; and he taught us to read, and me grammar and scripture,” she added with dignity, “and Mama didn’t say anything, but we knew she liked it, and Papa knew too, and Mama wants to teach me French, because it’s time I got an education.”
“And do you know how to pray?”

“Oh, of course we do! For a long time now; I pray to myself, because I’m big now, and Kolya and Lidochka pray aloud with Mama; first they say ‘Mother of God’, and then another prayer: ‘God, forgive and bless Sister Sonya’, and then another: ‘God, forgive and bless our other papa’, because our older papa has died already, and this one is our other one, and we pray for that one too.”
“Polechka, my name is Rodion; pray for me too sometime: ‘and thy servant Rodion’, nothing more.”
“I’ll pray for you all my future life,” the little girl said fervently, and suddenly laughed again, rushed to him and hugged him tight again.

Raskolnikov told her his name, gave her his address and promised to come round without fail the next day. The little girl went away completely delighted with him. It was past ten when he came out into the street. Five minutes later he was standing on the bridge, exactly on the spot from which the woman had thrown herself earlier.

“Enough!” he said resolutely and solemnly. “Away with mirages, away with feigned fears, away with phantoms!.. There is life! Have I not just been living? My life has not died yet together with the old woman! God rest her soul and, enough, my dear, it’s time you were at rest! Now it is the reign of reason and light and... and will, and strength... and now we shall see! Now we shall measure our strength!” he added defiantly, as if addressing some dark force and challenging it. “And I had already agreed to live on a square yard of space!

“...I am very weak at this moment, but... I think the whole illness has passed. I knew it would pass when I went out earlier. By the way: Pochinkov’s house is only two steps away. I will certainly go to Razumikhin’s, even if it weren’t two steps... let him win his bet!.. Let him have his fun too; no matter, let him!.. Strength, strength is what is needed: without strength you can take nothing; and strength must be won by strength; that is what they don’t know,” he added proudly and self-confidently, and walked off the bridge, hardly able to move his legs. Pride and self-confidence grew in him every minute; already the next minute he was not the same man he had been the minute before. But what had happened, so special, that had turned him round like this? He did not know himself; like a man clutching at a straw, it had suddenly seemed to him that he too “could live, that there was still life, that his life had not died together with the old woman”. Perhaps he was too hasty in his conclusion, but he did not think about that.

“But I did ask her to remember thy servant Rodion,” suddenly flashed through his head. “Well, that was... just in case!” he added, and laughed at once at his own boyish prank. He was in the most excellent spirits.

He easily found Razumikhin; at Pochinkov’s house the new lodger was already known, and the caretaker showed him the way at once. Already from halfway up the stairs one could make out the noise and lively talk of a large gathering. The door onto the stairs was wide open; shouts and arguments could be heard. Razumikhin’s room was fairly large, and there were about fifteen people there. Raskolnikov stopped in the entrance. Here, behind a partition, two of the landlady’s servants were busy around two big samovars, around bottles, plates and dishes of pie and snacks brought from the landlady’s kitchen. Raskolnikov sent for Razumikhin. He came running in delight. At the first glance one could see that he had drunk an unusual amount, and though Razumikhin could almost never get really drunk, this time something showed.

“Listen,” Raskolnikov hastened to say, “I have only come to tell you that you have won your bet, and that indeed nobody knows what may happen to him. But I can’t come in: I am so weak that I shall fall down in a moment. And so, hello and goodbye! And come to see me tomorrow...”
“Do you know what, I’ll see you home! If you say yourself that you’re weak, then...”
“And your guests? Who is that curly-haired one who just looked in here?”

“That one? The devil knows! A friend of my uncle’s, I suppose, or perhaps he just came by himself... I’ll leave my uncle with them; he’s a most precious man; a pity you can’t meet him now. But anyway, to the devil with them all! They don’t need me now, and I need some fresh air, so, brother, you’ve come just at the right time: two minutes more and I would have got into a fight there, by God! They talk such wild nonsense... You can’t imagine how far a man can talk himself into lies in the end! But then, how can you not imagine it? Don’t we lie ourselves? Well, let them lie: then they won’t lie later on... Sit down a minute, I’ll bring Zosimov.”
Zosimov fell upon Raskolnikov with a kind of eagerness; a kind of special curiosity was noticeable in him; soon his face cleared.
“Bed at once,” he decided, having examined the patient as far as he could, “and you should take one little thing for the night. Will you take it? I prepared it earlier... a little powder.”
“Two, if you like,” answered Raskolnikov.
The powder was taken right there.

“It’s very good that you are taking him home yourself,” Zosimov remarked to Razumikhin. “We shall see what tomorrow brings, but today he’s really not bad at all: a considerable change since earlier. Live and learn...”

“Do you know what Zosimov whispered to me just now, as we were going out?” Razumikhin blurted out as soon as they were in the street. “I’ll tell you everything straight, brother, because they are fools. Zosimov told me to chatter with you on the way and to make you chatter, and then to tell him, because he has an idea... that you are... mad, or close to it. Just imagine! In the first place, you are three times cleverer than he is; in the second, if you are not mad, you can spit on his having such nonsense in his head; and in the third, this lump of meat, a surgeon by profession, has gone crazy now about mental illness, and what finally turned him round about you was your conversation with Zamyotov today.”
“Zamyotov told you everything?”

“Everything, and he did very well. I understand the whole inside story now, and so does Zamyotov... Well, in a word, Rodya... the thing is... I am a tiny bit drunk now... But that’s nothing... the thing is that this idea... do you understand? really was beginning to peck its way out in them... do you understand? That is, none of them dared say it aloud, because it’s the most absurd nonsense, and especially when they arrested that painter, it all burst and went out for ever. But why are they fools? I gave Zamyotov a bit of a thrashing then (that’s between ourselves, brother; please don’t let on by the slightest hint that you know; I have noticed that he is touchy); it was at Laviza’s; but today, today everything became clear. Above all, that Ilya Petrovich! He took advantage of your fainting at the office then, and was ashamed of himself afterwards; I know...”
Raskolnikov listened greedily. Razumikhin was blurting things out in his drunkenness.
“I fainted then because it was stuffy and smelled of oil paint,” said Raskolnikov.

“He explains it, too! And it wasn’t only the paint: the inflammation had been coming on all month; Zosimov is witness! But you can’t imagine how crushed that boy is now! ‘I’m not worth that man’s little finger,’ he says. Yours, that is. He has good feelings sometimes, brother. But the lesson, the lesson you gave him today at the Crystal Palace, that was the height of perfection! You frightened him at first, you drove him to convulsions! You almost made him convinced again of all that hideous nonsense, and then suddenly you stuck your tongue out at him: ‘There, take that!’ Perfection! He is crushed, annihilated now! You’re a master, by God, that’s how to treat them. Eh, I wasn’t there! He was terribly eager to see you now; Porfiry wants to meet you too...”
“Ah... him too... But why have they put me down as mad?”

“Not as mad, that is. I have told you too much, brother, I think... You see, what struck him earlier was that only that one point interests you; now it’s clear why it interests you, knowing all the circumstances... and how it irritated you then, and got mixed up with your illness... I am a little drunk, brother, only the devil knows, he has some idea of his own... I tell you: he has gone crazy about mental illness. But you just spit on it...”
For half a minute both were silent.

“Listen, Razumikhin,” Raskolnikov began, “I want to tell you straight: I have just been with a dead man; an official died... I gave all my money there... and besides, I was kissed just now by a being who, even if I had killed someone, would also... in a word, I saw another being there too... with a fiery feather... but I am rambling; I am very weak; hold me up... the stairs are just here...”
“What’s the matter with you? What’s the matter with you?” asked Razumikhin in alarm.
“My head is spinning a little, only that’s not the point; the point is that I am so sad, so sad! Like a woman... really! Look, what’s that? Look! Look!”
“What is it?”
“Don’t you see? A light in my room, do you see? Through the crack...”
They were already standing at the last flight, beside the landlady’s door, and indeed one could see from below that there was a light in Raskolnikov’s little room.
“Strange! Nastasya, perhaps,” remarked Razumikhin.
“She is never in my room at this time, and she has been asleep long ago, but... it’s all the same to me! Goodbye!”
“What do you mean? I’m seeing you in, we’ll go in together!”
“I know we’ll go in together, but I want to shake your hand here and say goodbye to you here. Well, give me your hand, goodbye!”
“What’s the matter with you, Rodya?”
“Nothing; come on; you’ll be a witness...”

They began to climb the stairs, and the thought flashed through Razumikhin’s mind that Zosimov might be right after all. “Eh! I have upset him with my chatter!” he muttered to himself. Suddenly, as they came up to the door, they heard voices in the room.
“What’s going on here?” cried Razumikhin.
Raskolnikov took hold of the door first and flung it wide open; he opened it and stood on the threshold as if rooted to the spot.

His mother and sister were sitting on his sofa and had been waiting for an hour and a half. Why was it that he had least of all expected them and least of all thought of them, in spite of the news, repeated even that day, that they were setting out, travelling, would arrive at any moment? All that hour and a half they had been vying with each other in questioning Nastasya, who was standing before them even now and had already managed to tell them the whole inside story. They were beside themselves with fright when they heard that he had “run away today”, ill and, as was evident from her story, certainly delirious! “God, what is the matter with him!” Both had been crying; both had gone through the torment of the cross in that hour and a half of waiting.

A joyful, rapturous cry greeted Raskolnikov’s appearance. Both rushed to him. But he stood like a dead man; an unbearable sudden realisation had struck him like thunder. And his arms would not rise to embrace them: they could not. His mother and sister clasped him in their arms, kissed him, laughed, wept... He took a step, swayed, and crashed to the floor in a faint.
Alarm, cries of horror, groans... Razumikhin, who was standing on the threshold, flew into the room, seized the sick man in his powerful arms, and in an instant he was on the sofa.

“It’s nothing, nothing!” he shouted to the mother and sister. “It’s a faint, it’s rubbish! The doctor has only just said that he is much better, that he is perfectly well! Water! There, he is coming to already, there, he has come round!..”

And seizing Dunechka by the arm so that he nearly wrenched it out of joint, he bent her down to look at how “he has come round already”. And both mother and sister looked at Razumikhin as at Providence, with tenderness and gratitude; they had already heard from Nastasya what this “quick young man” had been to their Rodya all through his illness, as Pulkheria Alexandrovna Raskolnikova herself called him that same evening in an intimate talk with Dunya.
## PART III · CHAPTER I
Raskolnikov raised himself and sat up on the sofa.

He waved weakly at Razumikhin to stop the whole flood of his incoherent, heated consolations addressed to his mother and sister, took them both by the hands, and for about two minutes looked silently now at one, now at the other. His mother was frightened by his look. In that look there showed a feeling strong to the point of suffering, but at the same time there was something fixed in it, even almost mad. Pulkheria Alexandrovna began to cry.
Avdotya Romanovna was pale; her hand trembled in her brother’s hand.
“Go home... with him,” he said in a broken voice, pointing to Razumikhin. “Until tomorrow; tomorrow, everything... Have you been here long?”
“Since the evening, Rodya,” answered Pulkheria Alexandrovna. “The train was terribly late. But, Rodya, nothing will make me leave you now! I’ll spend the night here, beside you...”
“Don’t torment me!” he said, waving his hand irritably.
“I’ll stay with him!” cried Razumikhin. “I won’t leave him for a minute, and to the devil with all my people there, let them climb the walls! My uncle is presiding over them.”
“How, how can I ever thank you!” Pulkheria Alexandrovna began, pressing Razumikhin’s hands again, but Raskolnikov interrupted her once more:
“I can’t, I can’t,” he kept repeating irritably. “Don’t torment me! Enough, go away... I can’t!..”
“Let’s go, Mama, at least let’s go out of the room for a minute,” whispered the frightened Dunya. “We are killing him, anyone can see it.”
“Am I not even to look at him, after three years!” wept Pulkheria Alexandrovna.
“Wait!” he stopped them again. “You keep interrupting, and my thoughts get muddled... Have you seen Luzhin?”
“No, Rodya, but he already knows we have arrived. We heard, Rodya, that Pyotr Petrovich was so kind as to visit you today,” Pulkheria Alexandrovna added with some timidity.
“Yes... he was so kind... Dunya, earlier today I told Luzhin I would throw him down the stairs, and I sent him to the devil...”
“Rodya, what are you saying! Surely you... you don’t mean to say...” Pulkheria Alexandrovna began in alarm, but stopped, looking at Dunya.

Avdotya Romanovna was gazing intently at her brother, waiting for what came next. Both had already been told of the quarrel by Nastasya, as far as she had been able to understand and tell it, and they had been tormented by bewilderment and suspense.
“Dunya,” Raskolnikov went on with an effort, “I do not want this marriage, and so you must refuse Luzhin tomorrow, at the very first word, so that there isn’t a whiff of him left.”
“My God!” cried Pulkheria Alexandrovna.
“Brother, think what you are saying!” Avdotya Romanovna began hotly, but at once restrained herself. “Perhaps you are not in a fit state just now; you are tired,” she said gently.

“Delirious? No... You are marrying Luzhin for my sake. And I do not accept the sacrifice. And so, by tomorrow, write a letter... refusing him... Give it to me to read in the morning, and that’s the end of it!”
“I cannot do that!” cried the offended girl. “By what right...”
“Dunechka, you are hot-tempered too, stop it, tomorrow... Can’t you see...” the mother cried in fright, rushing to Dunya. “Oh, let us go, it’s better!”

“He’s raving!” shouted the tipsy Razumikhin. “How else would he dare! Tomorrow all this nonsense will jump out of him... But today he really did throw him out. That’s just how it was. Well, and the other one got angry... He made speeches here, showed off his learning, and went away with his tail between his legs...”
“So it’s true?” cried Pulkheria Alexandrovna.
“Until tomorrow, brother,” Dunya said with compassion. “Come, Mama... Goodbye, Rodya!”

“Do you hear, sister,” he repeated after her, gathering his last strength, “I am not delirious; this marriage is a vileness. I may be a scoundrel, but you must not... one of us is enough... and though I am a scoundrel, I would not count such a sister as my sister. It is me or Luzhin! Go...”

“You’ve gone out of your mind! Tyrant!” roared Razumikhin, but Raskolnikov no longer answered, and perhaps had no strength to answer. He lay down on the sofa and turned to the wall in utter exhaustion. Avdotya Romanovna looked at Razumikhin with curiosity; her black eyes flashed: Razumikhin even started under that look. Pulkheria Alexandrovna stood as if thunderstruck.
“I cannot go, nothing will make me!” she whispered to Razumikhin, almost in despair. “I’ll stay here, somewhere... see Dunya home.”

“And spoil everything!” Razumikhin whispered too, losing his temper. “Let’s at least go out onto the stairs. Nastasya, a light! I swear to you,” he went on in a half-whisper, already on the stairs, “that earlier today he nearly beat us, me and the doctor! Do you understand that? The doctor himself! And the doctor gave way so as not to irritate him, and went off, and I stayed downstairs on guard, and he dressed meanwhile and slipped away. And he will slip away now too, if you irritate him, at night, and do something to himself...”
“Oh, what are you saying!”

“And Avdotya Romanovna can’t possibly stay in those rooms alone without you! Think where you are staying! Couldn’t that scoundrel Pyotr Petrovich have found you better lodgings... But you know, I am a little drunk, and so I... swore; don’t pay any...”
“But I will go to the landlady here,” Pulkheria Alexandrovna insisted. “I will beg her to give Dunya and me a corner for tonight. I cannot leave him like this, I cannot!”

As they talked they were standing on the stairs, on the landing, right in front of the landlady’s door. Nastasya was lighting them from the bottom step. Razumikhin was in an extraordinary state of excitement. Half an hour earlier, seeing Raskolnikov home, he had been, though over-talkative (and he knew it), perfectly brisk and almost fresh, in spite of the dreadful amount of wine he had drunk that evening. Now his state was like a kind of rapture, and at the same time it was as if all the wine he had drunk had rushed to his head again, all at once and with doubled force. He stood with both ladies, having seized both of them by the hand, persuading them and laying out his reasons with astonishing frankness, and, probably to be more convincing, at almost every word he squeezed their hands, tight, as in a vice, until it hurt, and he seemed to devour Avdotya Romanovna with his eyes, without the slightest embarrassment. Sometimes, from the pain, they would pull their hands out of his enormous bony paw, but he not only failed to notice what the matter was, he drew them still more firmly towards him. If they had told him at that moment to throw himself head first down the stairs in their service, he would have done it at once, without reasoning or doubting. Pulkheria Alexandrovna, all alarm at the thought of her Rodya, though she felt that the young man was very eccentric indeed and was squeezing her hand far too painfully, nevertheless, since he was at the same time Providence to her, did not wish to notice all these eccentric details. But Avdotya Romanovna, in spite of the same alarm, and though she was not of a timid character, met with amazement and almost with fear the looks blazing with wild fire from her brother’s friend, and only the boundless trust inspired by Nastasya’s stories about this strange man kept her from attempting to run away from him and drag her mother after her. She also understood that perhaps it was impossible to run away from him now. Within ten minutes, however, she had calmed down considerably: Razumikhin had the quality of expressing his whole self in a moment, whatever his mood, so that everyone very soon knew whom they were dealing with.

“Impossible to go to the landlady, and the most dreadful nonsense!” he cried, persuading Pulkheria Alexandrovna. “Though you are his mother, if you stay you will drive him to frenzy, and then the devil knows what will happen! Listen, this is what I’ll do: Nastasya will sit with him now, and I will take you both to your rooms, because you can’t go through the streets alone; here in Petersburg, in that respect... Well, never mind!.. Then from your place I’ll run straight back here, and in a quarter of an hour, on my most honest word, I’ll bring you a report: how is he? asleep or not? and everything else. Then, listen! Then from you I’ll dash home, there are guests at my place, all drunk, I’ll fetch Zosimov, that’s the doctor who is treating him, he is sitting at my place now, not drunk; that one isn’t drunk, that one is never drunk! I’ll drag him to Rodka and then straight to you, so within an hour you will have two reports on him, and from the doctor, you understand, from the doctor himself; that’s not the same as from me! If he’s bad, I swear I’ll bring you here myself, and if he’s well, then you go to bed. And I will spend the whole night here, in the passage, he won’t even hear me, and I’ll tell Zosimov to spend the night at the landlady’s, so as to be at hand. Well, what is better for him now, you or the doctor? Why, the doctor is more useful, more useful. So go home! And going to the landlady is impossible; possible for me, but impossible for you: she won’t let you in, because... because she is a fool. She will be jealous over me with Avdotya Romanovna, if you want to know, and with you too... And with Avdotya Romanovna certainly. It’s a completely, completely unexpected character! Though I am a fool too... Never mind! Let’s go! Do you trust me? Well, do you trust me or not?”

“Let’s go, Mama,” said Avdotya Romanovna. “He will certainly do as he promises. He has already brought my brother back to life, and if it’s true that the doctor will agree to spend the night here, what could be better?”

“There, you... you... understand me, because you are an angel!” cried Razumikhin in rapture. “Let’s go! Nastasya! Upstairs this instant, and sit there with him, with a light; I’ll be back in a quarter of an hour...”

Pulkheria Alexandrovna, though not completely convinced, did not resist any further. Razumikhin took them both by the arm and pulled them down the stairs. He worried her, though: “He may be quick and kind, but is he able to do what he promises? In such a state!..”

“Ah, I understand, you are thinking that I am in such a state!” Razumikhin interrupted her thoughts, guessing them and striding along the pavement with his enormous strides, so that both ladies could hardly keep up with him, which, however, he did not notice. “Nonsense! that is... I am drunk as a blockhead, but that’s not the point; I am not drunk from wine. It was seeing you that went to my head... But never mind me! Don’t pay any attention: I am lying; I am not worthy of you... I am in the highest degree unworthy of you!.. And as soon as I have taken you home, at once, right here in the canal, I’ll pour two tubs of water over my head, and I’ll be ready... If you only knew how I love you both!.. Don’t laugh and don’t be angry!.. Be angry with everyone, but don’t be angry with me! I am his friend, and so I am your friend. That’s what I want... I had a presentiment of this... last year, there was one such moment... Though I had no presentiment at all, because you dropped from the sky. And I won’t sleep all night, I dare say... That Zosimov was afraid earlier that he might go out of his mind... That’s why he must not be irritated...”
“What are you saying!” cried the mother.
“Did the doctor himself really say that?” asked Avdotya Romanovna, frightened.

“He did, but that’s not it, not it at all. He gave him a medicine, too, a powder, I saw it, and then you arrived... Eh!.. You would have done better to come tomorrow! It’s good that we left. And within an hour Zosimov himself will report to you on everything. Now he is not drunk! And I won’t be drunk... And why did I get so sozzled? Because they dragged me into an argument, the damned lot! I had sworn an oath not to argue!.. Such rubbish they talk! I nearly got into a fight! I left my uncle there as chairman... Well, would you believe it: they demand complete impersonality and find the very relish of it in that! Anything so as not to be oneself, anything so as to be as little like oneself as possible! That is what they consider the very highest progress. And if only they lied in their own way, but as it is...”
“Listen,” Pulkheria Alexandrovna interrupted timidly, but this only added fuel to the fire.

“What do you think?” shouted Razumikhin, raising his voice still more. “You think I am against them because they lie? Nonsense! I love it when people lie! Lying is the one human privilege over all other organisms. Tell a lie, and you will get to the truth! It is because I lie that I am a man. Nobody ever got to a single truth without first lying fourteen times, or perhaps a hundred and fourteen, and that is honourable in its way; but we can’t even lie with our own minds! Lie to me, but lie in your own way, and then I will kiss you. To lie in your own way is almost better than to tell the truth in someone else’s way; in the first case you are a man, and in the second you are no better than a bird! The truth won’t run away, but life can be nailed shut; there have been examples. Well, what are we now? All of us, every one without exception, in science, development, thought, invention, ideals, aspirations, liberalism, reason, experience, and everything, everything, everything, everything, everything else, are still sitting in the first preparatory class of the gymnasium! We have taken a liking to living on other people’s minds, and we have got used to it! Isn’t that so? Am I right?” shouted Razumikhin, shaking and squeezing the hands of both ladies. “Am I?”
“Oh my God, I don’t know,” said poor Pulkheria Alexandrovna.
“Yes, yes... though I don’t agree with you in everything,” Avdotya Romanovna added seriously, and at once cried out, so painfully did he squeeze her hand this time.

“Yes? You say yes? Well, after that you... you...” he shouted in rapture, “you are a fountain of goodness, purity, reason and... perfection! Give me your hand, give it... you give me yours too, I want to kiss your hands here, now, on my knees!”
And he knelt down in the middle of the pavement, which, fortunately, was deserted at that moment.
“Stop it, I beg you, what are you doing?” cried Pulkheria Alexandrovna, alarmed to the extreme.
“Get up, get up!” laughed Dunya, alarmed too.

“Not for anything, until you give me your hands! There, that’s it, and that’s enough, and I’m up, and let’s go! I am an unhappy blockhead, I am not worthy of you, and drunk, and ashamed... I am not worthy to love you, but to bow down before you is the duty of everyone, unless he is a complete brute! And I have bowed down... Here are your rooms, and Rodion was right in that alone, that he threw out your Pyotr Petrovich today! How dared he put you in such rooms? It’s a scandal! Do you know who they let in here? And you are a bride! You are his bride, yes? Well then, I tell you, your fiancé is a scoundrel after this!”
“Listen, Mr Razumikhin, you are forgetting yourself...” Pulkheria Alexandrovna began.

“Yes, yes, you are right, I have forgotten myself, I am ashamed!” Razumikhin recollected himself. “But... but... you can’t be angry with me for speaking like this! Because I speak sincerely, and not because... hm! that would be base; in a word, not because I am... hm!.. well, so be it, never mind, I won’t say why, I don’t dare!.. But we all understood earlier, as soon as he came in, that this man was not of our sort. Not because he came in curled at the hairdresser’s, not because he was in a hurry to show off his intelligence, but because he is a spy and a speculator; because he is a Jew and a mountebank, and that shows. Do you think he is clever? No, he is a fool, a fool! Well, is he a match for you? Oh my God! You see, ladies,” he stopped suddenly, already going up the stairs to the rooms, “though they are all drunk at my place, still they are all honest, and though we lie, because I lie too, still we will lie our way through to the truth at last, because we are on an honourable road, and Pyotr Petrovich... is not on an honourable road. Though I was cursing them just now up hill and down dale, I respect them all; even Zamyotov, though I don’t respect him, I love, because he is a puppy! Even that brute Zosimov, because he is honest and knows his work... But enough, everything has been said and forgiven. Forgiven? Is that so? Well, let’s go. I know this corridor, I have been here; there was a scandal here, in number three... Well, where are you? Which number? Eight? Well then, lock yourselves in for the night, let no one in. In a quarter of an hour I’ll be back with news, and then in another half-hour with Zosimov, you’ll see! Goodbye, I’m running!”
“My God, Dunechka, what will come of this?” said Pulkheria Alexandrovna, turning anxiously and fearfully to her daughter.

“Calm yourself, Mama,” answered Dunya, taking off her hat and cape. “God himself has sent us this gentleman, even if he has come straight from some drinking party. He can be relied on, I assure you. And all that he has already done for my brother...”

“Ah, Dunechka, God knows whether he will come! And how could I bring myself to leave Rodya!.. And not at all, not at all how I imagined finding him! How stern he was, as if he were not glad to see us...”
Tears appeared in her eyes.
“No, that’s not so, Mama. You didn’t look closely, you were crying all the time. He is very upset after a serious illness; that is the cause of it all.”

“Ah, this illness! What will happen, what will happen! And how he spoke to you, Dunya!” said the mother, looking timidly into her daughter’s eyes to read all her thoughts, and already half consoled by the fact that Dunya herself was defending Rodya and so must have forgiven him. “I am sure he will think better of it tomorrow,” she added, probing to the end.

“And I am sure that tomorrow too he will say the same thing... about that,” Avdotya Romanovna cut her short, and of course this was the sticking point, because here was the very matter Pulkheria Alexandrovna was now far too afraid to speak of. Dunya went up and kissed her mother. Her mother hugged her tightly in silence. Then she sat down in anxious expectation of Razumikhin’s return, and timidly watched her daughter, who, with folded arms, and waiting too, began walking up and down the room, thinking to herself. Such walking from corner to corner, deep in thought, was Avdotya Romanovna’s habit, and her mother was always somehow afraid to disturb her musing at such times.

Razumikhin, of course, was ridiculous with his sudden passion for Avdotya Romanovna, kindled by drink; but anyone who looked at Avdotya Romanovna, especially now, as she walked about the room with folded arms, sad and thoughtful, might well have excused him, to say nothing of his eccentric state. Avdotya Romanovna was remarkably good-looking: tall, wonderfully well-made, strong, self-assured, which showed in her every gesture and yet took nothing away from the softness and grace of her movements. In face she was like her brother, but she could even be called a beauty. Her hair was dark brown, a little lighter than her brother’s; her eyes almost black, flashing, proud, and at the same time sometimes, for moments, extraordinarily kind. She was pale, but not sickly pale; her face shone with freshness and health. Her mouth was rather small, and her lower lip, fresh and scarlet, jutted forward a very little, together with her chin: the only irregularity in that beautiful face, but one that gave it a special character and, among other things, a kind of haughtiness. The expression of her face was always more serious than merry, thoughtful; but how well a smile suited that face, how well laughter suited her, merry, young, wholehearted laughter! It is understandable that the hot-headed, frank, simple, honest Razumikhin, strong as a hero of the old songs, and drunk, who had never seen anything like her, lost his head at first sight. Besides, chance, as if on purpose, had shown him Dunya for the first time at a beautiful moment of love and joy at meeting her brother. Then he had seen her lower lip quiver with indignation in answer to her brother’s insolent and ungratefully cruel commands, and he could not resist.

He had, however, told the truth when he blurted out drunkenly on the stairs earlier that Raskolnikov’s eccentric landlady, Praskovya Pavlovna, would be jealous over him not only with Avdotya Romanovna but perhaps with Pulkheria Alexandrovna herself. Although Pulkheria Alexandrovna was already forty-three, her face still kept traces of its former beauty; besides, she seemed much younger than her years, which almost always happens with women who have kept clarity of spirit, freshness of impressions and an honest, pure warmth of heart into old age. Let us say in parentheses that to keep all this is the only means of not losing one’s beauty even in old age. Her hair was already beginning to turn grey and thin, little radiating wrinkles had long since appeared around her eyes, her cheeks had grown hollow and dry from care and grief, and still this face was beautiful. It was a portrait of Dunechka’s face, only twenty years later, except for the expression of the lower lip, which did not jut forward in hers. Pulkheria Alexandrovna was sensitive, though not to the point of sentimentality, timid and yielding, but only up to a certain line: she could give way on much, could agree to much, even to what contradicted her convictions, but there was always a line of honesty, principle and deepest conviction which no circumstances could make her cross.
Exactly twenty minutes after Razumikhin had left, there came two soft but hurried knocks at the door; he had come back.

“I won’t come in, no time!” he hurried, when the door was opened. “He is sleeping like a log, splendidly, peacefully, and God grant he sleeps ten hours. Nastasya is with him; I told her not to leave until I come. Now I’ll drag Zosimov here, he will report to you, and then off to bed with you; you are worn out beyond anything, I can see.”
And he set off from them down the corridor.
“What a quick and... devoted young man!” exclaimed Pulkheria Alexandrovna, extremely gladdened.
“He seems a splendid person!” Avdotya Romanovna answered with some warmth, beginning to walk up and down the room again.

Almost an hour later there were steps in the corridor and another knock at the door. Both women had been waiting, this time fully believing Razumikhin’s promise; and indeed he had managed to drag Zosimov along. Zosimov had at once agreed to abandon the feast and go and look at Raskolnikov, but he went to the ladies reluctantly and with great suspicion, not trusting the drunken Razumikhin. But his vanity was at once soothed and even flattered: he understood that he really had been awaited like an oracle. He stayed exactly ten minutes and fully succeeded in convincing and calming Pulkheria Alexandrovna. He spoke with extraordinary sympathy, but with restraint and a kind of studied seriousness, exactly like a twenty-seven-year-old doctor at an important consultation, and not by a single word did he stray from the subject or show the slightest wish to enter into more personal and private relations with the two ladies. Having noticed as he came in how dazzlingly beautiful Avdotya Romanovna was, he at once made a point of not even noticing her at all during the whole visit, and addressed himself solely to Pulkheria Alexandrovna. All this gave him extraordinary inner satisfaction. Of the patient himself he said that he found him at the present moment in a very satisfactory condition. According to his observations, the patient’s illness, apart from the poor material circumstances of the last months of his life, also had certain moral causes, “was, so to speak, the product of many complex moral and material influences, anxieties, apprehensions, cares, certain ideas... and so forth.” Noticing in passing that Avdotya Romanovna had begun listening with special attention, Zosimov enlarged somewhat further on this theme. To Pulkheria Alexandrovna’s anxious and timid question about “some supposed suspicions of insanity”, he answered with a calm and candid smile that his words had been greatly exaggerated; that of course a certain fixed idea was noticeable in the patient, something suggesting monomania, since he, Zosimov, was now following that extremely interesting branch of medicine with particular attention; but one must remember that almost up to today the patient had been delirious, and... and of course the arrival of his family would strengthen him, distract him, and have a salutary effect, “if only fresh special shocks can be avoided,” he added significantly. Then he stood up, took his leave solidly and cordially, accompanied by blessings, warm gratitude, entreaties, and even by Avdotya Romanovna’s little hand held out for him to shake without his seeking it, and went out extremely pleased with his visit and still more with himself.
“And we’ll talk tomorrow; go to bed, now, without fail!” Razumikhin sealed it, leaving with Zosimov. “Tomorrow, as early as possible, I’ll be with you with a report.”
“What a ravishing girl that Avdotya Romanovna is, though!” remarked Zosimov, almost licking his lips, when they had both come out into the street.

“Ravishing? You said ravishing!” roared Razumikhin, and suddenly hurled himself at Zosimov and seized him by the throat. “If you ever dare... Do you understand? Do you understand?” he shouted, shaking him by the collar and pinning him to the wall. “Did you hear?”

“Let go, you drunken devil!” Zosimov fought him off, and then, when the other had let him go, he looked at him intently and suddenly burst out laughing. Razumikhin stood before him with his arms hanging down, in gloomy and serious thought.
“Of course I am an ass,” he said, gloomy as a storm cloud, “but then... so are you.”
“Oh no, brother, not at all so am I. I don’t dream about foolishness.”
They walked on in silence, and only as they were approaching Raskolnikov’s lodging did Razumikhin, greatly preoccupied, break the silence.

“Listen,” he said to Zosimov, “you are a fine fellow, but besides all your bad qualities you are also a lecher, that I know, and one of the dirty kind. You are a nervous, weak piece of rubbish, you are capricious, you have grown fat and can deny yourself nothing, and that is what I call dirt, because it leads straight to dirt. You have pampered yourself so much that, I confess, what I least of all understand is how, with all that, you can be a good and even self-sacrificing doctor. He sleeps on a feather bed (a doctor!) and gets up at night for a patient! In three years’ time you won’t be getting up for a patient... Well, the devil, that’s not the point; the point is this: tonight you are sleeping in the landlady’s flat (I barely talked her into it!), and I in the kitchen: here is your chance to get better acquainted! Not what you think! There isn’t a shadow of that here, brother...”
“But I’m not thinking anything at all.”

“Here, brother, there is modesty, silence, bashfulness, a fierce chastity, and with all that, sighs, and she melts like wax, simply melts! Rid me of her, for the sake of all the devils in the world! She’s so very prepossessing!.. I’ll repay you, I’ll repay you with my head!”
Zosimov laughed harder than before.
“Look how it’s got hold of you! But what do I want with her?”

“I assure you, it’s not much trouble; just talk any slop you like, just sit beside her and talk. Besides, you are a doctor, start treating her for something. I swear you won’t regret it. She has a clavichord; you know I strum a little; I have a song there, a Russian one, a real one: ‘I will drown in burning tears...’ She loves the real ones, well, it all began with the song; and you are a virtuoso on the piano, a maestro, a Rubinstein... I assure you, you won’t regret it!”
“But have you made her some sort of promises? Signed something in due form? Promised to marry her, perhaps...”
“Nothing, nothing, absolutely nothing of the kind! And she isn’t like that at all; Chebarov tried his luck with her...”
“Well, then drop her!”
“But you can’t just drop her like that!”
“But why can’t you?”
“Well, somehow you just can’t, and that’s all! There is a drawing-in principle here, brother.”
“Then why did you lure her on?”

“But I didn’t lure her on at all; perhaps I was lured on myself, out of my own stupidity, and it will be absolutely all the same to her, you or me, as long as someone sits beside her and sighs. Here, brother... I can’t put it to you, here, well, you know mathematics well, and you are still studying it now, I know... well, start taking her through the integral calculus, by God I am not joking, I am speaking seriously, it will be absolutely all the same to her: she will look at you and sigh, and so for a whole year on end. I talked to her, among other things, for a very long time, two days on end, about the Prussian House of Lords (because what else is there to talk to her about?), and she only sighed and grew warm! Only don’t start talking about love, she is bashful to the point of convulsions, but do give the impression that you can’t tear yourself away, and that’s enough. It is terribly comfortable; exactly like home: read, sit, lie down, write... You can even kiss her, carefully...”
“But what do I want with her?”

“Eh, I can’t explain it to you at all! You see: you are both perfectly suited to each other! I thought of you before... After all, you will end up with this! So isn’t it all the same to you, sooner or later? Here, brother, there lies a sort of feather-bed principle, eh! and not only feather-bed! It draws you in; here is the end of the world, an anchor, a quiet haven, the navel of the earth, the three-fish foundation of the world, the essence of pancakes, rich pies, the evening samovar, quiet sighs and warm jackets, well-heated stove-beds; well, just as if you had died and at the same time were alive, both advantages at once! Well, brother, the devil, I’ve talked myself into nonsense, it’s time for bed! Listen: I sometimes wake up at night, so I’ll go and look in on him. But it’s nothing, rubbish, all is well. Don’t you worry too much either, but if you like, go and look in once too. But if you notice anything at all, delirium, for instance, or fever, or anything, wake me at once. Though it can’t be...”
## CHAPTER IV

At that moment the door opened quietly, and a girl came into the room, looking round timidly. Everyone turned to her with surprise and curiosity. Raskolnikov did not recognise her at first glance. It was Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladova. He had seen her yesterday for the first time, but at such a moment, in such surroundings and in such a costume, that his memory had kept the image of quite a different person. Now she was a modestly and even poorly dressed girl, still very young, almost like a child, with a modest and decent manner and a clear but somewhat frightened face. She wore a very simple everyday dress, and on her head an old hat of an outdated style; only in her hands, as yesterday, was a parasol. Seeing unexpectedly a room full of people, she was not so much embarrassed as completely lost; she grew timid, like a small child, and even made a movement to go back out.
“Ah... it’s you?..” said Raskolnikov in extreme surprise, and suddenly he was embarrassed himself.

It at once occurred to him that his mother and sister already knew in passing, from Luzhin’s letter, about a certain young person of “notorious” behaviour. Only just now he had protested against Luzhin’s slander and mentioned that he had seen this girl for the first time, and suddenly she walks in herself. He remembered too that he had not protested at all against the expression “of notorious behaviour”. All this slid through his head vaguely and in an instant. But looking more closely, he suddenly saw that this humiliated being was so humiliated already that he suddenly felt sorry for her. And when she made a movement to run away in fear, something in him seemed to turn over.
“I wasn’t expecting you at all,” he hurried, stopping her with his eyes. “Do me the kindness, sit down. You have come from Katerina Ivanovna, I expect. Allow me, not there, sit here...”

When Sonya came in, Razumikhin, who was sitting on one of Raskolnikov’s three chairs, right by the door, half rose to let her in. At first Raskolnikov had pointed her to a place at the corner of the sofa, where Zosimov had been sitting, but remembering that the sofa was too familiar a place, and served him as a bed, he hastened to point her to Razumikhin’s chair.
“And you sit here,” he said to Razumikhin, putting him in the corner where Zosimov had been sitting.

Sonya sat down, almost trembling with fear, and looked timidly at the two ladies. It was evident that she herself did not understand how she could sit down beside them. Realising this, she was so frightened that she suddenly stood up again and in utter confusion turned to Raskolnikov.

“I... I... have only come in for one minute; forgive me for disturbing you,” she began, stammering. “I have come from Katerina Ivanovna, she had no one else to send... And Katerina Ivanovna told me to beg you very much to be at the funeral service tomorrow, in the morning... at the liturgy... at the Mitrofaniev cemetery, and afterwards at our place... at hers... to have something to eat... To do her the honour... She told me to ask you.”
Sonya stumbled and fell silent.

“I will try without fail... without fail,” answered Raskolnikov, half rising too, stammering too, and not finishing his words... “Do me the kindness, sit down,” he said suddenly. “I must talk with you. Please, perhaps you are in a hurry, do me the kindness, give me two minutes...”
And he moved a chair towards her. Sonya sat down again and again glanced timidly, lost, quickly, at the two ladies, and suddenly lowered her eyes.
Raskolnikov’s pale face flushed; something seemed to jerk through him; his eyes lit up.

“Mama,” he said firmly and insistently, “this is Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladova, the daughter of that same unfortunate Mr Marmeladov who was run over by horses yesterday before my eyes, and of whom I have already told you...”

Pulkheria Alexandrovna looked at Sonya and narrowed her eyes slightly. In spite of all her confusion before Rodya’s insistent and challenging look, she could not deny herself this pleasure. Dunechka fixed her eyes seriously and intently on the poor girl’s face and examined her in perplexity. Sonya, hearing herself introduced, raised her eyes again, but was more embarrassed than before.
“I wanted to ask you,” Raskolnikov turned to her quickly, “how did things go for you today? Did they trouble you?.. the police, for instance.”
“No, sir, it all went off... It was too plain, after all, what the death was from; they didn’t trouble us; only the lodgers are angry.”
“Why?”

“Because the body has been lying so long... it’s hot now, the smell... so today, by vespers, they will carry it to the cemetery, to the chapel, until tomorrow. Katerina Ivanovna didn’t want it at first, but now she sees herself that it can’t be helped...”
“Today, then?”
“She asks you to do us the honour of being at the funeral service in the church tomorrow, and then to come to her place, to the memorial meal.”
“She is giving a memorial meal?”

“Yes, sir, a little meal; she told me to thank you very much for helping us yesterday... without you we would have had nothing at all to bury him with.” And her lips and chin suddenly began to quiver, but she controlled herself and held it back, quickly lowering her eyes to the ground again.

While they talked, Raskolnikov was examining her closely. It was a thin, quite thin and pale little face, rather irregular, somehow sharp, with a sharp little nose and chin. She could not even be called pretty, but her blue eyes were so clear, and when they came alive, the expression of her face became so kind and so simple-hearted that one was drawn to her in spite of oneself. In her face, and in her whole figure, there was besides one special characteristic feature: in spite of her eighteen years she seemed almost still a little girl, much younger than her years, almost quite a child, and this sometimes showed itself even comically in some of her movements.
“But can Katerina Ivanovna really manage with such small means, and even intends to give a meal?..” asked Raskolnikov, insistently keeping up the conversation.

“The coffin will be a plain one, sir... and everything will be plain, so it won’t cost much... Katerina Ivanovna and I worked it all out earlier, so there will be something left for the memorial... and Katerina Ivanovna very much wants it to be so. You see, it can’t be helped, sir... it’s a comfort to her... she is like that, you know...”
“I understand, I understand... of course... Why are you looking round my room like that? Mama says too that it looks like a coffin.”

“You gave us everything yesterday!” Sonechka said suddenly in reply, in a kind of strong, rapid whisper, and suddenly looked down hard again. Her lips and chin began to quiver again. She had been struck for some time by Raskolnikov’s poor surroundings, and now these words burst out of her of themselves. A silence followed. Dunechka’s eyes somehow grew brighter, and Pulkheria Alexandrovna even looked at Sonya kindly.

“Rodya,” she said, standing up, “of course we shall dine together. Come, Dunechka... And you, Rodya, should go out for a little walk, and then rest, lie down, and then come to us soon... We have tired you out, I am afraid...”
“Yes, yes, I’ll come,” he answered, standing up and hurrying... “I have some business, though...”
“Surely you are not going to dine separately?” cried Razumikhin, looking at Raskolnikov in surprise. “What’s the matter with you?”
“Yes, yes, I’ll come, of course, of course... And you stay a minute. You don’t need him just now, do you, Mama? Or am I taking him from you?”
“Oh no, no! And you, Dmitry Prokofich, will you come to dinner, will you be so kind?”
“Please do come,” Dunya asked.
Razumikhin bowed and beamed all over. For a moment everyone was suddenly and strangely embarrassed.
“Goodbye, Rodya, that is, until we meet; I don’t like saying ‘goodbye’. Goodbye, Nastasya... ah, I’ve said ‘goodbye’ again!..”
Pulkheria Alexandrovna meant to bow to Sonechka too, but somehow did not manage it, and hurried out of the room.

But Avdotya Romanovna seemed to have been waiting her turn, and, passing Sonya as she followed her mother, she made her an attentive, courteous and full bow. Sonechka was confused and bowed in a hurried, frightened way; something even like pain was reflected in her face, as if Avdotya Romanovna’s courtesy and attention were burdensome and tormenting to her.
“Dunya, goodbye, then!” Raskolnikov called out, already in the passage. “Give me your hand!”
“But I did give it to you, have you forgotten?” answered Dunya, turning to him tenderly and awkwardly.
“Well, what of it, give it again!”
And he pressed her little fingers hard. Dunechka smiled at him, blushed, quickly pulled her hand away and went after her mother, also, for some reason, completely happy.
“Well, that’s splendid!” he said to Sonya, coming back into his room and looking at her brightly. “God rest the dead, but the living must go on living! Isn’t that so? Isn’t it? It is, isn’t it?”

Sonya looked with something like surprise at his suddenly brightened face; for a few moments he gazed at her silently and intently: the whole story her late father had told about her swept suddenly through his memory at that moment...

“Lord, Dunechka!” Pulkheria Alexandrovna began at once, as soon as they were out in the street. “Here I am now actually glad we have left: it’s somehow easier. Well, did I think yesterday, in the train, that I would be glad even of this!”
“I tell you again, Mama, he is still very ill. Can’t you see? Perhaps he upset himself suffering for our sake. One must be indulgent, and much, much can be forgiven.”

“But you weren’t indulgent yourself!” Pulkheria Alexandrovna interrupted at once, hotly and jealously. “You know, Dunya, I was looking at you both: you are his perfect portrait, and not so much in face as in soul: you are both melancholics, both gloomy and hot-tempered, both proud and both generous... Surely he can’t be an egoist, Dunechka? eh?.. And when I think of what is going to happen at our place this evening, my whole heart sinks!”
“Don’t worry, Mama; what must be will be.”
“Dunechka! But just think what a position we are in now! Well, what if Pyotr Petrovich breaks it off?” poor Pulkheria Alexandrovna suddenly blurted out incautiously.
“Then what will he be worth after that!” Dunechka answered sharply and contemptuously.

“We did well to leave just now,” Pulkheria Alexandrovna hurried on, interrupting. “He was hurrying off somewhere on business; let him take a walk, at least breathe some air... it’s dreadfully stuffy in his room... but where is one to breathe air here? Here even the streets are like rooms without windows. Lord, what a city!.. Wait, step aside, they’ll crush us, they’re carrying something! Why, it was a piano they carried past, really... how they push... I am very much afraid of that girl too...”
“What girl, Mama?”
“Why, that one, Sofya Semyonovna, who was there just now...”
“Afraid of what?”
“I have a presentiment, Dunya. Well, believe it or not, the moment she came in, I thought at once that this is where the main thing lies...”

“Nothing lies there at all!” Dunya cried in vexation. “What you are like with your presentiments, Mama! He has known her only since yesterday, and just now, when she came in, he didn’t recognise her.”

“Well, you will see!.. She troubles me; you’ll see, you’ll see! And how frightened I was: she looks at me and looks, such eyes, I could hardly stay on my chair, do you remember when he began introducing her? And it seems strange to me: Pyotr Petrovich writes about her like that, and he introduces her to us, and to you too! So she must be dear to him!”
“What does it matter what he writes! People talked about us too, and wrote, have you forgotten? And I am sure that she is... a fine person, and that all this is nonsense!”
“God grant it!”
“And Pyotr Petrovich is a worthless gossip,” Dunechka suddenly snapped.
Pulkheria Alexandrovna simply shrank. The conversation broke off.
“Here’s what, here’s the business I have with you...” said Raskolnikov, drawing Razumikhin aside to the window...
“Then I will tell Katerina Ivanovna that you will come...” Sonya hurried, bowing in order to leave.

“In a moment, Sofya Semyonovna; we have no secrets, you are not in the way... I would like to say two more words to you... Here’s what,” he turned suddenly to Razumikhin, without finishing, as if breaking off. “You know that... what’s his name!.. Porfiry Petrovich?”
“I should think so! He’s a relation. Why?” the other added with a kind of burst of curiosity.
“He is the one handling that case now... well, the one about the murder... that you were talking about yesterday... isn’t he?”
“Yes... well?” Razumikhin suddenly goggled.

“He was questioning the people who had pledges there, and I have pledges there too, just rubbish, but still, my sister’s little ring that she gave me as a keepsake when I left for here, and my father’s silver watch. It’s all worth five or six roubles, but it’s dear to me, a keepsake. So what am I to do now? I don’t want the things to be lost, especially the watch. I was trembling earlier in case Mother asked to see it, when they began talking about Dunechka’s watch. It is the only thing left after my father. She will fall ill if it is lost! Women! So how am I to do it, teach me! I know I ought to report it at the police station. But wouldn’t it be better to go to Porfiry himself, eh? What do you think? I would like to get the business done as soon as possible. You’ll see, Mama will ask before dinner!”

“Not the police station on any account, Porfiry without fail!” cried Razumikhin in a kind of extraordinary excitement. “Well, how glad I am! Why wait, let’s go now, it’s two steps, we’ll be sure to find him in!”
“Very well... let’s go...”

“And he will be very, very, very, very glad to meet you! I have talked to him a lot about you at various times... And I talked about you yesterday. Let’s go!.. So you knew the old woman? That’s it!.. It’s all turned out mag-ni-fi-cently!.. Ah, yes... Sofya Ivanovna...”
“Sofya Semyonovna,” Raskolnikov corrected him. “Sofya Semyonovna, this is my friend Razumikhin, and he is a good man...”
“If you have to go now...” Sonya began, without even looking at Razumikhin, and becoming still more embarrassed because of it.
“And let us go!” Raskolnikov decided. “I will come to see you today, Sofya Semyonovna; only tell me where you live.”
He was not exactly confused, but seemed to be in a hurry and to avoid her eyes. Sonya gave her address, and blushed as she did so. They all went out together.
“Don’t you lock your door?” asked Razumikhin, coming down the stairs after them.
“Never!.. Though I have been meaning to buy a lock for two years now,” he added carelessly. “Happy people, aren’t they, who have nothing to lock up?” he turned to Sonya, laughing.
In the street they stopped in the gateway.
