Only some big fly was buzzing and beating about, flying against the glass. At last it became unbearable: Raskolnikov suddenly raised himself and sat up on the sofa.
“Well, speak, what do you want?”
“And I knew all along that you were not asleep but only pretending,” the stranger answered strangely, laughing calmly. “Arkady Ivanovich Svidrigailov, allow me to introduce myself...”
## PART IV · CHAPTER I
“Can this be the dream going on?” Raskolnikov thought once more. Cautiously and mistrustfully he gazed at the unexpected visitor.
“Svidrigailov? What nonsense! It can’t be!” he said aloud at last, in bewilderment.
The visitor seemed not at all surprised by this exclamation.

“I have called on you for two reasons: in the first place, I wished to make your acquaintance personally, since I have long heard of you from a very curious point of view, and one favourable to you; and in the second, I dream that you will perhaps not refuse to help me in an undertaking that directly concerns the interest of your sister, Avdotya Romanovna. On my own, without a recommendation, she might not let me even into her yard now, because of prejudice; well, but with your help, on the contrary, I count on...”
“You count badly,” Raskolnikov interrupted.
“They arrived only yesterday, may I ask?”
Raskolnikov did not answer.

“Yesterday, I know. I myself arrived only the day before. Well, sir, this is what I will tell you on that score, Rodion Romanovich: I consider it superfluous to justify myself, but allow me too to declare: what is there, in all this, really so especially criminal on my part, that is, judging without prejudices, soberly?”
Raskolnikov went on examining him in silence.

“That in my own house I pursued a defenceless girl and ‘insulted her with my vile proposals’: isn’t that it, sir? (I am running ahead of myself!) But only suppose that I too am a man, et nihil humanum... nothing human, in a word, that I too am capable of being tempted and of falling in love (which, of course, does not happen at our command); then everything is explained in the most natural way. The whole question here is: am I a monster, or a victim myself? Well, and what if a victim? After all, in proposing to the object of my passion that she run away with me to America or to Switzerland, I may have cherished the most respectful feelings, and even thought of arranging our mutual happiness!.. Reason, you know, is the servant of passion; I was ruining myself even more, if you please!..”

“But that is not the point at all,” Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust. “Quite simply, you are repulsive, whether you are right or not; and so people don’t want to have anything to do with you, and they drive you away; so off you go!..”
Svidrigailov suddenly burst out laughing.
“Well, you... you can’t be thrown off!” he said, laughing in the frankest way. “I was thinking of being cunning, but no, you have gone straight to the very real point!”
“But you are still being cunning at this very moment.”

“Well, what of it? What of it?” Svidrigailov repeated, laughing wide open. “It is bonne guerre, fair war, as they say, and the most permissible cunning!.. But all the same you interrupted me; one way or another, I affirm again: there would have been no unpleasantness if it had not been for the incident in the garden. Marfa Petrovna...”
“And Marfa Petrovna, they say, you finished off too?” Raskolnikov interrupted rudely.

“So you have heard about that too? But then, how could you not... Well, as to this question of yours, really, I don’t know what to tell you, although my own conscience is in the highest degree at peace on that score. That is, don’t think that I fear anything of that sort: everything was done in perfect order and with complete exactness: the medical inquest found an apoplexy, brought on by bathing immediately after a heavy dinner with nearly a bottle of wine drunk, and it could have found nothing else... No, sir, this is what I have been thinking to myself for some time, especially on the journey, sitting in the train: did I not contribute to all this... misfortune, somehow, by irritating her morally, or something of that kind? But I concluded that this too was positively impossible.”
Raskolnikov laughed.
“Fancy worrying so much!”

“But what are you laughing at? Consider: I struck her only twice with a little riding whip; there weren’t even any marks... Please don’t think me a cynic; I know exactly how vile it is on my part, and so on; but I also know for certain that Marfa Petrovna was perhaps even glad of this, so to speak, impulse of mine. The story about your sister had been worn out to the last letter. For three days Marfa Petrovna had been forced to sit at home; she had nothing to show herself in the little town with, and besides, she had bored everyone there with that letter of hers (you have heard about the reading of the letter?). And suddenly these two lashes fall as if from heaven! The first thing she did was order the carriage to be harnessed!.. I won’t even mention that women have moments when it is very, very pleasant to be insulted, in spite of all their visible indignation. Everyone has them, these moments; man in general very, very much likes being insulted, have you noticed that? But with women it is especially so. One might even say that they live on it.”
At one point Raskolnikov thought of getting up and leaving and so ending the meeting. But a certain curiosity, and even a kind of calculation, held him back for the moment.
“Are you fond of fighting?” he asked absently.

“No, not very,” Svidrigailov answered calmly. “And Marfa Petrovna and I almost never fought. We lived in great harmony, and she always remained satisfied with me. In all our seven years I used the whip only twice (if one doesn’t count one more, third case, a very ambiguous one, though): the first time two months after our marriage, as soon as we arrived in the country, and then this last case now. And you thought I was such a monster, a reactionary, a serf-owner? He-he... And by the way: do you remember, Rodion Romanovich, how a few years ago, still in the days of beneficent publicity, a certain nobleman was publicly and literarily disgraced among us, I’ve forgotten his name! the one who thrashed a German woman in a railway carriage, remember? It was then, in that same year I think, that ‘The Disgraceful Act of The Age’ happened too (well, ‘Egyptian Nights’, the public reading, remember? Those black eyes! Oh, where are you, golden time of our youth!). Well, sir, here is my opinion: I have no deep sympathy for the gentleman who thrashed the German woman, because really it is... what is there to sympathise with! But at the same time I cannot help declaring that sometimes there are such provoking ‘German women’ that, it seems to me, there is not a single progressive who could fully vouch for himself. Nobody looked at the subject from that point of view at the time, and yet that point is the truly humane one, really it is, sir!”
Having said this, Svidrigailov suddenly laughed again. It was clear to Raskolnikov that this was a man who had firmly resolved on something and kept his own counsel.
“You must have gone several days on end without talking to anyone?” he asked.
“Almost. Why: are you surprised, I suppose, that I am such an easy-going man?”
“No, I am surprised that you are far too easy-going a man.”

“Because I was not offended by the rudeness of your questions? Is that it? Well... why be offended? As you asked, so I answered,” he added with an amazing expression of simple-heartedness. “I am not especially interested in almost anything, by God,” he went on, somehow thoughtfully. “Especially now; I am not occupied with anything at all... However, you are entitled to think that I am currying favour with some purpose, all the more since I have business with your sister, as I declared myself. But I will tell you frankly: I am very bored! Especially these three days, so that I was even glad to see you... Don’t be angry, Rodion Romanovich, but for some reason you yourself seem terribly strange to me. Say what you like, there is something in you; and precisely now, that is, not exactly at this minute, but now in general... Well, well, I won’t, I won’t, don’t frown! I am not such a bear as you think.”
Raskolnikov looked at him gloomily.
“Perhaps you are not a bear at all,” he said. “It even seems to me that you belong to very good society, or at least know how to be a decent man on occasion.”

“But I am not especially interested in anyone’s opinion,” Svidrigailov answered drily and even with a shade of haughtiness, “and so why not be a vulgar fellow for a while, when that suit of clothes is so convenient to wear in our climate and... and especially if one has a natural inclination for it,” he added, laughing again.
“I have heard, though, that you have many acquaintances here. You are what is called ‘not without connections’. Why do you need me, in that case, if not for some purpose?”

“You are right that I have acquaintances,” Svidrigailov took up, not answering the main point. “I have already met some; I have been loafing about for three days now; I recognise people, and they seem to recognise me. Of course, I am decently dressed and reckoned not a poor man; the emancipation of the serfs passed us by, you know: woods and water meadows, the income is not lost; but... I won’t go there; I was sick of it before: I have been walking about for three days and don’t make myself known to anyone... And then the city! I mean, how did it ever get composed among us, tell me, please! A city of clerks and all sorts of seminarists! Really, there was a lot I didn’t notice here before, eight years ago, when I was knocking about here... Now I put my hopes only in anatomy, by God!”
“What anatomy?”
“And as for these clubs, Dussot’s, these points of yours, or perhaps progress too, well, let it go on without us,” he went on, again not noticing the question. “And who wants to be a card sharper?”
“So you were a card sharper too?”

“How could I not be? There was a whole company of us, the most respectable, eight years ago; we passed the time; and all, you know, people with manners, there were poets, there were capitalists. And in general, among us in Russian society, the best manners are found in those who have been beaten, have you noticed that? It is only now in the country that I have let myself go. But all the same they put me in prison for debt then, a little Greek from Nezhin did. That was when Marfa Petrovna turned up, bargained and bought me out for thirty thousand pieces of silver. (I owed seventy thousand in all.) We were joined in lawful wedlock, and she carried me off at once to her place in the country, like some treasure. She was five years older than me, you know. She loved me very much. For seven years I never left the country. And note that all her life she kept a document against me, in someone else’s name, for those thirty thousand, so that if I had thought of rebelling in anything, I would have been in the trap at once! And she would have done it! With women, you know, all this lives together.”
“And if it hadn’t been for the document, would you have run off?”

“I don’t know what to tell you. The document hardly constrained me. I didn’t want to go anywhere, and Marfa Petrovna herself invited me abroad twice, seeing that I was bored. But what of it! I used to go abroad before, and it always made me sick. Not exactly, but the dawn is breaking, the Bay of Naples, the sea, you look, and somehow it is sad. What is most repulsive is that you really are sad about something! No, it’s better at home: here at least you blame others for everything and justify yourself. Perhaps I would go on an expedition to the North Pole now, because j’ai le vin mauvais, I am a bad drunk, and drinking disgusts me, and apart from wine there is nothing left. I have tried. And is it true, they say, that Berg is going up in a huge balloon in the Yusupov Garden on Sunday and inviting fellow passengers for a fee?”
“Why, would you go up?”
“I? No... just so...” muttered Svidrigailov, really as if lost in thought.
“What is he, really?” thought Raskolnikov.

“No, the document didn’t constrain me,” Svidrigailov went on thoughtfully. “It was I myself who never left the country. And it will be about a year now since Marfa Petrovna gave me back that document on my name day, and made me a present of a considerable sum besides. She had capital, you know. ‘You see how I trust you, Arkady Ivanovich’: really, that is how she put it. You don’t believe she put it like that? And you know, I became a decent landowner in the country; I am known in the district. I sent for books too. Marfa Petrovna approved at first, but then she kept being afraid I would study too much.”
“You seem to miss Marfa Petrovna very much?”
“I? Perhaps. Really, perhaps. And by the way, do you believe in ghosts?”
“What ghosts?”
“Ordinary ghosts, what else!”
“And do you believe in them?”
“Well, perhaps not, pour vous plaire, to please you... That is, not exactly not...”
“They appear to you, do they?”
Svidrigailov looked at him somehow strangely.
“Marfa Petrovna is pleased to visit me,” he said, twisting his mouth into a kind of strange smile.
“What do you mean, pleased to visit you?”

“Why, she has come three times already. The first time I saw her was on the very day of the funeral, an hour after the cemetery. That was the day before I left for here. The second time was the day before yesterday, on the journey, at dawn, at Malaya Vishera station; and the third time two hours ago, at the lodging where I am staying, in my room; I was alone.”
“Awake?”
“Completely. All three times awake. She comes, talks for a minute, and goes out by the door; always by the door. You can even seem to hear it.”
“Why did I think that something of this kind was sure to be happening to you!” Raskolnikov said suddenly, and at that very moment was surprised that he had said it. He was in great agitation.
“Re-eally? You thought that?” Svidrigailov asked in surprise. “Can it be? Well, didn’t I say there was some point in common between us, eh?”
“You never said that!” Raskolnikov answered sharply and heatedly.
“Didn’t I?”
“No!”
“I thought I did. Earlier, when I came in and saw that you were lying with your eyes closed and pretending, I said to myself at once: ‘This is the very one!’”
“What does that mean, the very one? What are you talking about?” cried Raskolnikov.
“About what? Really, I don’t know about what...” Svidrigailov muttered openly, as if confused himself.
For a minute they were silent. They stared at each other with all their eyes.
“This is all nonsense!” Raskolnikov cried in vexation. “What does she say to you when she comes?”

“She? Imagine, she talks about the most trifling nonsense, and you may marvel at human beings: that is just what makes me angry. The first time she came in (I was tired, you know: the funeral service, the ‘with the saints give rest’, then the litany, the meal; at last I was left alone in my study, lit a cigar, fell to thinking), she came in at the door: ‘And you, Arkady Ivanovich,’ she says, ‘with all the bustle today, forgot to wind the clock in the dining room.’ And indeed for all seven years I had wound that clock myself every week, and if I forgot, she would always remind me. The next day I was already on my way here. I went into the station at dawn, I had dozed in the night, I was aching, my eyes heavy with sleep; I took some coffee; I look, and Marfa Petrovna suddenly sits down beside me, a pack of cards in her hands: ‘Shall I tell your fortune for the journey, Arkady Ivanovich?’ And she was a past mistress at telling fortunes. Well, I shall never forgive myself for not letting her! I ran away in fright, and the bell was ringing just then, it’s true. Today I am sitting after the most wretched dinner from a cookshop, with a heavy stomach, sitting smoking, and suddenly Marfa Petrovna again, she comes in all dressed up, in a new green silk dress with a very long train: ‘Good day, Arkady Ivanovich! How do you like my dress? Aniska couldn’t make one like it.’ (Aniska is a dressmaker in our village, one of the former serfs, she was apprenticed in Moscow, a pretty little girl.) She stands turning round in front of me. I looked over the dress, then looked attentively into her face: ‘Why do you want,’ I say, ‘to come to me over such trifles, Marfa Petrovna, and trouble yourself?’ ‘Oh my God, my dear, so one can’t even disturb you now!’ To tease her, I say: ‘Marfa Petrovna, I want to get married.’ ‘That would be like you, Arkady Ivanovich; it does you little credit that before you have even buried your wife, you go off at once to get married. And if only you had chosen well, but I know you: neither for her nor for yourself, you’ll only make good people laugh.’ And she took herself off and went out, and her train seemed to rustle. What nonsense, eh?”
“But perhaps you are lying about all of it?” Raskolnikov responded.
“I rarely lie,” answered Svidrigailov, thoughtfully, and as if not noticing the rudeness of the question at all.
“And before this, you had never seen ghosts?”

“N... no, I did, only once in my life, six years ago. I had a house serf, Filka; he had only just been buried when I shouted, forgetting: ‘Filka, my pipe!’ He came in and went straight to the cabinet where I keep my pipes. I sit and think: ‘He is doing it to take revenge on me,’ because just before his death we had a bad quarrel. ‘How dare you,’ I say, ‘come into my presence with a hole in your elbow; get out, you rascal!’ He turned, went out and never came again. I didn’t tell Marfa Petrovna then. I was going to have a requiem served for him, but I felt ashamed.”
“Go and see a doctor.”

“I understand without you that I am unwell, though really I don’t know with what; in my opinion I am surely five times healthier than you. I didn’t ask you that: whether or not you believe that ghosts appear. I asked you: do you believe that ghosts exist?”
“No, I will never believe it!” Raskolnikov cried, even with a kind of anger.

“How do people usually put it?” Svidrigailov muttered, as if to himself, looking aside and bending his head a little. “They say: ‘You are ill, so what appears to you is only non-existent delirium.’ But there is no strict logic in that. I agree that ghosts appear only to the sick; but that only proves that ghosts cannot appear except to the sick, not that they do not exist in themselves.”
“Of course they don’t!” Raskolnikov insisted irritably.

“No? You think so?” Svidrigailov went on, looking at him slowly. “Well, and what if one reasons like this (now help me out here): ‘Ghosts are, so to speak, shreds and fragments of other worlds, their beginnings. A healthy man, of course, has no reason to see them, because a healthy man is the most earthly of men, and therefore must live only this life here, for the sake of completeness and order. Well, but as soon as he falls ill, as soon as the normal earthly order in the organism is disturbed, at once the possibility of another world begins to make itself felt, and the more ill he is, the more contacts there are with the other world, so that when a man dies altogether, he passes straight into the other world.’ I reasoned about this long ago. If you believe in a future life, you can believe this reasoning too.”
“I do not believe in a future life,” said Raskolnikov.
Svidrigailov sat lost in thought.
“And what if there is nothing there but spiders, or something of that sort,” he said suddenly.
“This is a madman,” thought Raskolnikov.

“We keep imagining eternity as an idea that cannot be understood, something huge, huge! But why must it be huge? And suddenly, instead of all that, imagine, there will be one little room there, something like a village bathhouse, black with soot, and spiders in every corner, and that is all eternity. I sometimes imagine it like that, you know.”
“And can it be, can it be that nothing more consoling and more just than that occurs to you!” Raskolnikov cried with a painful feeling.
“More just? And how do we know, perhaps that is just, and you know, I would certainly make it so on purpose!” answered Svidrigailov, smiling vaguely.
A kind of chill suddenly seized Raskolnikov at this hideous answer. Svidrigailov raised his head, looked at him intently and suddenly burst out laughing.

“No, just think of this,” he shouted. “Half an hour ago we had never even seen each other; we count ourselves enemies; there is an unsettled matter between us; we have dropped the matter and gone off into this kind of literature! Well, wasn’t I right in saying that we are berries from the same field?”

“Do me the favour,” Raskolnikov went on irritably, “allow me to ask you to explain yourself quickly and tell me why you have honoured me with your visit... and... and... I am in a hurry, I have no time, I want to go out...”
“By all means, by all means. Your sister, Avdotya Romanovna, is marrying Mr Luzhin, Pyotr Petrovich?”
“Could you not somehow avoid any question about my sister, and not mention her name? I don’t even understand how you dare to pronounce her name in my presence, if you really are Svidrigailov.”
“But I have come precisely to talk about her; how can I not mention her?”
“Very well; speak, but quickly!”

“I am sure that you have already formed your opinion of this Mr Luzhin, a relation of mine through my wife, if you have seen him for even half an hour or heard anything accurate and exact about him. He is no match for Avdotya Romanovna. In my opinion Avdotya Romanovna is sacrificing herself in this affair very generously and recklessly for... for her family. It seemed to me, from everything I had heard about you, that you for your part would be very glad if this marriage could be broken off without damage to anyone’s interests. Now that I know you personally, I am even sure of it.”
“All this is very naive on your part; forgive me, I meant to say: impudent,” said Raskolnikov.

“That is, you mean by this that I am working for my own pocket. Don’t worry, Rodion Romanovich: if I were working for my own advantage, I wouldn’t speak out so directly; I am not a complete fool, after all. On this score I will reveal to you a psychological oddity. Earlier, justifying my love for Avdotya Romanovna, I said that I was a victim myself. Well, then, know that I feel no love now, n-none at all, so that I find it strange myself, because I really did feel something...”
“From idleness and depravity,” Raskolnikov interrupted.
“It’s true, I am a depraved and idle man. But then your sister has so many advantages that even I could not help yielding to a certain impression. But all that is nonsense, as I see myself now.”
“Have you seen it long?”

“I began to notice it even before, but became finally convinced the day before yesterday, almost at the very moment of my arrival in Petersburg. Though even in Moscow I still imagined I was coming to seek Avdotya Romanovna’s hand and to compete with Mr Luzhin.”
“Forgive me for interrupting you; do me the favour: could you not cut it short and go straight to the purpose of your visit? I am in a hurry, I must go out...”

“With the greatest pleasure. Having arrived here and having now decided to undertake a certain... voyage, I wished to make the necessary preliminary arrangements. My children have stayed with their aunt; they are rich, and they have no personal need of me. And what kind of father am I! For myself I took only what Marfa Petrovna gave me a year ago. That is enough for me. Forgive me, I am coming to the point now. Before the voyage, which perhaps will come off, I want to have done with Mr Luzhin too. Not that I can’t stand him very much, but it was through him, all the same, that my quarrel with Marfa Petrovna came about, when I learned that she had cooked up this marriage. I wish now to see Avdotya Romanovna, through your mediation, and perhaps in your presence, to explain to her, in the first place, that not only will she get not the slightest advantage from Mr Luzhin, but there will even certainly be obvious harm. Then, having asked her forgiveness for all these recent unpleasantnesses, I would ask permission to offer her ten thousand roubles and so make easier the break with Mr Luzhin, a break which I am sure she would not be averse to herself, if only the possibility arose.”
“But you really, really are mad!” cried Raskolnikov, not so much angered as surprised. “How dare you talk like that!”

“I knew you would shout; but in the first place, though I am not rich, these ten thousand roubles are free, that is, I have absolutely, absolutely no need of them. If Avdotya Romanovna won’t accept them, I shall perhaps use them still more stupidly. That is one thing. Second: my conscience is perfectly at peace; I make the offer without any calculations. Believe it or not, but later both you and Avdotya Romanovna will find out. The whole point is that I really did cause your much-respected sister some trouble and unpleasantness; and so, feeling sincere repentance, I wish with all my heart, not to buy myself off, not to pay for the unpleasantness, but simply to do something to her advantage, on the grounds that I have not, after all, taken out a privilege to do nothing but evil. If there were even a millionth part of calculation in my offer, I would not make it so directly; and I would not offer only ten thousand, when only five weeks ago I offered her more. Besides, I may very, very soon be marrying a certain girl, and consequently all suspicions of any designs against Avdotya Romanovna must by that very fact be destroyed. In conclusion I will say that in marrying Mr Luzhin, Avdotya Romanovna is taking the very same money, only from another side... But don’t be angry, Rodion Romanovich; reason calmly and coolly.”
As he said this, Svidrigailov was himself extremely cool and calm.
“I ask you to finish,” said Raskolnikov. “In any case this is unforgivably insolent.”

“Not in the least. At that rate a man may do nothing but evil to another man in this world, and on the contrary has no right to do a crumb of good, because of empty accepted formalities. That is absurd. Why, if I, for example, died and left this sum to your sister in my will, surely she wouldn’t refuse to accept it then?”
“Very possibly.”
“Well, that she wouldn’t, sir. But then, no is no, so be it. Only ten thousand is a fine thing, on occasion. In any case, I will ask you to pass on what I have said to Avdotya Romanovna.”
“No, I will not pass it on.”
“In that case, Rodion Romanovich, I shall be forced to seek a personal meeting myself, and so to trouble her.”
“And if I pass it on, you will not seek a personal meeting?”
“Really, I don’t know what to tell you. I would very much like to see her once.”
“Don’t hope for it.”
“A pity. However, you don’t know me. Perhaps we shall become closer.”
“You think we shall become closer?”

“And why not?” said Svidrigailov with a smile, standing up and taking his hat. “It isn’t that I so very much wished to trouble you, and coming here I did not even count on much, though, to be sure, your face struck me this morning...”
“Where did you see me this morning?” Raskolnikov asked uneasily.

“By chance, sir... I keep feeling that there is something in you that suits mine... But don’t worry, I am not a bore; I got along with card sharpers, and I didn’t bore Prince Svirbey, a distant relation of mine and a grandee, and I managed to write about Raphael’s Madonna in Madame Prilukova’s album, and I lived with Marfa Petrovna for seven years without leaving the place, and in the old days I used to spend nights in Vyazemsky’s house on the Haymarket, and perhaps I shall go up in the balloon with Berg.”
“Well, very good, sir. Allow me to ask, will you be setting out on your journey soon?”
“What journey?”
“Why, that ‘voyage’... You said so yourself.”

“The voyage? Ah, yes!.. indeed, I spoke to you about a voyage... Well, that is a wide question... And if only you knew what you are asking about!” he added, and suddenly laughed loudly and shortly. “Perhaps instead of the voyage I shall get married; they are finding me a bride.”
“Here?”
“Yes.”
“When did you find time for that?”

“But I very much wish to see Avdotya Romanovna once. I ask it seriously. Well, goodbye... ah, yes! Here is what I forgot! Tell your sister, Rodion Romanovich, that she is mentioned in Marfa Petrovna’s will for three thousand. That is positively certain. Marfa Petrovna made the arrangement a week before her death, and it was done in my presence. In two or three weeks Avdotya Romanovna can have the money.”
“Are you telling the truth?”
“The truth. Pass it on. Well, sir, your servant. I am staying not very far from you, you know.”
As he went out, Svidrigailov ran into Razumikhin in the doorway.
## CHAPTER IV

And Raskolnikov went straight to the house on the canal where Sonya lived. It was a three-storey house, old and painted green. He sought out the caretaker and got vague directions from him as to where Kapernaumov the tailor lived. Having found, in a corner of the courtyard, the entrance to a narrow, dark staircase, he climbed at last to the second floor and came out onto the gallery that ran round it on the courtyard side. While he was wandering in the dark, puzzling where the entrance to Kapernaumov’s could be, a door suddenly opened three steps away from him; he caught hold of it mechanically.
“Who is there?” asked a woman’s voice anxiously.
“It’s me... to see you,” answered Raskolnikov, and went into a tiny entrance. There, on a chair with a sunken seat, in a bent brass candlestick, stood a candle.
“It’s you! Lord!” Sonya cried out faintly, and stood rooted to the spot.
“Which way to you? In here?”
And Raskolnikov, trying not to look at her, went quickly into the room.

A minute later Sonya came in too with the candle, set it down and stood before him, completely at a loss, in inexpressible agitation and evidently frightened by his unexpected visit. Suddenly colour rushed into her pale face, and tears even came into her eyes... She felt sick, and ashamed, and sweet... Raskolnikov quickly turned away and sat down on a chair by the table. In passing he managed to take in the room at a glance.

It was a large room, but extremely low, the only one let by the Kapernaumovs, whose locked door was in the wall on the left. On the opposite side, in the wall on the right, there was another door, always locked tight. Beyond it was another flat, a neighbouring one, under another number. Sonya’s room looked rather like a shed; it had the shape of a very irregular quadrilateral, and this gave it something misshapen. The wall with three windows, looking out on the canal, cut across the room at a slant, so that one corner, terribly sharp, ran off somewhere into the depths, so that in the weak light one could not even make it out properly; the other corner was far too hideously obtuse. In all this large room there was hardly any furniture. In the corner on the right was a bed; beside it, nearer the door, a chair. Along the same wall as the bed, right by the door into the other flat, stood a plain deal table covered with a little blue cloth; by the table, two wicker chairs. Then, against the opposite wall, near the sharp corner, stood a small chest of drawers of plain wood, as if lost in the emptiness. That was all there was in the room. The yellowish, scuffed and worn wallpaper had gone black in all the corners; it must have been damp and full of fumes here in winter. The poverty was plain to see; there were not even curtains at the bed.

Sonya silently watched her visitor, who was examining her room so attentively and so unceremoniously, and at last even began to tremble with fear, as if she were standing before a judge who would decide her fate.
“I am late... Is it eleven yet?” he asked, still not raising his eyes to her.
“Yes,” muttered Sonya. “Oh yes, it is!” she hurried suddenly, as if this were the whole way out for her. “The landlord’s clock has just struck... and I heard it myself... Yes, it is.”
“I have come to you for the last time,” Raskolnikov went on gloomily, though even now this was only the first time. “I may not see you again...”
“You are... going away?”
“I don’t know... everything is tomorrow...”
“So you won’t be at Katerina Ivanovna’s tomorrow?” Sonya’s voice trembled.
“I don’t know. Everything is tomorrow morning... That is not the point: I have come to say one word...”
He raised his thoughtful look to her and suddenly noticed that he was sitting, while she was still standing before him.
“Why are you standing? Sit down,” he said, in a suddenly changed, quiet and gentle voice.
She sat down. He looked at her kindly and almost with compassion for a minute.
“How thin you are! What a hand you have! Quite transparent. Fingers like a dead girl’s.”
He took her hand. Sonya smiled faintly.
“I have always been like this,” she said.
“Even when you lived at home?”
“Yes.”
“Well, of course!” he said abruptly, and the expression of his face and the sound of his voice suddenly changed again. He looked round once more.
“You rent this from Kapernaumov?”
“Yes, sir...”
“They are there, behind the door?”
“Yes... They have the same kind of room too.”
“All in one?”
“In one, sir.”
“I would be afraid in your room at night,” he remarked gloomily.

“The landlord and his wife are very good, very kind,” answered Sonya, still as if she had not come to herself or collected her wits. “And all the furniture, and everything... everything is theirs. And they are very kind, and the children often come to see me too...”
“The ones with the speech defect?”

“Yes, sir... He stammers, and he is lame too. And his wife too... Not that she stammers, but it’s as if she can’t say everything out. She is kind, very. And he used to be a house serf. And there are seven children... and only the eldest stammers, and the others are just sickly... but they don’t stammer... But how do you know about them?” she added with some surprise.
“Your father told me everything then. He told me everything about you... And about how you went out at six o’clock and came back after eight, and about how Katerina Ivanovna knelt by your bed.”
Sonya was confused.
“I thought I saw him today,” she whispered hesitantly.
“Whom?”
“Father. I was walking along the street, near there, at the corner, after nine, and it was as if he were walking ahead of me. And it was just like him. I was going to go in to Katerina Ivanovna’s...”
“You were walking out?”
“Yes,” Sonya whispered abruptly, confused again and looking down.
“Katerina Ivanovna nearly beat you, didn’t she, when you lived with your father?”
“Oh no, what are you saying, what are you saying, no!” Sonya looked at him even with a kind of fright.
“So you love her?”

“Her? But how could I no-o-ot!” Sonya drew out plaintively, suddenly clasping her hands in suffering. “Ah! you... her... If only you knew. Why, she is just like a child... Why, her mind is quite unhinged... from grief. And how clever she used to be... how generous... how kind! You don’t know anything, anything... ah!”

Sonya said this as if in despair, agitated and suffering and wringing her hands. Her pale cheeks flushed again, and torment showed in her eyes. It was evident that a terrible lot had been stirred in her, that she terribly wanted to express something, to say something, to stand up for someone. A kind of insatiable compassion, if one may put it so, suddenly appeared in every feature of her face.

“Beat me! What are you saying! Lord, beat me! And even if she did beat me, what of it! Well, what of it? You don’t know anything, anything... She is so unhappy, ah, how unhappy! And ill... She is looking for justice... She is pure. She believes so much that there must be justice in everything, and she demands it... And you could torture her, but she would not do anything unjust. She doesn’t notice herself how impossible it all is for there to be justice among people, and she gets irritated... Like a child, like a child! She is just, just!”
“And what will become of you?”
Sonya looked at him questioningly.
“They are left on your hands, you know. It’s true that everything was on you before too, and your late father came to you to beg when he had a hangover. Well, and now what will happen?”
“I don’t know,” Sonya said sadly.
“Will they stay there?”
“I don’t know; they owe money for that lodging; only the landlady, I hear, said today that she wants to give them notice, and Katerina Ivanovna says that she won’t stay a minute herself.”
“How is it she is so bold? Is she relying on you?”

“Ah no, don’t say that!.. We are one, we live as one,” Sonya suddenly grew agitated again and even irritated, exactly as if a canary or some other little bird had got angry. “And what is she to do? Well, what, what is she to do?” she asked, growing heated and agitated. “And how, how she cried today! Her mind is getting confused, didn’t you notice? It is getting confused; now she worries like a little girl about everything being done properly tomorrow, about there being food and everything... now she wrings her hands, coughs blood, cries, suddenly starts beating her head against the wall, as if in despair. And then she is comforted again; she keeps relying on you: she says that you will be her helper now, and that she will borrow a little money somewhere and go to her home town, with me, and open a boarding school for girls of noble birth, and take me as a supervisor, and a whole new, beautiful life will begin for us, and she kisses me, hugs me, comforts me, and she believes it so! she believes her fancies so! Well, how can anyone contradict her? And she herself spent the whole day today washing, cleaning, mending; she dragged the washtub into the room herself, with her poor little strength, she got out of breath, and just fell down on the bed; and this morning we went to the market stalls too, to buy shoes for Polechka and Lena, because theirs have all fallen to pieces, only we didn’t have enough money for what we had worked out, a great deal short, and she chose such dear little boots, because she has taste, you don’t know... And right there in the shop she burst out crying, in front of the shopmen, because there wasn’t enough... Ah, how pitiful it was to see.”
“Well, after that it’s understandable that you... live like this,” said Raskolnikov with a bitter smile.

“But aren’t you sorry? Aren’t you sorry?” Sonya flared up again. “Why, you, I know, you gave away your last money yourself, without having seen anything yet. And if you had seen everything, oh Lord! And how many, many times I have brought her to tears! Why, only last week! Oh, me! Only a week before his death. I acted cruelly! And how many, many times I have done that. Ah, how painful it was to remember all day today!”
Sonya was even wringing her hands as she spoke, from the pain of the memory.
“You, cruel?”

“Yes, me, me! I came to see them then,” she went on, crying, “and my late father says: ‘Read to me, Sonya,’ he says, ‘my head is aching somehow, read to me... here is a book’; he had some book, he had got it from Andrei Semyonych, from Lebezyatnikov, who lives here; he was always getting such funny books. And I say: ‘I must go’, and so I wouldn’t read to him; and I had come in to them mainly to show Katerina Ivanovna some collars; Lizaveta, the dealer, had brought me some collars and cuffs cheap, pretty ones, new, with a pattern. And Katerina Ivanovna liked them very much; she put them on and looked at herself in the mirror, and she liked them very, very much: ‘Give them to me, Sonya,’ she says, ‘please.’ She said please, and she wanted them so much. And where was she to wear them! It was just that the old, happy time came back to her! She looks at herself in the mirror, admires herself, and she has no dresses at all, none, no things at all, for so many years now! And she never asks anyone for anything; she is proud, she would sooner give away her last thing herself; and here she asked, she liked them so much! And I grudged giving them: ‘What do you want them for, Katerina Ivanovna?’ I said. I said just that, ‘what for’. That I should never have said to her! She looked at me like that, and she felt so heavy, so heavy, that I had refused, and it was so pitiful to see... And it wasn’t the collars that made it heavy for her, but that I had refused, I could see. Ah, I think I would take it all back now, do it all over again, all those words of before... Oh, me... but what of it!.. it’s all the same to you!”
“You knew this Lizaveta, the dealer?”
“Yes... But did you know her?” Sonya asked in her turn, with some surprise.
“Katerina Ivanovna has consumption, a bad case; she will die soon,” said Raskolnikov after a silence, not answering the question.
“Oh, no, no, no!” And with an unconscious gesture Sonya seized him by both hands, as if begging him that it should not be.
“But it will be better if she dies.”
“No, not better, not better, not better at all!” she repeated, frightened and without thinking.
“And the children? Where will you take them then, if not to your place?”
“Oh, I don’t know!” Sonya cried almost in despair, and clutched her head. It was evident that this thought had flashed through her many, many times already, and he had only startled it up again.
“Well, and if you, while Katerina Ivanovna is still alive, now, fall ill and are taken to the hospital, what will happen then?” he insisted mercilessly.
“Ah, what are you saying, what are you saying! That can’t possibly happen!” and Sonya’s face was distorted with terrible fright.

“Why can’t it?” Raskolnikov went on with a harsh smile. “You’re not insured, are you? Then what will become of them? They will go out into the street, the whole troop of them; she will cough and beg and beat her head against a wall somewhere, as she did today, and the children will cry... And then she will collapse, be taken to the police station, to the hospital, she will die, and the children...”

“Oh, no!.. God will not let that happen!” broke at last from Sonya’s tight breast. She listened, looking at him in supplication and folding her hands in mute entreaty, as if everything depended on him.
Raskolnikov stood up and began walking about the room. A minute passed. Sonya stood with her arms and head lowered, in terrible anguish.
“And can’t you save? Put something by for a rainy day?” he asked, stopping suddenly in front of her.
“No,” whispered Sonya.
“Of course not! And have you tried?” he added, almost mockingly.
“I have.”
“And it came to nothing! Well, of course! Why even ask!”
And again he walked about the room. Another minute passed.
“You don’t earn something every day?”
Sonya was more embarrassed than before, and the colour rushed into her face again.
“No,” she whispered with a tormented effort.
“It will probably be the same with Polechka,” he said suddenly.
“No! no! It can’t be, no!” Sonya cried aloud, like someone desperate, as if she had suddenly been stabbed with a knife. “God, God will not allow such a horror!..”
“He allows it for others.”
“No, no! God will protect her, God!..” she repeated, beside herself.
“But perhaps there is no God at all,” Raskolnikov answered with a kind of malicious glee, laughed, and looked at her.

Sonya’s face suddenly changed terribly: spasms ran across it. With inexpressible reproach she looked at him, meant to say something, but could not get out a word, and only suddenly began to sob bitterly, bitterly, covering her face with her hands.
“You say Katerina Ivanovna’s mind is getting confused; your own mind is getting confused,” he said after some silence.

About five minutes passed. He kept walking up and down, silently, without looking at her. At last he came up to her; his eyes were flashing. He took her by the shoulders with both hands and looked straight into her weeping face. His look was dry, inflamed, piercing; his lips were trembling violently... Suddenly he bent down quickly with his whole body and, sinking to the floor, kissed her foot. Sonya recoiled from him in horror, as from a madman. And indeed he looked quite like a madman.
“What are you doing, what are you doing? Before me!” she muttered, turning pale, and suddenly her heart was wrung painfully, painfully.
He stood up at once.

“I did not bow down to you; I bowed down to all human suffering,” he said somehow wildly, and went off to the window. “Listen,” he added, coming back to her a minute later, “I told a certain insulting fellow today that he wasn’t worth your little finger... and that I did my sister an honour today by seating her beside you.”
“Ah, why did you tell them that! And in front of her?” Sonya cried in fright. “To sit with me! An honour! Why, I am... dishonoured... I am a great, great sinner! Ah, why did you say that!”

“It was not for your dishonour and your sin that I said it of you, but for your great suffering. And that you are a great sinner, that is so,” he added almost rapturously, “and above all you are a sinner because you have destroyed and betrayed yourself for nothing. Isn’t that a horror! Isn’t it a horror that you live in this filth which you hate so much, and at the same time you know yourself (you have only to open your eyes) that you are not helping anyone by it, and are not saving anyone from anything! But tell me at last,” he said, almost in a frenzy, “how can such shame and such baseness live in you side by side with other feelings, opposite and holy? Why, it would be more just, a thousand times more just and more reasonable, to go head first into the water and end it all at once!”
“And what will become of them?” Sonya asked weakly, looking at him in suffering, but at the same time as if not at all surprised by his suggestion. Raskolnikov looked at her strangely.

He read everything in that one look of hers. So she herself really had already had this thought. Perhaps many times and seriously she had considered in despair how to end it all at once, and so seriously that now she was hardly surprised at his suggestion. She did not even notice the cruelty of his words (the meaning of his reproaches and his particular view of her shame she of course did not notice either, and that was visible to him). But he understood fully to what monstrous pain the thought of her dishonourable and shameful position had tormented her, and for a long time. What, what could have held back until now, he thought, her resolve to end it all at once? And only then did he understand fully what these poor little orphaned children meant to her, and this pitiful, half-mad Katerina Ivanovna, with her consumption and her beating her head against the wall.

But nonetheless it was again clear to him that Sonya, with her character and with the education, such as it was, that she had received, could not in any case go on like this. Still it was a question for him: how could she have stayed in such a position so very long without going out of her mind, if she did not have the strength to throw herself into the water? Of course he understood that Sonya’s position was an accidental phenomenon in society, though unfortunately far from solitary or exceptional. But that very accidentalness, that certain degree of education and her whole previous life might, it seems, have killed her at once, at the first step on that loathsome road. What, then, sustained her? Not depravity, surely? This shame had obviously touched her only mechanically; real depravity had not yet penetrated a single drop into her heart: he saw that; she stood before him in reality...

“There are three roads for her,” he thought: “to throw herself into the canal, to end up in a madhouse, or... or, at last, to throw herself into depravity, which stupefies the mind and turns the heart to stone.” The last thought was the most repulsive of all to him; but he was already a sceptic, he was young, abstract and therefore cruel, and so he could not help believing that the last way out, that is, depravity, was the most likely of all.

“But can this really be true,” he exclaimed to himself, “can this creature too, who has still kept her purity of spirit, be drawn consciously at last into that vile, stinking pit? Has this drawing-in already begun, and is it only because of that that she has been able to endure until now, because vice no longer seems so repulsive to her? No, no, it cannot be!” he exclaimed, as Sonya had earlier. “No, what has kept her from the canal until now is the thought of sin, and they, those... And if she has not yet gone out of her mind... But who said that she has not already gone out of her mind? Is she in her right mind? Can a person talk as she does? Can anyone in her right mind reason as she does? Can one sit over one’s own ruin like this, right over the stinking pit into which one is already being drawn, and wave one’s hands and stop one’s ears when one is told of the danger? What is she waiting for, a miracle? Surely that is it. Aren’t all these signs of madness?”
He fixed stubbornly on this thought. He even liked this way out better than any other. He began to look at her more intently.
“So you pray to God a great deal, Sonya?” he asked her.
Sonya was silent; he stood beside her and waited for an answer.
“What would I be without God?” she whispered quickly and energetically, glancing up at him for a moment with suddenly flashing eyes, and she pressed his hand tightly with hers.
“Well, so it is!” he thought.
“And what does God do for you in return?” he asked, probing further.
Sonya was silent for a long time, as if she could not answer. Her weak little breast heaved all over with agitation.
“Be quiet! Don’t ask! You are not worthy!..” she cried suddenly, looking at him sternly and angrily.
“So it is! so it is!” he repeated insistently to himself.
“He does everything!” she whispered quickly, looking down again.
“There is the way out! There is the explanation of the way out!” he decided to himself, examining her with greedy curiosity.

With a new, strange, almost painful feeling he gazed at that pale, thin, irregular, angular little face, at those gentle blue eyes that could flash with such fire, with such stern, energetic feeling, at that small body still trembling with indignation and anger, and all this seemed to him more and more strange, almost impossible. “A holy fool! a holy fool!” he kept saying to himself.

On the chest of drawers lay some book. Each time he passed up and down he had noticed it; now he picked it up and looked. It was the New Testament in Russian translation. The book was old, well used, in a leather binding.
“Where is this from?” he called to her across the room. She was still standing in the same place, three steps from the table.
“It was brought to me,” she answered, as if reluctantly and without looking at him.
“Who brought it?”
“Lizaveta brought it; I asked her to.”
“Lizaveta! Strange!” he thought. Everything about Sonya was becoming somehow stranger and more wonderful to him with every minute. He carried the book over to the candle and began turning the pages.
“Where is the part about Lazarus?” he asked suddenly.
Sonya looked stubbornly at the floor and did not answer. She was standing a little sideways to the table.
“Where is the raising of Lazarus? Find it for me, Sonya.”
She glanced at him sideways.
“You are not looking in the right place... in the fourth gospel...” she whispered sternly, without moving towards him.
“Find it and read it to me,” he said, sat down, leaned his elbows on the table, propped his head on his hand and stared gloomily to one side, ready to listen.
“In three weeks’ time, out at the seventh verst, you’re welcome! I think I shall be there myself, if nothing worse happens,” he muttered to himself.
Sonya stepped hesitantly to the table, having listened mistrustfully to Raskolnikov’s strange wish. She took the book, however.
“Haven’t you read it?” she asked, glancing at him across the table, from under her brows. Her voice was growing sterner and sterner.
“Long ago... When I was at school. Read!”
“And haven’t you heard it in church?”
“I... didn’t go. Do you go often?”
“N-no,” whispered Sonya.
Raskolnikov smiled.
“I understand... And so you won’t go to bury your father tomorrow?”
“I will. I was there last week too... I had a requiem sung.”
“For whom?”
“For Lizaveta. She was killed with an axe.”
His nerves were growing more and more irritated. His head began to spin.
“You were friends with Lizaveta?”
“Yes... She was just... she used to come... rarely... it wasn’t possible. We used to read together and... talk. She will see God.”
These bookish words sounded strange to him, and here was something new again: some mysterious meetings with Lizaveta, and both of them holy fools.
“One could become a holy fool oneself here! It’s catching!” he thought. “Read!” he exclaimed suddenly, insistently and irritably.
Sonya still hesitated. Her heart was pounding. Somehow she did not dare to read to him. Almost in torment he looked at the “unhappy madwoman”.
“What do you want it for? You don’t believe, do you?..” she whispered quietly and somehow breathlessly.
“Read! I want you to!” he insisted. “You read to Lizaveta!”
Sonya opened the book and found the place. Her hands were trembling; her voice failed her. Twice she began, and still the first syllable would not come out.

“Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany...” she uttered at last, with an effort, but suddenly, at the third word, her voice rang and broke like a string stretched too tight. Her breath caught and her chest tightened.

Raskolnikov understood in part why Sonya could not bring herself to read to him, and the more he understood it, the more roughly and irritably, as it were, he insisted on the reading. He understood only too well how hard it was for her now to give away and expose everything that was her own. He understood that these feelings really did form, as it were, her real and long-standing secret, perhaps since her girlhood, back in the family, beside her unhappy father and her stepmother driven mad by grief, among hungry children, hideous shouts and reproaches. But at the same time he knew now, and knew for certain, that though she was full of anguish and terribly afraid of something as she began to read, yet at the same time she herself tormentingly wanted to read, in spite of all her anguish and all her fears, and to him precisely, so that he would hear it, and certainly now, “whatever might come of it afterwards!”... He read this in her eyes, understood it from her rapturous agitation... She mastered herself, suppressed the spasm in her throat that had cut off her voice at the beginning of the verse, and went on reading the eleventh chapter of the Gospel of John. So she read on to the nineteenth verse:

“And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother. Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him: but Mary sat still in the house. Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee.”
Here she stopped again, foreseeing with shame that her voice would tremble and break again...

“Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again. Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this? She saith unto him,”
(and drawing breath as if in pain, Sonya read distinctly and forcefully, as if she herself were confessing before all the world):
“Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.”

She was about to stop, quickly raised her eyes to him, but hastily mastered herself and went on reading. Raskolnikov sat and listened motionless, not turning round, his elbows on the table, looking to one side. They read on to the thirty-second verse.

“Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, and said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him! And some of them said, Could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?”

Raskolnikov turned to her and looked at her with agitation: yes, so it was! She was already trembling all over in a real, genuine fever. He had expected it. She was approaching the word about the greatest and unheard-of miracle, and a feeling of great triumph took hold of her. Her voice grew ringing, like metal; triumph and joy rang in it and strengthened it. The lines swam before her, because her eyes were darkening, but she knew by heart what she was reading. At the last verse, “Could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind...”, she lowered her voice and conveyed hotly and passionately the doubt, the reproach and the blasphemy of the unbelieving, blind Jews, who in a moment, in a minute, would fall as if struck by thunder, sob and believe... “And he, he too is blinded and unbelieving; he too will hear in a moment, he too will believe, yes, yes! at once, right now,” she dreamed, and she trembled with joyful expectation.

“Jesus therefore again groaning in himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it. Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.”
She struck the word four with energy.

“Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God? Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me. And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth,”
(she read loudly and rapturously, trembling and turning cold, as if she were seeing it with her own eyes):

“bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go. Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on him.”
Further she did not read, and could not read; she closed the book and quickly got up from her chair.

“That is all about the raising of Lazarus,” she whispered abruptly and sternly, and stood motionless, turned aside, not daring, and as if ashamed, to raise her eyes to him. Her feverish trembling still went on. The candle end had long been guttering in the bent candlestick, dimly lighting up in this beggarly room the murderer and the harlot, strangely come together over the reading of the eternal book. Five minutes or more passed.

“I came to talk about something,” Raskolnikov said suddenly, loudly and frowning; he stood up and went over to Sonya. She raised her eyes to him in silence. His look was especially stern, and a kind of wild resolve was expressed in it.
“Today I abandoned my family,” he said, “my mother and my sister. I will not go to them now. I have broken off everything there.”

“Why?” Sonya asked, as if stunned. The meeting with his mother and sister earlier had left an extraordinary impression on her, though one unclear even to herself. She heard the news of the break almost with horror.
“Now I have only you,” he added. “Let us go together... I have come to you. We are both cursed; let us go together!”
His eyes were flashing. “Like a half-wit!” Sonya thought in her turn.
“Go where?” she asked in fear, and involuntarily stepped back.
“How should I know? I only know that it is the same road, I know that for certain, and nothing more. One goal!”
She looked at him and understood nothing. She understood only that he was terribly, infinitely unhappy.
“None of them will understand anything, if you talk to them,” he went on, “but I have understood. I need you; that is why I have come to you.”
“I don’t understand...” whispered Sonya.

“You will understand later. Haven’t you done the same thing? You too have stepped over... you were able to step over. You have laid hands on yourself, you have destroyed a life... your own (it is all the same!). You could have lived by spirit and reason, and you will end up on the Haymarket... But you can’t bear it, and if you are left alone you will go out of your mind, like me. You are like a madwoman even now; so we must go together, by the same road! Let us go!”
“Why? Why are you saying this!” said Sonya, strangely and rebelliously stirred by his words.

“Why? Because one cannot stay like this, that is why! One must reason seriously and directly at last, and not cry like a child and shout that God won’t allow it! Well, what will happen if you really are taken to the hospital tomorrow? She is out of her mind and consumptive, she will die soon, and the children? Won’t Polechka be ruined? Haven’t you seen children here, at the street corners, whose mothers send them out to beg? I have found out where these mothers live and in what surroundings. There children cannot remain children. There a seven-year-old is depraved and a thief. And yet children are the image of Christ: ‘For of such is the kingdom of God.’ He commanded us to honour and love them; they are the humanity of the future...”
“What, then, what is to be done?” Sonya repeated, weeping hysterically and wringing her hands.

“What is to be done? Break what must be broken, once and for all, and that’s all: and take the suffering on yourself! What? You don’t understand? You will understand later... Freedom and power, and above all power! Over all trembling creatures and over the whole anthill!.. That is the goal! Remember it! That is my parting word to you! Perhaps I am speaking to you for the last time. If I don’t come tomorrow, you will hear about everything yourself, and then remember these words of now. And some day, later, years later, with life, perhaps you will understand what they meant. But if I come tomorrow, I will tell you who killed Lizaveta. Goodbye!”
Sonya shuddered all over with fright.
“But do you know who killed her?” she asked, going cold with horror and looking at him wildly.

“I know and I will tell... You, only you! I have chosen you. I am not coming to you to ask forgiveness; I will simply tell you. I chose you long ago to tell you this; already then, when your father talked about you and Lizaveta was alive, I thought of it. Goodbye. Don’t give me your hand. Tomorrow!”

He went out. Sonya looked at him as at a madman; but she herself was as if out of her mind and felt it. Her head was spinning. “Lord! how does he know who killed Lizaveta? What did those words mean? It is frightening!” But at the same time the thought did not come into her head. Not at all! Not at all!.. “Oh, he must be terribly unhappy!.. He has abandoned his mother and sister. Why? What happened? And what does he intend? What was he saying to her? He kissed her foot and said... said (yes, he said it clearly) that he cannot live without her any more... Oh Lord!”

Sonya spent the whole night in fever and delirium. At times she jumped up, wept, wrung her hands, then sank again into a feverish sleep, and she dreamed of Polechka, Katerina Ivanovna, Lizaveta, the reading of the Gospel, and him... him, with his pale face, with his burning eyes... He kisses her feet, he weeps... Oh Lord!

Behind the door on the right, behind that very door which separated Sonya’s lodging from the lodging of Gertrude Karlovna Resslich, there was an intermediate room, long empty, belonging to Madame Resslich’s flat and offered by her for rent, for which notices had been put up on the gate and little papers stuck on the window panes looking out onto the canal. Sonya had long been used to regarding this room as uninhabited. And yet, all this time, Mr Svidrigailov had been standing at the door in the empty room, hidden, eavesdropping. When Raskolnikov went out, he stood for a while, thought, went on tiptoe to his own room, next to the empty one, fetched a chair and noiselessly carried it right up to the door leading into Sonya’s room. He had found the conversation entertaining and significant, and he liked it very, very much: so much that he even carried the chair over, so that in future, tomorrow for instance, he would not again be subjected to the unpleasantness of standing for a whole hour on his feet, but could settle himself more comfortably, so as to get complete satisfaction in every respect.
## CHAPTER V

When, the next morning, at eleven o’clock precisely, Raskolnikov entered the building of the — district, the department of the investigating magistrate, and asked to be announced to Porfiry Petrovich, he was even surprised at how long they kept him waiting: at least ten minutes passed before he was called. And by his reckoning, it seemed, they ought to have pounced on him at once. Meanwhile he stood in the waiting room, and people walked past him, back and forth, who apparently had nothing whatever to do with him. In the next room, which looked like an office, several clerks sat writing, and it was obvious that not one of them had the slightest idea who or what Raskolnikov was. With an uneasy and suspicious look he watched everything around him, on the lookout for some guard near him, some mysterious eye appointed to watch him so that he should not get away. But there was nothing of the kind: he saw only office faces, petty and preoccupied, then some other people, and no one had any need of him at all: he could go off to the four corners of the earth that very moment. The thought grew firmer and firmer in him that if that enigmatic man of yesterday, that phantom who had come up out of the ground, really knew everything and had seen everything, would they let him, Raskolnikov, stand here like this and wait calmly? And would they have waited for him here till eleven o’clock, until it suited him to come of his own accord? It followed that either the man had not yet reported anything, or... or simply he too knew nothing and had seen nothing with his own eyes (and how could he have seen?), and so all that had happened to him, Raskolnikov, yesterday, was again a phantom, magnified by his irritated and sick imagination. This guess had begun to take hold of him even yesterday, during his most violent alarm and despair. Thinking all this over now and preparing for a new battle, he suddenly felt that he was trembling, and indignation even boiled up in him at the thought that he was trembling with fear before the hateful Porfiry Petrovich. The most terrible thing of all for him was to meet that man again: he hated him beyond measure, infinitely, and was even afraid that his hatred might somehow give him away. And so strong was his indignation that it stopped the trembling at once; he prepared to go in with a cold and insolent air, and gave himself his word to keep silent as much as possible, to watch and listen, and, at least this time, at any cost, to conquer his morbidly irritated nature. At that very moment he was called in to Porfiry Petrovich.

It turned out that at that moment Porfiry Petrovich was alone in his study. His study was a room neither large nor small; in it stood a large writing table in front of a sofa covered with oilcloth, a bureau, a cupboard in the corner and a few chairs, all government furniture of polished yellow wood. In the corner, in the back wall, or rather in the partition, there was a locked door: beyond it, behind the partition, there must therefore be some further rooms. When Raskolnikov came in, Porfiry Petrovich at once closed the door by which he had entered, and they were left alone. He met his visitor with what seemed the merriest and most welcoming air, and only some minutes later did Raskolnikov notice in him, by certain signs, something like confusion, as if he had suddenly been thrown off his stride or caught at something very private and secret.

“Ah, my most esteemed friend! Here you are... in our parts...” Porfiry began, holding out both hands to him. “Well, sit down, my dear fellow! Or perhaps you don’t like being called most esteemed and... my dear fellow, just like that, tout court, without ceremony? Please don’t take it for familiarity... Here, sir, on the little sofa.”
Raskolnikov sat down, not taking his eyes off him.

“In our parts”, the apology for familiarity, the little French phrase “tout court”, and so on and so on: all these were characteristic signs. “He held out both hands to me, though, and didn’t give me either; he drew them back in time,” flashed through him suspiciously. Both were watching each other, but as soon as their eyes met, both, with the speed of lightning, looked away from each other.
“I have brought you this paper... about the watch... here it is, sir. Is it written properly, or must I write it out again?”

“What? The paper? Yes, yes... don’t worry, it’s quite right, sir,” said Porfiry Petrovich, as if hurrying somewhere, and only after saying it did he take the paper and look it over. “Yes, quite right, sir. Nothing more is needed,” he confirmed in the same patter, and put the paper on the table. Then, a minute later, already talking of something else, he took it from the table again and moved it to his bureau.

“You said yesterday, I think, that you would like to question me... formally... about my acquaintance with that... murdered woman?” Raskolnikov began again. “Now why did I put in ‘I think’?” flashed through him like lightning. “Now why am I so worried about having put in that ‘I think’?” another thought flashed through him at once, like lightning.

And he suddenly felt that his suspiciousness, from mere contact with Porfiry, from only two words, only two looks, had already grown in an instant to monstrous proportions... and that this was terribly dangerous: his nerves were getting irritated, his agitation was growing. “Trouble! Trouble!.. I’ll give myself away again.”

“Yes, yes, yes! Don’t worry! There’s plenty of time, plenty of time, sir,” muttered Porfiry Petrovich, walking up and down near the table, but somehow without any purpose, as if rushing now to the window, now to the bureau, now back to the table, now avoiding Raskolnikov’s suspicious look, now suddenly stopping still and looking straight at him point-blank. His small, fat, round little figure seemed extraordinarily strange as he did this, like a little ball rolling in different directions and at once bouncing off all the walls and corners.

“We’ll have time, sir, we’ll have time!.. And do you smoke? Have you any? Here, sir, a little cigarette, sir...” he went on, offering his visitor a cigarette. “You know, I am receiving you here, but my lodging is right here, behind the partition... a government lodging, sir, and I am in a private one for the time being. Some little repairs had to be done here. Now it is almost ready... a government lodging, you know, is a splendid thing, eh? What do you think?”
“Yes, a splendid thing,” answered Raskolnikov, looking at him almost mockingly.

“A splendid thing, a splendid thing...” Porfiry Petrovich repeated, as if suddenly thinking about something quite different. “Yes! a splendid thing!” he almost cried out at the end, suddenly raising his eyes to Raskolnikov and stopping two steps away from him. This repeated, silly assertion that a government lodging was a splendid thing was, in its vulgarity, too much at odds with the serious, thinking and enigmatic look which he now fixed on his visitor.
But this boiled up Raskolnikov’s anger still more, and he could no longer keep himself from a mocking and rather incautious challenge.

“And do you know what,” he asked suddenly, looking at him almost insolently and as if taking pleasure in his insolence, “there exists, I believe, a legal rule, a legal device, for all possible investigators: first to begin from far off, with trifles, or even with something serious, but quite irrelevant, so as to encourage, so to speak, or rather to distract the person being questioned, to lull his caution, and then suddenly, in the most unexpected way, to stun him on the crown of the head with some most fatal and dangerous question; isn’t that so? This, I believe, is still mentioned religiously in all the rules and manuals?”

“Just so, just so... what, do you think I was using the government lodging to, er... eh?” And having said this, Porfiry Petrovich narrowed his eyes and winked; something merry and sly ran over his face, the little wrinkles on his forehead smoothed out, his little eyes narrowed, his features stretched, and he suddenly broke into a nervous, prolonged laugh, heaving and shaking all over and looking straight into Raskolnikov’s eyes. Raskolnikov began to laugh himself, forcing himself somewhat; but when Porfiry, seeing that he too was laughing, went off into such a fit of laughter that he almost turned purple, Raskolnikov’s disgust suddenly overcame all caution: he stopped laughing, frowned, and looked long and hatefully at Porfiry, not taking his eyes off him, all through his long laughter, which seemed to go on as if on purpose. The incaution, however, was obvious on both sides: it turned out that Porfiry Petrovich was as if laughing in the face of his visitor, who received this laughter with hatred, and was very little embarrassed by the circumstance. This last was very significant for Raskolnikov: he understood that Porfiry Petrovich had surely not been embarrassed at all earlier either, but that on the contrary he himself, Raskolnikov, had perhaps fallen into a trap; that there was obviously something here that he did not know, some purpose; that perhaps everything was already prepared and would be revealed at any moment, this very minute, and come crashing down...
He went straight to the point at once, got up from his seat and took his cap.

“Porfiry Petrovich,” he began resolutely, but with rather strong irritability, “yesterday you expressed the wish that I should come for some kind of questioning.” (He laid special stress on the word questioning.) “I have come, and if you need anything, then ask; if not, allow me to withdraw. I have no time, I have business... I must be at the funeral of that same official run over by horses, of whom you... also know...” he added, at once angry at having added this, and therefore at once more irritated still. “I am sick of all this, sir, do you hear, and have been for a long time... it was partly why I was ill... in a word,” he almost shouted, feeling that the phrase about illness was still more out of place, “in a word: be so good as either to question me or to let me go, at once... and if you are going to question me, then only in due form, sir! Otherwise I shall not permit it; and so, for the time being, goodbye, since the two of us have nothing to do together now.”

“Lord! What are you saying! What is there to question you about?” Porfiry Petrovich suddenly began clucking, at once changing both his tone and his look and instantly ceasing to laugh. “Please don’t worry,” he fussed, now rushing in all directions again, now suddenly trying to make Raskolnikov sit down. “There’s plenty of time, plenty of time, sir, and all this is mere trifles, sir! I, on the contrary, am so glad that you have come to us at last... I am receiving you as a guest. And forgive me for that cursed laughter, my dear Rodion Romanovich. Rodion Romanovich? That is your patronymic, isn’t it?.. I’m a nervous man, sir; you made me laugh very much with the wit of your remark; sometimes, really, I start shaking like india rubber, and for half an hour at a time... I’m given to laughing, sir. With my build I am even afraid of a stroke. But sit down, what is the matter?.. Please, my dear fellow, or else I shall think you are angry...”
Raskolnikov was silent, listening and observing, still frowning angrily. He did sit down, however, but without letting go of his cap.

“I will tell you one thing about myself, my dear Rodion Romanovich, by way of explaining my character, so to speak,” Porfiry Petrovich went on, bustling about the room and, as before, seeming to avoid meeting his visitor’s eyes. “I am, you know, a bachelor, a man not of the world and not known, and besides, a finished man, a stiffened man, sir, gone to seed and... and... and have you noticed, Rodion Romanovich, that among us, that is, here in Russia, sir, and most of all in our Petersburg circles, if two intelligent men who are not yet very well acquainted, but, so to speak, respect each other mutually, as you and I do now, sir, come together, they can’t find a subject for conversation for a whole half hour; they stiffen before each other, sit there and are mutually embarrassed. Everyone has a subject of conversation; the ladies, for instance... people of the world, for instance, of the higher tone, always have a subject of conversation, c’est de rigueur, it is the rule; but people of the middling sort, like us, are all bashful and untalkative... the thinking ones, that is. Why is that, my dear fellow? Is it that we have no public interests, sir, or are we so very honest that we don’t wish to deceive each other, I don’t know, sir. Eh? What do you think? But put down your little cap, sir, as if you were about to leave this minute; really, it’s awkward to look at... I, on the contrary, am so glad, sir...”

Raskolnikov put down his cap, continuing to be silent and listening seriously, frowning, to Porfiry’s empty and confused chatter. “What, does he really want to distract my attention with his stupid chatter?”

“I won’t offer you coffee, sir, this isn’t the place; but why not sit for five minutes with a friend, for diversion,” Porfiry poured out without stopping, “and you know, sir, all these official duties... but don’t be offended, my dear fellow, that I keep walking up and down like this, back and forth; forgive me, my dear fellow, I am so afraid of offending you, but exercise is simply indispensable to me, sir. I sit all the time, and I’m so glad to walk for five minutes... haemorrhoids, sir... I keep meaning to treat myself with gymnastics; there, they say, state councillors, actual state councillors and even privy councillors are happy to skip with a rope, sir; that’s how it is, science, in our age, sir... yes, sir... And as for these duties here, the interrogations and all this formality... you yourself, my dear fellow, were pleased just now to mention interrogations, sir... so, you know, really, my dear Rodion Romanovich, these interrogations sometimes throw the interrogator off more than the interrogated... You were pleased, my dear fellow, to remark on that just now with perfect justice and wit.” (Raskolnikov had remarked nothing of the kind.) “One gets muddled, sir! Really, one gets muddled! And it’s always one and the same thing, always one and the same, like a drum! There’s the reform coming, and at least we’ll be renamed, he-he-he! And as for our legal methods, as you so wittily put it, I agree with you entirely, sir. Well, tell me, who among all the accused, even the most homespun peasant, doesn’t know that, for instance, they will first start lulling him with irrelevant questions (in your happy expression), and then suddenly stun him on the very crown, with the butt of the axe, sir, he-he-he! on the very crown, in your happy comparison, he-he! So you really thought that I wanted to use the lodging to... he-he! You are an ironical man. Well, I won’t!
