Ah, yes, by the way, one little word calls up another, one thought calls up another: you were also pleased to mention form earlier, regarding, you know, the little interrogation, sir... But what of form! Form, you know, in many cases, is nonsense, sir. Sometimes it is more profitable just to have a friendly talk. Form will never run away, allow me to reassure you on that, sir; and what is form, essentially, I ask you? An investigator cannot be hampered by form at every step. The investigator’s business, you know, is, so to speak, a free art, in its way, sir, or something of the kind... he-he-he!..”

Porfiry Petrovich paused for breath for a moment. He poured out his words tirelessly, now senselessly empty phrases, now suddenly slipping in some enigmatic little words, and at once getting lost again in nonsense. He was almost running about the room by now, moving his fat little legs faster and faster, looking at the ground all the time, his right hand thrust behind his back, his left hand constantly waving and making various gestures, each time amazingly unsuited to his words. Raskolnikov suddenly noticed that as he ran about the room he had twice seemed to stop by the door, for an instant, as if listening... “Is he expecting something?”

“And you are really perfectly right, sir,” Porfiry took up again, looking merrily and with extraordinary simple-heartedness at Raskolnikov (which made him start and instantly prepare himself), “really right, sir, to have been pleased to laugh with such wit at our legal forms, he-he! These profoundly psychological methods of ours (some of them, of course) are extremely ridiculous, sir, and perhaps useless too, sir, if one is very constrained by form, sir. Yes, sir... I am back to form again: well, suppose I recognised, or rather suspected, someone or other, this one, that one, as a criminal, sir, in some little case entrusted to me... You are preparing to be a lawyer, aren’t you, Rodion Romanovich?”
“Yes, I was...”

“Well, then here is a little example for the future, so to speak; that is, don’t think that I would dare to teach you: why, you publish such articles about crimes! No, sir, but just as a fact, I will venture to present a little example. So suppose I considered this one, that one, the other, to be a criminal; why, I ask, should I disturb him before the time, even if I had evidence against him, sir? One I am obliged, for instance, to arrest as soon as possible, but another is not of that character, really, sir; so why not let him walk about the town a bit, he-he, sir! No, I see you don’t quite understand, so I’ll picture it more clearly for you, sir: if I put him away too early, for instance, why, I might give him, so to speak, moral support, he-he! You are laughing?” (Raskolnikov had no thought of laughing: he sat with his lips compressed, not taking his inflamed gaze from Porfiry Petrovich’s eyes.) “And yet that is how it is, sir, especially with some subjects, because people are very various, sir, and over everything there is only practice, sir. You are pleased to say now: evidence; well, let us suppose there is evidence, sir, but evidence, my dear fellow, cuts both ways, for the most part, sir, and I am an investigator, and therefore a weak man, I confess: I would like to present the case, so to speak, with mathematical clarity; I would like to get hold of such a piece of evidence that it would be like two times two is four! Like a direct and indisputable proof! But if I lock him up at the wrong time, even if I were sure that it was he, why, I may deprive myself of the means of exposing him further, and why? Because I will give him, so to speak, a definite position, define him psychologically, so to speak, and set him at ease, and so he will withdraw from me into his shell: he will understand at last that he is a prisoner. They say that in Sevastopol, right after Alma, the clever people were terribly afraid that the enemy would attack in open force at any moment and take Sevastopol at once; but when they saw that the enemy preferred a regular siege and was opening the first parallel, my, they say, how glad and relieved the clever people were, sir: it meant the business would drag on for at least two months, because when would a regular siege take it! You’re laughing again, you don’t believe me again? Well, of course, you are right too. You are right, sir, right, sir! These are all particular cases, I agree with you; the case I presented is indeed a particular one, sir! But here is what one must observe, my kindest Rodion Romanovich: the general case, sir, that very one for which all the legal forms and rules are fitted and from which they are calculated and written down in books, does not exist at all, sir, for the very reason that every case, every one, a crime, for instance, as soon as it happens in reality, at once turns into a completely particular case, sir; and sometimes into such a one: just like nothing that has gone before, sir. Most comical cases of that kind sometimes occur, sir. Why, if I leave some gentleman quite alone: don’t take him and don’t disturb him, but let him know every hour and every minute, or at least suspect, that I know everything, every last detail, and am watching him day and night, guarding him without sleeping, and let him be consciously under eternal suspicion and fear before me, why, by God, he will get dizzy, really, sir, he will come of his own accord and perhaps even do something that will be like two times two, will have, so to speak, a mathematical look, and that is pleasant, sir. That can happen even with a clod-footed peasant, and all the more with one of us, a modern intelligent man, and developed in a certain direction at that! Because, my dear, it is a very important thing to understand in which direction a man is developed. And nerves, sir, nerves, sir, you have quite forgotten them, sir! Why, nowadays all this is sick, and thin, and irritated!.. And the bile, how much bile there is in them all! Why, I tell you, that is a kind of mine on occasion, sir! And what does it worry me that he walks about the town unbound! Let him, let him walk about for now, let him; I know anyway that he is my little victim and won’t run away from me anywhere! And where would he run to, he-he! Abroad, perhaps? A Pole will run abroad, but not he, especially since I am watching and have taken measures. Into the depths of the fatherland, perhaps? But peasants live there, real, homespun, Russian ones; why, a modern developed man would sooner choose prison than live with such foreigners as our peasants, he-he! But this is all nonsense and externals. What is ‘run away’! That is the formal side; that is not the main thing; it’s not only because there is nowhere to run that he won’t run away from me: he won’t run away from me psychologically, he-he! What a little expression! He won’t run away from me by a law of nature, even if there were somewhere to run. Have you seen a moth before a candle? Well, so he will keep, keep circling round me as round a candle; freedom will lose its charm for him, he will begin to brood, to get entangled, he will entangle himself all round as in a net, he will worry himself to death!.. More than that: he himself will prepare for me some mathematical little thing, like two times two, if only I give him a long enough interval... And he will keep, keep making circles round me, narrowing and narrowing the radius, and... slap! He will fly straight into my mouth, and I will swallow him, sir, and that is very pleasant indeed, sir, he-he-he! You don’t believe me?”
Raskolnikov did not answer; he sat pale and motionless, still gazing with the same intensity into Porfiry’s face.

“A fine lesson!” he thought, growing cold. “This is not even cat and mouse any more, as it was yesterday. And he is not just showing me his strength for nothing and... prompting me: he is far too clever for that! There is another purpose here; what is it? Eh, nonsense, brother, you are trying to frighten me and being cunning! You have no proofs, and yesterday’s man does not exist! You simply want to throw me off, want to irritate me before the time and slam me down in that state; only you’re lying, you’ll come to grief, you’ll come to grief! But why, why prompt me to such an extent?.. Are we counting on my sick nerves?.. No, brother, you’re lying, you’ll come to grief, though you have prepared something... Well, we shall see what you have prepared there.”

And he braced himself with all his strength, preparing for a terrible and unknown catastrophe. At moments he wanted to throw himself on Porfiry and strangle him on the spot. Even as he came in here he had feared this anger. He felt that his lips had dried up, his heart was pounding, froth had dried on his lips. But still he resolved to keep silent and not utter a word until the right time. He understood that this was the best tactic in his position, because not only would he not give himself away, but on the contrary he would irritate the enemy himself with his silence, and perhaps the other would give himself away to him. At least he hoped so.

“No, I see you don’t believe me, sir; you keep thinking I am playing innocent little jokes on you,” Porfiry took up, growing merrier and merrier and constantly giggling with pleasure, and beginning to circle the room again. “Of course you are right, sir; God himself has made my figure so that it arouses only comic thoughts in others; a buffoon, sir; but I will tell you this, and repeat it again, sir: you, my dear Rodion Romanovich, forgive me, an old man, are still a young man, sir, in your first youth, so to speak, and therefore you value the human mind above all, like all young people. The playful sharpness of the mind and the abstract arguments of reason tempt you, sir. And that is exactly like the old Austrian Hofkriegsrat, for instance, as far as I can judge of military events, that is: on paper they defeated Napoleon and took him prisoner, and how wittily they calculated and arranged everything there in their office, and then you look, and General Mack surrenders with his whole army, he-he-he! I see, I see, my dear Rodion Romanovich, you are laughing at me for picking little examples from military history, such a civilian as I am. But what is to be done, it’s a weakness; I love military matters, and how I love reading all these military dispatches... I have decidedly missed my career. I should have served in the army, sir, really, sir. I might not have become a Napoleon, but I would have been a major, sir, he-he-he! Well, sir, now, my dear, I will tell you the whole detailed truth about the particular case, that is: reality and nature, my dear sir, are an important thing, and oh, how they sometimes cut down the most far-sighted calculation! Eh, listen to an old man, I am speaking seriously, Rodion Romanovich.” (As he said this, Porfiry Petrovich, who was hardly thirty-five, really did seem suddenly to grow old all over: even his voice changed, and he seemed to shrink all over.) “Besides, I am a frank man, sir... Am I a frank man or not? What do you think? It seems to me that I am entirely: I tell you such things for nothing, and don’t even ask for a reward for it, he-he! Well, then, sir, I continue, sir: wit, in my opinion, is a magnificent thing, sir; it is, so to speak, the beauty of nature and the consolation of life, and what tricks, it seems, it can play, so that how, it seems, is some poor little investigator to guess sometimes, who is besides carried away by his own fancy, as always happens, because he is a man too, sir! But nature comes to the rescue of the poor little investigator, there’s the trouble! And youth carried away by its wit never thinks of that, youth ‘stepping over all obstacles’ (as you were pleased to put it in the wittiest and most cunning way). Let us suppose he will lie, I mean the man, sir, the particular case, sir, the incognito, sir, and lie excellently, in the most cunning manner; here, it seems, is triumph, and he can enjoy the fruits of his wit, but he goes... slap! and at the most interesting, the most scandalous point, he faints. Let us suppose it is illness; rooms are sometimes stuffy too; but all the same, sir! All the same he has given someone the idea! He lied incomparably, but he didn’t know how to reckon with nature. There is where the treachery lies, sir! Another time, carried away by the playfulness of his wit, he will begin to make a fool of the man who suspects him; he will turn pale as if on purpose, as if in play, but he turns pale too naturally, too much like the truth, and again he has given the idea! Even if he deceives him the first time, the other will think it over during the night, if he is no fool himself. Why, it happens like that at every step, sir! What’s more: he will begin running ahead himself, poking in where no one asks him, talking constantly about what he ought, on the contrary, to keep quiet about, slipping in various allegories, he-he! He will come himself and begin asking: why don’t you take me for so long? he-he-he! And that can happen with the wittiest man, with a psychologist and a man of letters, sir! Nature is a mirror, a mirror, sir, the most transparent one, sir! Look into it and admire, that’s what, sir! But why have you turned so pale, Rodion Romanovich? Isn’t it stuffy for you? Shall I open the little window?”
“Oh, don’t trouble, please,” cried Raskolnikov, and suddenly burst out laughing. “Please don’t trouble!”
Porfiry stopped in front of him, waited, and suddenly burst out laughing himself, following him. Raskolnikov got up from the sofa, suddenly breaking off his laughter, which was completely like a fit.

“Porfiry Petrovich!” he said loudly and distinctly, though he could hardly stand on his trembling legs. “I see clearly at last that you positively suspect me of the murder of that old woman and her sister Lizaveta. For my part I declare to you that I have long been sick of all this. If you find that you have the right to prosecute me lawfully, then prosecute me; to arrest me, then arrest me. But I will not allow you to laugh in my face and torment me.”
Suddenly his lips began to tremble, his eyes blazed with fury, and his voice, held back until then, rang out.
“I will not allow it, sir!” he shouted suddenly, banging his fist on the table with all his strength. “Do you hear that, Porfiry Petrovich? I will not allow it!”
“Ah, Lord, what is this again!” cried Porfiry Petrovich, apparently in utter fright. “My dear fellow! Rodion Romanovich! My dear! My good man! What is the matter with you?”
“I will not allow it!” Raskolnikov began to shout a second time.
“My dear fellow, quieter! They’ll hear, they’ll come! Well, what shall we tell them then, think!” Porfiry Petrovich whispered in horror, bringing his face right up to Raskolnikov’s face.
“I will not allow it, I will not allow it!” Raskolnikov repeated mechanically, but also suddenly in a complete whisper.
Porfiry turned quickly and ran to open the window.

“Let in some air, some fresh air! And you ought to drink a little water, my dear, it’s a fit, sir!” And he rushed to the door to order water, but right there in the corner, conveniently, there turned out to be a carafe of water.

“My dear fellow, drink,” he whispered, rushing to him with the carafe, “perhaps it will help...” Porfiry Petrovich’s fright and his very sympathy were so natural that Raskolnikov fell silent and began to examine him with wild curiosity. He did not take the water, however.
“Rodion Romanovich! my dear! why, you will drive yourself out of your mind like this, I assure you, e-eh! A-ah! Do drink! Drink just a little!”
He did make him take the glass of water in his hand. Raskolnikov mechanically raised it to his lips, but, recollecting himself, put it down on the table with disgust.

“Yes, sir, we had a little fit, sir! At this rate, my dear, you will bring your former illness back on yourself,” Porfiry Petrovich clucked with friendly sympathy, though still with a somewhat bewildered look. “Lord! How can you not take care of yourself like that? And there was Dmitry Prokofich, who came to see me yesterday; I agree, I agree, sir, I have a caustic, nasty character, but what they concluded from it!.. Lord! He came yesterday, after you, we had dinner, he talked and talked, and I could only throw up my hands; well, I thought... oh, Lord! Did he come from you? But sit down, my dear fellow, sit down, for Christ’s sake!”
“No, not from me! But I knew that he was going to you, and why he was going,” Raskolnikov answered sharply.
“You knew?”
“I knew. Well, what of it?”

“Why, this, my dear Rodion Romanovich, that I know still other exploits of yours; I am informed about everything, sir! Why, I know how you went to rent the flat, right at nightfall, when it was getting dark, and began ringing the bell, and asked about the blood, and confused the workmen and the caretakers. Why, I understand your state of soul, your state then... but all the same, at this rate you will simply drive yourself out of your mind, by God, sir! You’ll get dizzy! The indignation in you is boiling up very strongly, sir, a noble indignation, sir, at the injuries received, first from fate, and then from the police officers, and so you rush about here and there, so as to make everyone speak out quickly, so to speak, and end everything at once, because you are sick of this foolishness and all these suspicions. Isn’t that so? Have I guessed your state of mind, sir?.. Only at this rate you will make not only yourself dizzy, but Razumikhin too; he is far too kind a man for this, you know yourself. With you it is illness, and with him it is virtue, and the illness turns out catching for him... I will tell you, my dear fellow, when you have calmed down... but sit down, my dear fellow, for Christ’s sake! Please, rest; you look terrible; do sit down.”

Raskolnikov sat down; his trembling was passing, and he was breaking into a heat all over his body. In deep amazement he listened intently to Porfiry Petrovich, who was frightened and fussing over him like a friend. But he did not believe a single word of his, though he felt some strange inclination to believe. Porfiry’s unexpected words about the flat had completely astounded him. “How is it, then, he knows about the flat?” he suddenly thought, “and he is telling me about it himself!”

“Yes, sir, there was such a case, almost exactly, a psychological one, in our legal practice, sir, such a morbid case, sir,” Porfiry went on in a patter. “A man also accused himself falsely of a murder, sir, and how he accused himself: he produced a whole hallucination, presented facts, told circumstances, muddled and confused each and everyone, and why? He himself, quite unintentionally, partly, had been the cause of a murder, but only partly, and when he found out that he had given the murderers an occasion, he grew melancholy, his mind clouded, he began to imagine things, he went quite off his head, and he convinced himself that he was the murderer! But the Governing Senate at last examined the case, and the unhappy man was acquitted and put under care. Thanks to the Governing Senate! Eh, dear me, ai-ai-ai! But what is this, my dear fellow? At this rate one can catch a fever, when such urges to irritate one’s nerves appear, going to ring bells at night and asking about blood! Why, I have studied all this psychology in practice, sir. Sometimes, you know, a man is drawn to jump out of a window or off a bell tower, and the sensation is so tempting. And the bells too, sir... Illness, Rodion Romanovich, illness! You have begun to neglect your illness too much, sir. You should consult an experienced medical man; what good is that fat fellow of yours!.. You are delirious! All this happens to you simply in delirium!..”
For a moment everything spun round Raskolnikov.

“Can it be, can it be,” flashed through him, “that he is lying even now? Impossible, impossible!” he pushed the thought away from him, feeling beforehand to what a degree of fury and rage it could bring him, feeling that he could go out of his mind with fury.
“It was not in delirium, it was awake!” he cried, straining all the powers of his reason to penetrate Porfiry’s game. “Awake, awake! Do you hear?”

“Yes, I understand and hear, sir! You said yesterday too that it was not in delirium; you even insisted especially that it was not in delirium! I understand everything you can say, sir! E-eh!.. But listen, Rodion Romanovich, my benefactor, take just this circumstance. Why, if you really were, in actual fact, guilty, or somehow mixed up in this cursed business, well, would you, I ask you, insist yourself that you did all this not in delirium but, on the contrary, in full consciousness? And insist especially, with such peculiar stubbornness, insist; well, could it be, well, could it be, I ask you? Why, quite the contrary, in my opinion. Why, if you felt anything against yourself, you ought precisely to insist: that it was certainly in delirium! Isn’t that so? It is, isn’t it?”
Something sly could be heard in this question. Raskolnikov recoiled right against the back of the sofa from Porfiry, who was leaning over him, and examined him silently, point-blank, in bewilderment.

“Or take Mr Razumikhin, that is, whether he came to talk yesterday on his own or at your prompting? Why, you ought precisely to say that he came on his own and hide that it was at your prompting! And yet you don’t hide it! You actually insist that it was at your prompting!”
Raskolnikov had never insisted on that. A chill ran down his back.

“You keep lying,” he said slowly and weakly, his lips twisted into a sickly smile. “You want to show me again that you know my whole game, that you know all my answers in advance,” he said, himself almost feeling that he was no longer weighing his words as he should, “you want to frighten me... or you are simply laughing at me...”
He went on looking at him point-blank as he said this, and suddenly boundless anger flashed in his eyes again.
“You are lying all the time!” he cried. “You know perfectly well yourself that the best dodge for a criminal is, as far as possible, not to hide what can be left unhidden. I don’t believe you!”

“What a wriggler you are!” giggled Porfiry. “Why, there is no managing you, my dear fellow; some monomania has got hold of you. So you don’t believe me? And I tell you that you already do believe me, you already believe me by a quarter of a yard, and I will make you believe the whole yard, because I truly love you and sincerely wish you well.”
Raskolnikov’s lips trembled.

“Yes, sir, I do, sir, I tell you finally, sir,” he went on, taking Raskolnikov lightly, in a friendly way, by the arm a little above the elbow, “I tell you finally, sir: look after your illness. Besides, your family has come to you now; think of them. You ought to give them peace and tenderness, and you only frighten them...”
“What business is that of yours? How do you know about it? Why are you so interested? So you are watching me and want to show me that?”

“My dear fellow! Why, I learned everything from you, from you yourself! You don’t notice that, in your agitation, you tell everything in advance yourself, both to me and to others. From Mr Razumikhin, Dmitry Prokofich, I also learned many interesting details yesterday. No, sir, you interrupted me, but I will tell you that through your suspiciousness, with all your wit, you have even lost a sound view of things. Well, for example, on the same subject again, about the bells: why, such a precious thing, such a fact (a whole fact, sir!) I handed over to you just like that, bag and baggage, I, the investigator! And you see nothing in that? Why, if I suspected you even a little, is that how I should have acted? On the contrary, I ought first to have lulled your suspicions and not let on that I already knew of this fact; distracted you, like this, in the opposite direction, and then suddenly, as with an axe butt on the crown (in your own expression), stunned you: ‘And what, sir, were you pleased to be doing in the murdered woman’s flat at ten o’clock at night, or even nearly eleven? And why did you ring the bell? And why did you ask about the blood? And why did you confuse the caretakers and invite them to the police station, to the district lieutenant?’ That is how I ought to have acted if I had even a drop of suspicion of you. I ought to have taken a statement from you in full form, made a search, and perhaps even arrested you... So I have no suspicions of you, since I acted otherwise! But you have lost a sound view and don’t see anything, I repeat, sir!”
Raskolnikov started with his whole body, so that Porfiry Petrovich noticed it all too clearly.
“You are lying all the time!” he cried. “I don’t know your purposes, but you are lying all the time... Earlier you weren’t speaking in that sense, and I can’t be mistaken... You are lying!”

“I am lying?” Porfiry took up, apparently growing heated, but keeping the merriest and most mocking air and seeming not in the least worried about what opinion Mr Raskolnikov had of him. “I am lying?.. Well, and how did I treat you earlier (I, the investigator), prompting you myself and handing you all the means of defence, setting out all this psychology for you myself: ‘Illness, he says, delirium, he had been insulted; melancholy and the police officers’, and all the rest of it? Eh? he-he-he! Though, by the way, I will say in passing, all these psychological means of defence, these excuses and dodges, are extremely unsound, and cut both ways: ‘Illness, delirium, dreams, I imagined it, I don’t remember’; all that is so, sir, but why, my dear fellow, in illness and delirium, does one imagine precisely such dreams and not others? There could have been others, couldn’t there, sir? Isn’t that so? He-he-he-he!”
Raskolnikov looked at him proudly and with contempt.

“In a word,” he said insistently and loudly, standing up and pushing Porfiry slightly as he did so, “in a word, I want to know: do you acknowledge me finally free of suspicion or not? Speak, Porfiry Petrovich, speak positively and finally, and quickly, now!”

“What a business! Well, what a business you are,” cried Porfiry with a perfectly merry, sly and not in the least worried air. “And why do you need to know, why do you need to know so much, when they haven’t even begun to trouble you at all! Why, you are like a child: give me, give me fire to hold! And why are you so worried? Why do you keep thrusting yourself on us like this, for what reasons? Eh? he-he-he!”
“I repeat to you,” Raskolnikov cried in fury, “that I cannot bear it any longer...”
“Bear what, sir? The uncertainty?” Porfiry interrupted.
“Don’t sting me! I don’t want it!.. I tell you I don’t want it!.. I can’t and I don’t want to!.. Do you hear! Do you hear!” he shouted, banging his fist on the table again.

“Quieter, quieter! They’ll hear! I warn you seriously: take care of yourself. I am not joking, sir!” said Porfiry in a whisper, but this time there was no longer in his face the womanish good-natured and frightened expression of before; on the contrary, now he was simply giving orders, sternly, frowning, as if at one stroke breaking through all secrets and ambiguities. But that was only for an instant. Raskolnikov, taken aback, suddenly fell into a real frenzy; but strangely: again he obeyed the order to speak more quietly, though he was in the most violent paroxysm of fury.

“I will not let myself be tormented!” he began whispering suddenly as before, realising in an instant, with pain and hatred, that he could not help submitting to the order, and coming to still greater fury at the thought. “Arrest me, search me, but be so good as to act according to form, and not play with me, sir! Don’t you dare...”

“But don’t worry about form,” Porfiry interrupted, with his former sly smile and as if even admiring Raskolnikov with relish. “I have invited you now, my dear fellow, in a homely way, quite in a friendly way, like this!”
“I don’t want your friendship and I spit on it! Do you hear? And here: I take my cap and go. Well, what will you say now, if you mean to arrest me?”
He seized his cap and went to the door.

“But don’t you want to see the little surprise?” giggled Porfiry, again seizing him a little above the elbow and stopping him at the door. He was visibly growing merrier and more playful, which finally drove Raskolnikov beside himself.
“What little surprise? what is it?” he asked, suddenly stopping and looking at Porfiry in fright.

“A little surprise, sir, sitting here behind my door, he-he-he!” (He pointed with his finger at the locked door in the partition, which led to his government lodging.) “I have even locked it, so that it won’t run away.”
“What is it? where? what?..” Raskolnikov went up to the door and wanted to open it, but it was locked.
“It’s locked, sir; here is the key!”
And indeed he showed him the key, taking it out of his pocket.

“You are lying all the time!” Raskolnikov howled, no longer holding back. “You’re lying, you damned Punchinello!” and he flung himself at Porfiry, who was retreating towards the door, but was not in the least frightened.
“I understand everything, everything!” He sprang up to him. “You are lying and teasing me, so that I’ll give myself away...”
“But you can’t give yourself away any further, my dear Rodion Romanych. You have fallen into a frenzy. Don’t shout, or I shall call people, sir!”

“You’re lying, nothing will happen! Call people! You knew I was ill and wanted to irritate me, to the point of fury, so that I would give myself away; that is your purpose! No, produce your facts! I have understood everything! You have no facts, you have only trashy, worthless guesses, Zamyotov’s guesses!.. You knew my character, you wanted to drive me to a frenzy, and then suddenly stun me with priests and deputies... Are you waiting for them? eh? What are you waiting for? Where? Produce them!”

“What deputies, my dear fellow! The things a man will imagine! Why, it is impossible even to act according to form, as you say; you don’t know the business, my dear... But form will not run away, sir, you’ll see for yourself!..” muttered Porfiry, listening at the door.
Indeed, at that moment something like a noise was heard right at the door in the other room.

“Ah, they’re coming!” cried Raskolnikov. “You sent for them!.. You were waiting for them! You calculated... Well, bring them all here: deputies, witnesses, whatever you like... come on! I’m ready! ready!..”
But here a strange incident occurred, something so unexpected in the ordinary course of things that neither Raskolnikov nor Porfiry Petrovich could, of course, have counted on such an outcome.
## CHAPTER VI
Afterwards, when he remembered that moment, it all appeared to Raskolnikov like this.
The noise heard behind the door suddenly grew quickly louder, and the door opened a little.
“What is it?” Porfiry Petrovich shouted in vexation. “I gave orders...”
For a moment there was no answer, but it was evident that there were several people behind the door, and that someone seemed to be being pushed back.
“But what is going on there?” Porfiry Petrovich repeated in alarm.
“They’ve brought the prisoner, Nikolai,” someone’s voice was heard.
“Not now! Away! Wait!.. Why has he got in here! What disorder!” shouted Porfiry, rushing to the door.
“But he...” the same voice began again, and suddenly broke off.

For two seconds, no more, a real struggle went on; then suddenly someone seemed to push someone else away with force, and right after that a very pale man stepped straight into Porfiry Petrovich’s study.

The man’s appearance at first sight was very strange. He was looking straight ahead of him, but as if seeing no one. Resolve flashed in his eyes, but at the same time a deathly pallor covered his face, as if he were being led to execution. His lips, gone quite white, were trembling slightly.

He was still very young, dressed like a common man, of middle height, lean, his hair cut round in the peasant way, with thin, as it were dry, features. The man he had unexpectedly pushed away rushed into the room after him first and managed to seize him by the shoulder: it was the guard; but Nikolai jerked his arm and broke free of him once more.
Several curious people crowded in the doorway. Some of them were trying to get in. All that has been described happened almost in one instant.

“Away, it’s too early! Wait until you are called!.. Why was he brought in before time?” muttered Porfiry Petrovich in extreme vexation, as if thrown off his stride. But Nikolai suddenly went down on his knees.
“What are you doing?” Porfiry shouted in amazement.
“I am guilty! It is my sin! I am the murderer!” Nikolai said suddenly, as if somewhat out of breath, but in a fairly loud voice.
The silence lasted about ten seconds, as if everyone had been struck dumb; even the guard recoiled and no longer came up to Nikolai, but retreated mechanically to the door and stood there motionless.
“What is this?” cried Porfiry Petrovich, coming out of his momentary stupor.
“I... am the murderer...” Nikolai repeated, after a tiny pause.
“How... you... How... Whom did you kill?”
Porfiry Petrovich was obviously at a loss.
Nikolai paused a tiny bit again.
“Alyona Ivanovna and her sister, Lizaveta Ivanovna, I... killed... with an axe. A darkness came over me...” he added suddenly, and was silent again. He was still on his knees.

Porfiry Petrovich stood for a few moments as if thinking it over, but suddenly started up again and waved his arms at the uninvited witnesses. They vanished at once, and the door was shut. Then he looked at Raskolnikov, who was standing in the corner and staring wildly at Nikolai, and started towards him, but suddenly stopped, looked at him, at once moved his eyes to Nikolai, then back to Raskolnikov, then again to Nikolai, and suddenly, as if carried away, fell on Nikolai again.
“Why are you running ahead of me with your darkness?” he shouted at him almost angrily. “I haven’t asked you yet whether a darkness came over you or not... speak: did you kill them?”
“I am the murderer... I am making my statement...” said Nikolai.
“E-eh! What did you kill them with?”
“With an axe. I had it ready.”
“Eh, he’s in a hurry! Alone?”
Nikolai did not understand the question.
“Did you kill them alone?”
“Alone. And Mitka is innocent and had no part in any of it.”
“Don’t be in a hurry with Mitka! E-eh!”
“Then how, well, how did you run down the stairs that time? The caretakers met the two of you, didn’t they?”
“That was to throw them off... then... I ran with Mitka,” Nikolai answered, as if in a hurry and as if he had prepared it in advance.
“Well, so it is!” Porfiry cried angrily. “He is saying words that aren’t his own!” he muttered as if to himself, and suddenly caught sight of Raskolnikov again.
He had evidently been so carried away with Nikolai that for a moment he had even forgotten about Raskolnikov. Now he suddenly recollected himself, and was even embarrassed...
“Rodion Romanovich, my dear fellow! Forgive me, sir,” he rushed to him, “this won’t do, sir; please, sir... there is nothing for you here... I myself... you see what surprises!.. please, sir!..”
And taking him by the arm, he pointed him to the door.
“You didn’t expect this, it seems?” said Raskolnikov, who of course did not yet understand anything clearly, but had already managed to take heart greatly.
“And you didn’t expect it either, my dear fellow. Look how your little hand is trembling! he-he!”
“And you are trembling too, Porfiry Petrovich.”
“And I am trembling, sir; I didn’t expect it, sir!..”
They were already standing in the doorway. Porfiry was waiting impatiently for Raskolnikov to pass.
“And so you won’t show me the little surprise after all?” Raskolnikov said suddenly.
“He says that, and his own little teeth are still chattering in his mouth, he-he! You are an ironical man! Well, sir, until we meet again, sir.”
“For my part, I’ll say goodbye!”
“As God wills, sir, as God wills!” muttered Porfiry, with a smile that was somehow twisted.

As he passed through the office, Raskolnikov noticed that many people looked at him intently. In the hall, in the crowd, he managed to make out both caretakers from that house, whom he had called that night to go to the police officer. They were standing there waiting for something. But just as he came out onto the stairs, he suddenly heard Porfiry Petrovich’s voice behind him again. Turning round, he saw that he was catching up with him, all out of breath.

“One little word, Rodion Romanovich; as for all the rest of this, as God wills, but all the same I shall have to ask you about one or two things in due form, sir... so we shall see each other again, yes, sir.”
And Porfiry stopped in front of him with a smile.
“Yes, sir,” he added once more.
One might have supposed that he wanted to say something more, but somehow it would not come out.
“And you must forgive me, Porfiry Petrovich, about earlier... I lost my temper,” Raskolnikov began, now completely cheered, to the point of an irresistible wish to show off.

“Not at all, sir, not at all...” Porfiry took up almost joyfully. “I myself, sir... I have a venomous character, I confess, I confess! But we shall see each other, sir. If God wills, we shall see a great deal of each other, sir!..”
“And come to know each other finally?” Raskolnikov took up.
“And come to know each other finally,” Porfiry Petrovich agreed, and narrowing his eyes he looked at him very seriously. “Off to a name-day party now, sir?”
“To a funeral, sir.”
“Yes, of course, to a funeral! Take care of your health, your health, sir...”

“And I really don’t know what to wish you, for my part!” Raskolnikov took up; he had already begun to go down the stairs, but suddenly turned back to Porfiry again. “I would wish you great success, but you see what a comical post yours is!”
“Why comical, sir?” Porfiry Petrovich at once pricked up his ears; he too had turned to go.

“Why, of course: that poor Mikolka, how you must have tormented and tortured him, psychologically, in your own way, until he confessed; day and night, I suppose, you were proving to him: ‘You are the murderer, you are the murderer...’; and now that he has confessed, you will begin pulling him to pieces again, bone by bone: ‘You’re lying,’ you’ll say, ‘you are not the murderer! You couldn’t have been! These are not your own words!’ Well, after that, how can your post not be comical?”
“He-he-he! So you noticed that I said just now to Nikolai that he was ‘saying words that aren’t his own’?”
“How could I not notice?”

“He-he! Witty, witty, sir. You notice everything! A real playful mind, sir! And you strike the most comical string... he-he! It was Gogol, among writers, they say, who had that trait in the highest degree?”
“Yes, Gogol.”
“Yes, sir, Gogol, sir... until our most pleasant next meeting, sir.”
“Until our most pleasant next meeting...”

Raskolnikov went straight home. He was so thrown and confused that, having come home and thrown himself on the sofa, he sat for a quarter of an hour only resting and trying to collect his thoughts at least somewhat. He did not even attempt to reason about Nikolai: he felt that he was stunned; that in Nikolai’s confession there was something inexplicable, astonishing, which he could not possibly understand now. But Nikolai’s confession was a real fact. The consequences of this fact became clear to him at once: the lie could not fail to be discovered, and then they would set about him again. But at least until then he was free, and he must certainly do something for himself, because the danger was inevitable.

But, then, to what degree? The situation was beginning to clear. Recalling roughly, as a whole, his whole scene with Porfiry earlier, he could not help shuddering with horror once more. Of course he did not yet know all Porfiry’s purposes, could not grasp all his calculations of earlier. But part of the game had been revealed, and surely no one could understand better than he how terrible for him this “move” in Porfiry’s game had been. A little more, and he might have given himself away completely, in fact. Knowing the morbidity of his character, and having grasped and seen through it correctly at first sight, Porfiry had acted, though too decisively, almost surely. There was no denying that Raskolnikov had already compromised himself too much earlier, but it had still not come to facts; it was all still only relative. But was he, however, was he understanding all this correctly now? Wasn’t he mistaken? What result exactly had Porfiry been driving at today? Had he really had something prepared today? And what exactly? Had he really been waiting for something or not? How exactly would they have parted today, if the unexpected catastrophe through Nikolai had not come about?

Porfiry had shown almost his whole game; of course he had taken a risk, but he had shown it, and (so it all seemed to Raskolnikov) if Porfiry really had had anything more, he would have shown that too. What was this “surprise”? A mockery? Did it mean something or not? Could there be hidden under it even anything like a fact, a positive accusation? Yesterday’s man? Where had he vanished to? Where had he been today? For if Porfiry had anything positive, it was surely connected with yesterday’s man...

He sat on the sofa with his head hanging down, his elbows on his knees and his face in his hands. A nervous trembling still went on through his whole body. At last he stood up, took his cap, thought, and went towards the door.

He somehow had a feeling that, at least for today, he could almost certainly consider himself safe. Suddenly he felt almost joy in his heart: he wanted to go quickly to Katerina Ivanovna’s. He was too late for the funeral, of course, but he would be in time for the memorial meal, and there, now, he would see Sonya.
He stopped, thought, and a sickly smile forced itself onto his lips.
“Today! Today!” he repeated to himself. “Yes, this very day! It must be so...”

Just as he was about to open the door, it suddenly began to open by itself. He trembled and sprang back. The door opened slowly and quietly, and suddenly a figure appeared: yesterday’s man from under the ground.

The man stopped on the threshold, looked silently at Raskolnikov and took one step into the room. He was exactly as yesterday, the same figure, dressed the same way, but a great change had taken place in his face and in his look: he looked somehow sorrowful now, and after standing a little, he sighed deeply. All he needed was to put his palm to his cheek and tilt his head to one side to look completely like a peasant woman.
“What do you want?” asked Raskolnikov, numb with dread.
The man was silent, and suddenly bowed to him deeply, almost to the ground. At least he touched the ground with a finger of his right hand.
“What are you doing?” cried Raskolnikov.
“I am guilty,” the man said quietly.
“Of what?”
“Of wicked thoughts.”
They both looked at each other.

“I felt aggrieved. When you were pleased to come that time, in drink perhaps, and called the caretakers to the police and asked about the blood, I felt aggrieved that they let it go for nothing and took you for a drunk. And I felt so aggrieved that I lost my sleep. And having remembered the address, we came here yesterday and asked...”
“Who came?” Raskolnikov interrupted, instantly beginning to remember.
“I did, that is; I wronged you.”
“So you are from that house?”

“Why, I was standing right there with them at the gate that time, or have you forgotten? We have our trade there, from long ago. We are furriers, tradespeople, we take work home... and most of all I felt aggrieved...”

And suddenly Raskolnikov clearly remembered the whole scene in the gateway two days before; he realised that besides the caretakers several other people had been standing there then, women too. He remembered one voice suggesting that he be taken straight to the police. He could not remember the speaker’s face and did not recognise it even now, but he remembered that he had even answered him something then, had turned towards him...

So this, then, was how all yesterday’s horror had resolved itself. Most terrible of all was to think that he really had nearly perished, nearly destroyed himself, because of such a trifling circumstance. So, apart from the renting of the flat and the talk about the blood, this man could tell nothing. So Porfiry too had nothing, nothing but this delirium, no facts except psychology, which cuts both ways, nothing positive. So, if no more facts appeared (and they must not appear any more, they must not, they must not!), then... then what could they do to him? How could they finally convict him, even if they arrested him? And so Porfiry had learned about the flat only now, only just now, and had not known until then.
“Was it you who told Porfiry today... that I had been there?” he cried, struck by a sudden idea.
“What Porfiry?”
“The investigating magistrate.”
“I told him. The caretakers didn’t go then, so I went.”
“Today?”
“I was there just a minute before you. And I heard everything, everything, how he tormented you.”
“Where? What? When?”
“Why, right there, behind his partition; I sat there the whole time.”
“What? So you were the surprise? But how could that have happened? Good heavens!”

“Seeing,” the tradesman began, “that the caretakers didn’t want to go on my word, because, they said, it was already late, and perhaps he would be angry that they hadn’t come at the time, I felt aggrieved, and lost my sleep, and began to find things out. And having found out yesterday, I went today. The first time I came, he wasn’t there. I came an hour later, they wouldn’t admit me; the third time I came, they let me in. I began to report everything to him, how it was, and he began leaping about the room and beating his breast with his fist: ‘What are you doing to me, you robbers?’ he says. ‘If I had known of such a thing, I would have had him fetched under guard!’ Then he ran out, called someone and began talking with him in the corner, and then came back to me, and began asking and scolding. And he reproached me a lot; and I reported everything to him, and said that you didn’t dare answer me anything to my words yesterday and that you didn’t recognise me. And then he began running about again, and kept beating his breast, and was angry, and ran about, and when you were announced, ‘Well,’ he says, ‘get behind the partition, sit there for now, don’t move, whatever you hear,’ and he brought me a chair there himself and locked me in; ‘perhaps,’ he says, ‘I shall ask you.’ And when they brought Nikolai, then, after you, he let me out: ‘I shall send for you again,’ he says, ‘and question you again...’”
“And did he question Nikolai in front of you?”
“As soon as he let you out, he let me out at once too, and began questioning Nikolai.”
The tradesman stopped and suddenly bowed again, touching the floor with his finger.
“Forgive me for the slander and for my wickedness.”

“God will forgive,” answered Raskolnikov, and as soon as he had said it, the tradesman bowed to him, but not to the ground this time, only from the waist, slowly turned and went out of the room. “Everything cuts both ways, now everything cuts both ways,” Raskolnikov repeated, and went out of the room more cheerful than ever.
“Now we shall fight on,” he said with a malicious smile as he went down the stairs. The malice, though, was directed at himself: he remembered his “faint-heartedness” with contempt and shame.
## CHAPTER III

“Pyotr Petrovich!” she cried. “You at least protect me! Make this stupid creature understand that she dare not treat a gentlewoman in misfortune like this, that there is a law for it... I’ll go to the Governor-General himself... She will answer for it... Remembering my father’s hospitality, protect the orphans.”

“Allow me, madam... Allow me, allow me, madam,” Pyotr Petrovich waved her off. “Your papa, as you know, I never had the honour of knowing... allow me, madam!” (someone laughed loudly) “and I have no intention of taking part in your incessant quarrels with Amalia Ivanovna, madam... I have come on my own business... and I wish to have an explanation, immediately, with your stepdaughter, Sofya... Ivanovna... I believe that is right, madam? Allow me to pass, madam...”
And Pyotr Petrovich, edging round Katerina Ivanovna, made his way to the opposite corner, where Sonya was.

Katerina Ivanovna stayed where she was, as if thunderstruck. She could not understand how Pyotr Petrovich could disown her papa’s hospitality. Having once invented this hospitality, she now believed in it devoutly herself. She was struck too by Pyotr Petrovich’s businesslike, dry tone, full even of a kind of contemptuous threat. And everyone grew somehow quieter little by little at his appearance. Besides the fact that this “businesslike and serious” man was far too sharply out of harmony with the whole company, it was evident too that he had come about something important, that probably some extraordinary reason could have drawn him into such company, and that, therefore, something was about to happen, something was coming. Raskolnikov, who was standing beside Sonya, moved aside to let him pass; Pyotr Petrovich seemed not to notice him at all. A minute later Lebezyatnikov also appeared on the threshold; he did not come into the room, but stopped there too, with a kind of special curiosity, almost with surprise; he listened, but for a long time seemed unable to understand something.

“Excuse me if I am perhaps interrupting, but the matter is rather important, madam,” Pyotr Petrovich remarked to the room in general, not addressing anyone in particular. “I am even glad that there is an audience. Amalia Ivanovna, I most humbly request you, as landlady of the flat, to pay attention to the conversation I am about to have with Sofya Ivanovna. Sofya Ivanovna,” he went on, turning straight to Sonya, who was extremely surprised and already frightened in advance, “immediately after your visit, a hundred-rouble government banknote belonging to me disappeared from my table, in the room of my friend, Andrei Semyonovich Lebezyatnikov. If in any way whatever you know and will show us where it is now, then I assure you on my word of honour, and I call everyone to witness, that the matter will end there. Otherwise I shall be forced to resort to very serious measures, and then... you will have only yourself to blame, madam!”

Complete silence reigned in the room. Even the crying children fell quiet. Sonya stood deathly pale, looking at Luzhin, and could not answer anything. She seemed not yet to understand. Several seconds passed.
“Well, madam, what then, madam?” asked Luzhin, looking at her intently.
“I don’t know... I don’t know anything...” Sonya said at last in a weak voice.

“No? You don’t know?” Luzhin asked again, and was silent for a few more seconds. “Think, mademoiselle,” he began sternly, but still as if admonishing her, “consider; I am willing to give you more time to reflect. Kindly see, madam: if I were not so sure, then of course, with my experience, I would not have risked accusing you so directly; for a direct and public accusation of this kind, if false or even only mistaken, I am, in a certain sense, myself answerable. I know that, madam. This morning I changed, for my own needs, several five-per-cent bonds for a sum of, nominally, three thousand roubles. The account is written down in my pocketbook. On coming home, I (Andrei Semyonovich is witness to it) began counting the money, and having counted two thousand three hundred roubles, I put them in my pocketbook and the pocketbook in the side pocket of my frock coat. About five hundred roubles were left on the table, in banknotes, and among them three notes of a hundred roubles each. At that moment you arrived (at my invitation), and all the time you were with me afterwards you were in extreme confusion, so that three times, in the middle of the conversation, you even stood up and hurried for some reason to leave, although our conversation was not yet finished. Andrei Semyonovich can testify to all this. Probably you yourself, mademoiselle, will not refuse to confirm and declare that I invited you, through Andrei Semyonovich, solely in order to talk with you about the orphaned and helpless position of your relative, Katerina Ivanovna (whose memorial dinner I could not attend), and about how useful it would be to arrange something for her benefit, a kind of subscription, a lottery or the like. You thanked me and even shed tears (I am telling everything as it was, in the first place to remind you, and in the second to show you that not the slightest detail has been erased from my memory). Then I took a ten-rouble note from the table and gave it to you, in my own name, for the interests of your relative and by way of first relief. Andrei Semyonovich saw all this. Then I saw you to the door, all in the same confusion on your part, after which, remaining alone with Andrei Semyonovich and talking with him for about ten minutes, Andrei Semyonovich went out, and I turned again to the table with the money lying on it, intending to count it and put it aside separately, as I had planned before. To my surprise, one hundred-rouble note was missing among the rest. Kindly judge for yourselves: I cannot possibly suspect Andrei Semyonovich, madam; I am ashamed even of the supposition. Nor could I have made a mistake in counting, because a minute before your arrival, having finished all my accounts, I found the total correct. You will agree yourselves that, remembering your confusion, your haste to leave, and the fact that you kept your hands on the table for some time; taking into consideration, finally, your social position and the habits associated with it, I was, so to speak, with horror, and even against my will, forced to settle on a suspicion: a cruel one, of course, but a just one, madam! I will add, and repeat, that in spite of all my evident certainty, I understand that there is nonetheless some risk for me in my present accusation. But, as you see, I have not let it pass; I have risen up, and I will tell you why: solely, madam, solely on account of your blackest ingratitude! What? I invite you in the interests of your poorest relative, I give you my modest alms of ten roubles, and you, right there, right then, repay me for all this with such an act! No, madam, that is not good, madam! A lesson is needed, madam. Think it over; what’s more, as your true friend, I beg you (for you can have no better friend at this moment), come to your senses! Otherwise I shall be relentless! Well, madam, then?”

“I didn’t take anything from you,” Sonya whispered in horror. “You gave me ten roubles; here, take them.” Sonya took her handkerchief out of her pocket, found the knot, untied it, took out the ten-rouble note and held out her hand to Luzhin.
“And you still won’t admit to the other hundred roubles?” he said reproachfully and insistently, not accepting the note.

Sonya looked round. Everyone was looking at her with such terrible, stern, mocking, hateful faces. She glanced at Raskolnikov... he was standing by the wall, his arms crossed, looking at her with a fiery look.
“Oh Lord!” broke from Sonya.
“Amalia Ivanovna, it will be necessary to inform the police, and so I most humbly ask you to send for the caretaker for the time being,” Luzhin said quietly and even gently.
“Gott der Barmherzige! I knew it zat she vas stealing!” Amalia Ivanovna clasped her hands.
“You knew it?” Luzhin took it up. “Then you already had some grounds before for concluding so. I ask you, most worthy Amalia Ivanovna, to remember your words, uttered, moreover, before witnesses.”
A loud hubbub suddenly arose on all sides. Everyone began to stir.

“Wha-a-at!” Katerina Ivanovna cried out suddenly, coming to herself, and, as if breaking loose, rushed at Luzhin. “What! You accuse her of theft? Sonya? Ah, scoundrels, scoundrels!” And rushing to Sonya, she embraced her with her withered arms as in a vice.
“Sonya! How dared you take ten roubles from him! Oh, you silly girl! Give them here! Give me those ten roubles at once, there!”

And snatching the note from Sonya, Katerina Ivanovna crumpled it in her hands and flung it back-handed straight into Luzhin’s face. The little ball hit him in the eye and bounced onto the floor. Amalia Ivanovna rushed to pick up the money. Pyotr Petrovich lost his temper.
“Restrain this madwoman!” he shouted.
At that moment several more faces appeared in the doorway beside Lebezyatnikov, among whom both of the visiting ladies were peeping in.

“What! Madwoman? I am a madwoman? You fo-ol!” shrieked Katerina Ivanovna. “You are a fool yourself, you pettifogger, you low man! Sonya, Sonya take money from him! Sonya a thief! Why, she would give you money herself, you fool!” And Katerina Ivanovna laughed hysterically. “Have you ever seen such a fool?” she rushed in all directions, pointing Luzhin out to everyone. “What! And you too?” she caught sight of the landlady. “And you join in too, you sausage-seller, confirming that she ‘vas stealing’, you vile Prussian chicken leg in a crinoline! Oh, you! Oh, you! Why, she didn’t even leave the room, and when she came back from you, you scoundrel, she sat down right here beside Rodion Romanovich!.. Search her! If she didn’t go anywhere, then the money must be on her! Search, then, search, search! Only if you don’t find it, then excuse me, my dear, you will answer for it! I’ll run to the sovereign, to the sovereign, to the merciful tsar himself, I’ll throw myself at his feet, at once, this very day! I am an orphan! They will let me in! You think they won’t? You’re lying, I’ll get there! I’ll get the-ere! Were you counting on her being meek? Was that what you relied on? But I, brother, am no meek one! You’ll come to grief! Search, then! Search, search, go on, search!!”
And Katerina Ivanovna, in a frenzy, was tugging at Luzhin, dragging him towards Sonya.

“I am ready, madam, and I answer for it... but calm yourself, madam, calm yourself! I see all too well that you are no meek one!.. This... this... how is this to be done, madam?” muttered Luzhin. “This ought to be done in the presence of the police, madam... though, however, even now there are more than enough witnesses... I am ready, madam... But in any case it is awkward for a man... on account of sex... If with the help of Amalia Ivanovna... though, however, things are not done like this... How is this to be done, madam?”

“Whoever you like! Let whoever wants to search her!” shouted Katerina Ivanovna. “Sonya, turn out your pockets for them! There, there! Look, you monster, here, it’s empty, my handkerchief was here, the pocket is empty, you see! Here is the other pocket, here, here! You see! You see!”

And Katerina Ivanovna did not so much turn out as pull out both pockets, one after the other. But from the second, right-hand pocket a piece of paper suddenly jumped out and, describing a parabola in the air, fell at Luzhin’s feet. Everyone saw it; many cried out. Pyotr Petrovich bent down, picked up the paper from the floor with two fingers, held it up for everyone to see and unfolded it. It was a hundred-rouble banknote, folded in eight. Pyotr Petrovich moved his hand round in a circle, showing everyone the note.
“Thief! Out of ze rooms! Police, police!” howled Amalia Ivanovna. “Zey must be chased to Siberia! Out!”

Exclamations flew from all sides. Raskolnikov was silent, not taking his eyes off Sonya, now and then, but quickly, moving them to Luzhin. Sonya stood on the same spot as if unconscious: she was hardly even surprised. Suddenly colour flooded her whole face; she cried out and hid her face in her hands.

“No, it wasn’t me! I didn’t take it! I don’t know!” she cried with a heartrending wail, and rushed to Katerina Ivanovna. Katerina Ivanovna seized her and pressed her tightly to herself, as if wishing to shield her from everyone with her breast.

“Sonya! Sonya! I don’t believe it! You see, I don’t believe it!” cried Katerina Ivanovna (in spite of all the evidence), shaking her in her arms like a child, kissing her countless times, catching her hands and, simply fastening on them, kissing them. “That you would take it! What stupid people these are! Oh Lord! You are stupid, stupid,” she cried, turning to everyone. “Why, you don’t know yet, you don’t know what a heart this is, what a girl this is! She take it, she! Why, she would take off her last dress, sell it, go barefoot, and give it to you if you needed it, that is what she is like! She even got the yellow ticket because my children were dying of hunger; she sold herself for us!.. Ah, my late husband, my late husband! Ah, my late husband! Do you see? Do you see? Here is your memorial dinner! Lord! But protect her, why are you all standing there! Rodion Romanovich! Why don’t you stand up for her? Do you believe it too? You are not worth her little finger, all of you, all, all, all! Lord! Protect her, at last!”

The weeping of the poor, consumptive, orphaned Katerina Ivanovna seemed to produce a strong effect on the public. There was so much that was pitiful, so much suffering, in this withered consumptive face distorted with pain, in these parched lips caked with blood, in this hoarsely shouting voice, in this sobbing like a child’s crying, in this trusting, childlike and at the same time desperate plea to protect her, that, it seemed, everyone pitied the unhappy woman. At any rate Pyotr Petrovich at once pitied her.

“Madam! Madam!” he exclaimed in an impressive voice. “This fact does not concern you! No one would venture to accuse you of intent or complicity, the more so since it was you who discovered it, by turning out the pocket: so you suspected nothing. I am very, very ready to feel sorry if, so to speak, poverty drove Sofya Semyonovna to it too; but why, mademoiselle, did you not want to confess? Were you afraid of the shame? The first step? Perhaps you lost your head? It is understandable, madam; very understandable, madam... But all the same, why go in for such things! Gentlemen!” he turned to all present. “Gentlemen! Feeling sorry and, so to speak, sympathising, I am perhaps prepared to forgive, even now, in spite of the personal insults I have received. Let this present shame, mademoiselle, serve as a lesson to you for the future,” he turned to Sonya, “and I will let the rest go and, so be it, I drop the matter. Enough!”

Pyotr Petrovich gave a sidelong look at Raskolnikov. Their eyes met. Raskolnikov’s burning look was ready to reduce him to ashes. Meanwhile Katerina Ivanovna seemed not to hear anything more: she was embracing and kissing Sonya like a madwoman. The children too had clasped Sonya from all sides with their little arms, and Polechka, who did not quite understand, however, what the matter was, seemed to have drowned completely in tears, breaking down in sobs and hiding her pretty little face, swollen with crying, on Sonya’s shoulder.
“How base!” a loud voice rang out suddenly in the doorway.
Pyotr Petrovich looked round quickly.
“What baseness!” repeated Lebezyatnikov, looking him intently in the eyes.
Pyotr Petrovich even seemed to start. Everyone noticed it. (They remembered it afterwards.) Lebezyatnikov stepped into the room.
“And you dared to put me down as a witness?” he said, going up to Pyotr Petrovich.
“What does this mean, Andrei Semyonovich? What are you talking about?” muttered Luzhin.

“It means that you are... a slanderer; that is what my words mean!” Lebezyatnikov said hotly, looking at him sternly with his short-sighted little eyes. He was terribly angry. Raskolnikov fastened his eyes on him, as if catching up and weighing every word. Again silence reigned. Pyotr Petrovich was almost at a loss, especially in the first moment.
“If you are saying this to me...” he began, stammering. “But what is the matter with you? Are you in your right mind?”

“I am in my right mind, sir, but you are... a swindler! Ah, how base this is! I have been listening to everything; I waited on purpose so as to understand everything, because, I confess, even now it is not quite logical... But why you did all this, I don’t understand.”
“But what have I done! Will you stop talking in your absurd riddles! Or perhaps you have been drinking?”

“It is you, you low man, who may drink, not I! I never drink vodka at all, because it is not in my convictions! Imagine, he, he himself, with his own hands, gave this hundred-rouble note to Sofya Semyonovna; I saw it, I am a witness, I will take an oath! He did, he did!” repeated Lebezyatnikov, turning to each and everyone.

“Have you gone mad or not, you milksop?” shrieked Luzhin. “She is here herself before you, in person; she herself, here, just now, in front of everyone, confirmed that apart from ten roubles she received nothing from me. How could I have given it to her, after that?”

“I saw it, I saw it!” Lebezyatnikov shouted and insisted. “And though it is against my convictions, I am ready this very hour to take any oath you like in court, because I saw how you slipped it to her quietly! Only I, fool that I am, thought you slipped it to her out of charity! In the doorway, saying goodbye to her, when she turned round and you were pressing her hand with one hand, with the other, the left, you put the paper quietly into her pocket. I saw it! I saw it!”
Luzhin turned pale.
“What lies you are telling!” he cried insolently. “And how could you, standing by the window, make out the paper? You imagined it... with your short-sighted eyes. You are raving!”

“No, I did not imagine it! And though I was standing far off, I saw everything, everything, and though from the window it is really hard to make out a paper (you are right about that), I knew for certain, owing to a special circumstance, that it was precisely a hundred-rouble note, because when you began giving Sofya Semyonovna the ten-rouble note (I saw it myself), you took a hundred-rouble note from the table at the same time (I saw that, because I was standing close by then, and because a certain thought came to me at once, I did not forget that you had a note in your hand). You folded it and kept it squeezed in your hand all the time. Then I forgot again, but when you began to get up, you moved it from your right hand to your left and nearly dropped it; then I remembered again, because the same thought came to me again, namely that you wanted to do her a kindness without my knowing. You can imagine how I began to watch, and so I saw how you managed to slip it into her pocket. I saw it, I saw it, I will take an oath!”

Lebezyatnikov was almost choking. Various exclamations began to ring out from all sides, mostly expressing surprise; but there were also exclamations that took on a threatening tone. Everyone pressed in around Pyotr Petrovich. Katerina Ivanovna rushed to Lebezyatnikov.
“Andrei Semyonovich! I was wrong about you! Protect her! You alone are for her! She is an orphan; God has sent you! Andrei Semyonovich, my dear, my good man!”
And Katerina Ivanovna, hardly knowing what she was doing, threw herself on her knees before him.

“Rubbish!” howled Luzhin, enraged to fury. “It’s rubbish you keep grinding out, sir. ‘I forgot, I remembered, I forgot’: what is that! So I planted it on her on purpose? Why? For what purpose? What have I in common with this...”

“Why? That is just what I don’t understand myself, but that I am telling a true fact, that is certain! I am so far from mistaken, you vile, criminal man, that I remember precisely how a question came into my head at once about it, just at the moment when I was thanking you and shaking your hand. Why exactly did you put it into her pocket stealthily? That is, why exactly stealthily? Was it only because you wanted to hide it from me, knowing that I hold opposite convictions and reject private charity, which cures nothing radically? Well, and I decided that you really were ashamed before me to hand out such sums, and besides, perhaps, I thought, he wants to give her a surprise, to astonish her when she finds a whole hundred roubles in her pocket. (Because some philanthropists are very fond of spreading out their good deeds like that; I know.) Then it also occurred to me that you wanted to test her, that is, whether she would come to thank you on finding it. Then, that you wanted to avoid gratitude and so that, well, how does the saying go: so that the right hand, or something, should not know... in a word, something like that... Well, all sorts of thoughts came into my head then, so that I resolved to think it all over later, but all the same I considered it indelicate to reveal to you that I knew the secret. But then, however, another question came into my head at once: that Sofya Semyonovna, before she noticed, might, for all one knows, lose the money; that is why I decided to come here, call her out and let her know that a hundred roubles had been put in her pocket. But on the way I first called at the room of the Kobylyatnikov ladies, to take them The General Conclusion of the Positive Method and especially to recommend Piderit’s article (and also Wagner’s, by the way); then I come here, and look what a story is going on! Well, could I, could I have had all these thoughts and reasonings if I had not really seen that you put a hundred roubles into her pocket?”

When Andrei Semyonovich had finished his long-winded reasoning, with such a logical deduction at the end of his speech, he was terribly tired, and sweat was even running down his face. Alas, he could not even express himself properly in Russian (though he knew no other language), so that he was all somehow exhausted at once, and even seemed to have grown thinner after his lawyer’s feat. Nevertheless his speech produced an extraordinary effect. He spoke with such passion, with such conviction, that evidently everyone believed him. Pyotr Petrovich felt that things were going badly.

“What business is it of mine that some stupid questions came into your head?” he cried. “That is no proof, sir! You could have dreamed it all in your sleep, that’s all, sir! And I tell you that you are lying, sir! Lying and slandering out of some spite against me, and precisely out of pique because I would not agree to your free-thinking and godless social proposals, that’s what it is, sir!”
But this dodge did Pyotr Petrovich no good. On the contrary, a murmur arose on all sides.

“Ah, so that’s where you’re heading!” shouted Lebezyatnikov. “You’re lying! Call the police, and I will take an oath! Only one thing I can’t understand: why he risked such a base act! Oh, pitiful, vile man!”
“I can explain why he risked such an act, and, if necessary, I will take an oath myself!” Raskolnikov said at last in a firm voice, and stepped forward.
He was apparently firm and calm. It somehow became clear to everyone, at a single look at him, that he really knew what the matter was, and that things had come to the denouement.

“Now I have made everything completely clear to myself,” Raskolnikov went on, turning straight to Lebezyatnikov. “From the very beginning of this business I had begun to suspect that there was some vile trick here; I began to suspect it because of certain special circumstances, known only to me, which I will now explain to everyone: the whole matter lies in them! And you, Andrei Semyonovich, with your precious testimony, have finally made everything clear to me. I ask everyone, everyone, to listen: this gentleman” (he pointed to Luzhin) “recently sought the hand of a certain girl, and precisely of my sister, Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikova. But on arriving in Petersburg, two days ago, at our first meeting, he quarrelled with me, and I drove him out of my room, of which there are two witnesses. This man is very spiteful... Two days ago I did not yet know that he was lodging here, in your rooms, Andrei Semyonovich, and that, therefore, on the very day we quarrelled, that is, two days ago, he witnessed how I gave, as a friend of the late Mr Marmeladov, some money to his wife Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral. He at once wrote a note to my mother and informed her that I had given all the money not to Katerina Ivanovna but to Sofya Semyonovna, and in doing so he referred in the vilest terms to... to Sofya Semyonovna’s character, that is, he hinted at the character of my relations with Sofya Semyonovna. All this, as you understand, with the aim of setting me at odds with my mother and sister, by suggesting to them that I am squandering, for ignoble purposes, their last money, with which they help me. Last night, before my mother and sister, and in his presence, I re-established the truth, proving that I had given the money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, and not to Sofya Semyonovna, and that two days ago I was not even acquainted with Sofya Semyonovna and had not even seen her face. At the same time I added that he, Pyotr Petrovich Luzhin, with all his merits, was not worth Sofya Semyonovna’s little finger, of whom he speaks so ill. And to his question whether I would seat Sofya Semyonovna beside my sister, I answered that I had already done so, that same day. Infuriated that my mother and sister would not quarrel with me on the strength of his slanders, he began, word by word, to say unforgivably insolent things to them. A final break took place, and he was turned out of the house. All this happened last night. Now I ask for special attention: imagine that if he had now succeeded in proving that Sofya Semyonovna was a thief, then, in the first place, he would have proved to my sister and mother that he had been almost right in his suspicions; that he had justly been angry at my putting my sister and Sofya Semyonovna on the same level; that, in attacking me, he had therefore been defending and safeguarding the honour of my sister, his bride. In a word, by all this he could even have set me at odds with my family again, and of course he hoped to get back into their good graces. Not to mention that he was taking revenge on me personally, because he has grounds for supposing that the honour and happiness of Sofya Semyonovna are very dear to me. That is his whole calculation! That is how I understand this business! That is the whole reason, and there can be no other!”

So, or almost so, Raskolnikov ended his speech, which was often interrupted by exclamations from the audience, who nevertheless listened very attentively. But in spite of all the interruptions, he spoke sharply, calmly, precisely, clearly, firmly. His sharp voice, his tone of conviction and his stern face produced an extraordinary effect on everyone.

“Yes, yes, that’s it!” Lebezyatnikov confirmed in rapture. “It must be so, because he asked me precisely, as soon as Sofya Semyonovna came into our room, ‘are you here? Had I seen you among Katerina Ivanovna’s guests?’ He called me over to the window for that and asked me there quietly. So he absolutely needed you to be here! That’s it, that’s all it is!”

Luzhin was silent and smiled contemptuously. He was very pale, however. He seemed to be considering how to wriggle out of it. Perhaps he would gladly have dropped everything and left, but at the present moment that was almost impossible; it would have meant openly admitting the justice of the accusations brought against him and that he really had slandered Sofya Semyonovna. Besides, the audience, already tipsy enough as it was, was too agitated. The commissariat clerk, though he did not understand everything, shouted loudest of all and proposed certain measures very unpleasant for Luzhin. But there were sober people too; people had come and gathered from all the rooms. All three little Poles were terribly heated and kept shouting at him: “Pan lajdak! Mister scoundrel!”, and muttering some threats in Polish besides. Sonya listened intently, but she too seemed not to understand everything, as if she were waking from a faint. She only did not take her eyes off Raskolnikov, feeling that all her protection lay in him. Katerina Ivanovna was breathing with difficulty and hoarsely, and seemed to be in terrible exhaustion. Most foolish of all stood Amalia Ivanovna, with her mouth open, understanding absolutely nothing. She only saw that Pyotr Petrovich had somehow been caught. Raskolnikov asked to speak again, but they no longer let him finish: everyone was shouting and pressing around Luzhin with curses and threats. But Pyotr Petrovich did not lose his nerve. Seeing that the case of the accusation against Sonya was completely lost, he resorted straight to insolence.

“Allow me, gentlemen, allow me; don’t crowd, let me pass!” he said, making his way through the crowd. “And do me the favour of not threatening; I assure you that nothing will come of it, you will do nothing; I am not one of the timid sort, sir; on the contrary, it is you, gentlemen, who will answer for having covered up a criminal case by violence. The thief has been more than exposed, and I shall prosecute, sir. In court they are not so blind and... not so drunk, sir, and they will not believe two notorious atheists, agitators and free-thinkers, who accuse me out of personal revenge, which they themselves, in their stupidity, admit... Yes, sir, allow me, sir!”

“See that not a whiff of you is left in my room at once; kindly move out, and everything between us is over! And when I think that I was jumping out of my skin, explaining things to him... for two whole weeks!..”

“But I told you myself earlier, Andrei Semyonovich, that I was moving out, when you were still trying to keep me; now I will only add that you are a fool, sir. I wish you a cure for your mind and your short-sighted eyes. Allow me, gentlemen, sir!”

He pushed his way through; but the commissariat clerk did not want to let him go so easily, with mere curses: he seized a glass from the table, swung his arm and hurled it at Pyotr Petrovich; but the glass flew straight at Amalia Ivanovna. She shrieked, and the commissariat clerk, losing his balance from the swing, fell heavily under the table. Pyotr Petrovich went to his own room, and within half an hour he was no longer in the house. Sonya, timid by nature, had known before that it was easier to ruin her than anyone else, and that anyone could offend her almost with impunity. But all the same, up to this very moment, it had seemed to her that disaster could somehow be avoided: by caution, by meekness, by submissiveness before each and everyone. Her disillusionment was too heavy. She could, of course, bear everything with patience and almost without complaint, even this. But in the first moment it was too heavy. In spite of her triumph and her vindication, when the first fright and the first stupor had passed, when she understood and grasped everything clearly, a feeling of helplessness and injury wrung her heart tormentingly. She became hysterical. At last, unable to bear it, she rushed out of the room and ran home. This was almost immediately after Luzhin’s departure. Amalia Ivanovna, when the glass hit her amid the loud laughter of those present, also could not bear paying for someone else’s feast. With a shriek, like a madwoman, she rushed at Katerina Ivanovna, considering her to blame for everything:

“Out of ze rooms! At vonce! March!” And with these words she began seizing everything of Katerina Ivanovna’s that came to hand and throwing it on the floor. Almost crushed as it was, nearly fainting, gasping, pale, Katerina Ivanovna sprang up from the bed (on which she had fallen in exhaustion) and rushed at Amalia Ivanovna. But the struggle was too unequal; the landlady pushed her away like a feather.

“What! Not enough that they have slandered us so godlessly, this creature is at me too! What!
