On the day of my husband’s funeral I am turned out of my lodging, after my hospitality, into the street, with orphans! But where am I to go!” the poor woman wailed, sobbing and gasping. “Lord!” she cried suddenly, her eyes flashing, “can it be that there is no justice! Whom are you to protect, if not us, orphans? But we shall see! There is judgement and truth in the world, there is, I shall find it! At once, wait, you godless creature! Polechka, stay with the children, I’ll come back. Wait for me, even in the street! We shall see whether there is truth in the world!”

And throwing over her head that same green drap-de-dames shawl which the late Marmeladov had mentioned in his story, Katerina Ivanovna pushed her way through the disorderly drunken crowd of lodgers, still crowding the room, and ran out into the street wailing and in tears, with the vague purpose of finding justice somewhere, now, at once, and at whatever cost. Polechka, in fright, huddled with the children in a corner on the trunk, where, embracing the two little ones and trembling all over, she began to wait for her mother to come back. Amalia Ivanovna rushed about the room, shrieking, lamenting, flinging everything that came her way on the floor, and raging. The lodgers bawled at random, every one in his own key: some were finishing saying what they could about the incident; others were quarrelling and swearing; some struck up songs...
“And now it is time for me!” thought Raskolnikov. “Well, Sofya Semyonovna, let us see what you will say now!”
And he set off for Sonya’s lodging.
## CHAPTER IV

Raskolnikov had been an active and spirited advocate for Sonya against Luzhin, in spite of carrying so much horror and suffering of his own in his soul. But after suffering so much that morning, he was as if glad of the chance to change his impressions, which were becoming unbearable, not to speak of how much that was personal and heartfelt lay in his impulse to stand up for Sonya. Besides, he had in view, and it alarmed him terribly, especially at moments, the coming meeting with Sonya: he had to tell her who had killed Lizaveta, and he foresaw a terrible torment for himself, and was as if waving it away with his hands. And so, when he exclaimed as he left Katerina Ivanovna’s, “Well, what will you say now, Sofya Semyonovna?”, he was evidently still in a kind of outwardly excited state of high spirits, defiance and his recent victory over Luzhin. But a strange thing happened to him. When he reached Kapernaumov’s lodging, he felt a sudden loss of strength and fear. He stopped before the door in thought, with a strange question: “Must I tell who killed Lizaveta?” The question was strange because at the same time he suddenly felt that not only was it impossible not to tell, but it was impossible even to put off the moment, even for a while. He did not yet know why it was impossible; he only felt it, and this tormenting awareness of his helplessness before necessity almost crushed him. So as not to reason and torment himself any more, he quickly opened the door and looked at Sonya from the threshold. She was sitting with her elbows on the little table and her face in her hands, but seeing Raskolnikov she got up quickly and went to meet him, as if she had been waiting for him.

“What would have become of me without you!” she said quickly, meeting him in the middle of the room. Evidently that was all she wanted to say to him as quickly as possible. That was why she had been waiting.
Raskolnikov went to the table and sat down on the chair from which she had just risen. She stood before him two steps away, exactly as yesterday.
“Well, Sonya?” he said, and suddenly felt that his voice was trembling. “The whole thing rested on ‘social position and the habits associated with it’. Did you understand that earlier?”
Suffering showed in her face.
“Only don’t talk to me as you did yesterday!” she interrupted him. “Please, don’t begin. There is enough torment as it is...”
She smiled quickly, frightened that he might not like the reproach.
“It was silly of me to leave there. What is happening there now? I was just about to go, but I kept thinking that... you would come in.”
He told her that Amalia Ivanovna was turning them out of the flat and that Katerina Ivanovna had run off somewhere “to look for justice”.
“Oh, my God!” Sonya started up. “Let us go quickly...”
And she seized her cape.
“Always the same thing!” Raskolnikov cried irritably. “They are all you have in your thoughts! Stay with me.”
“But... Katerina Ivanovna?”

“And Katerina Ivanovna, of course, won’t pass you by; she will come to you herself, since she has run out of the house,” he added peevishly. “If she doesn’t find you in, it will be you who are to blame, after all...”
Sonya sat down on a chair in tormenting indecision. Raskolnikov was silent, looking at the ground and thinking something over.

“Suppose Luzhin didn’t want to this time,” he began, without looking at Sonya. “Well, but if he had wanted to, or if it had somehow come into his calculations, he would have locked you up in prison, if Lebezyatnikov and I hadn’t happened to be there! Eh?”
“Yes,” she said in a weak voice. “Yes!” she repeated, absently and in alarm.
“And I really might not have happened to be there! And Lebezyatnikov turned up quite by chance.”
Sonya was silent.
“Well, and if it had been prison, what then? Do you remember what I said yesterday?”
Again she did not answer. He waited.

“And I thought you would cry out again: ‘Oh, don’t talk, stop it!’” Raskolnikov laughed, but somehow with a strain. “What, silence again?” he asked a minute later. “We must talk about something, mustn’t we? Now I would be particularly interested to know how you would resolve a certain ‘question’, as Lebezyatnikov says.” (He seemed to be beginning to get muddled.) “No, really, I am serious. Imagine, Sonya, that you knew all Luzhin’s intentions beforehand, knew (that is, for certain) that through them Katerina Ivanovna would perish completely, and the children too; and you as well, into the bargain (since you count yourself for nothing, so into the bargain). Polechka too... because the same road lies before her. Well, then: if suddenly all this were now left to your decision: that one or those to live in the world, that is, should Luzhin live and do vile things, or should Katerina Ivanovna die? How would you decide: which of them is to die? I am asking you.”
Sonya looked at him uneasily: she heard something peculiar in this unsteady speech, approaching something from far off.
“I had a feeling that you would ask something like that,” she said, looking at him searchingly.
“Very well, let it be so; but still, how would you decide?”
“Why do you ask what cannot be?” said Sonya with disgust.
“So it is better for Luzhin to live and do vile things! You didn’t dare decide even that?”

“But I cannot know God’s providence... And why do you ask what cannot be asked? Why such empty questions? How could it happen that it should depend on my decision? And who has made me a judge here: who is to live, who is not to live?”
“Once God’s providence gets mixed up in it, there’s nothing to be done,” Raskolnikov grumbled sullenly.
“You had better say straight out what you want!” Sonya cried in anguish. “You are leading up to something again... Can it be that you came only to torment me!”
She could not bear it and suddenly began to cry bitterly. He looked at her in gloomy anguish. About five minutes passed.

“But you are right, Sonya,” he said quietly at last. He had suddenly changed; his affectedly insolent and helplessly defiant tone had vanished. Even his voice suddenly grew weak. “I told you myself yesterday that I would not come to ask forgiveness, and I have begun almost with just that, with asking forgiveness... What I said about Luzhin and providence, I said for myself... That was me asking forgiveness, Sonya...”
He tried to smile, but something helpless and unfinished showed in his pale smile. He bowed his head and covered his face with his hands.

And suddenly a strange, unexpected sensation of a kind of caustic hatred for Sonya passed through his heart. As if surprised and frightened himself by this sensation, he suddenly raised his head and looked at her intently; but he met her uneasy look, anxious for him to the point of torment; there was love here; his hatred vanished like a phantom. That was not it; he had mistaken one feeling for another. It only meant that the moment had come.

Again he covered his face with his hands and bowed his head. Suddenly he turned pale, got up from the chair, looked at Sonya, and, without saying a word, moved mechanically to her bed and sat down on it.
This moment was terribly like, in his sensation, the moment when he had stood behind the old woman, having already freed the axe from its loop, and felt that “there was not a moment more to lose”.
“What is the matter with you?” asked Sonya, terribly frightened.

He could not utter a word. He had meant to tell her quite, quite differently, and he did not himself understand what was happening to him now. She came up to him quietly, sat down on the bed beside him and waited, not taking her eyes off him. Her heart was pounding and stopping. It became unbearable: he turned his deathly pale face to her; his lips twisted helplessly, straining to utter something. Horror passed through Sonya’s heart.
“What is the matter with you?” she repeated, drawing back from him slightly.

“Nothing, Sonya. Don’t be frightened... Nonsense! Really, if you think about it, it’s nonsense,” he muttered, like a man in delirium who does not know what he is doing. “Why have I come to torment you, of all people?” he added suddenly, looking at her. “Really. Why? I keep asking myself this question, Sonya...”
He might have been asking himself this question a quarter of an hour ago, but now he said it in complete helplessness, barely aware of himself and feeling a continuous trembling in his whole body.
“Oh, how you are suffering!” she said in anguish, gazing at him.
“It’s all nonsense!.. Here is the thing, Sonya” (he suddenly smiled for some reason, somehow palely and helplessly, for about two seconds), “do you remember what I wanted to tell you yesterday?”
Sonya waited uneasily.
“I said, as I was leaving, that perhaps I was saying goodbye to you for ever, but that if I came today, I would tell you... who killed Lizaveta.”
She suddenly trembled all over.
“Well, so I have come to tell you.”
“So you really meant it yesterday...” she whispered with difficulty. “How do you know?” she asked quickly, as if suddenly coming to herself.
Sonya began to breathe with difficulty. Her face was growing paler and paler.
“I know.”
She was silent for a minute.
“Have they found him?” she asked timidly.
“No, they haven’t.”
“Then how do you know about it?” she asked again, barely audibly, and again almost after a minute’s silence.
He turned to her and looked at her very, very intently.
“Guess,” he said, with the same twisted and helpless smile as before.
It was as if convulsions ran through her whole body.
“But you... me... why do you... frighten me like this?” she said, smiling like a child.

“So I must be a great friend of his... if I know,” Raskolnikov went on, still looking steadily into her face, as if no longer able to take his eyes away. “He did not mean to kill that Lizaveta... He killed her... by accident... He meant to kill the old woman... when she was alone... and he came... And then Lizaveta came in... And he... killed her too.”
Another terrible minute passed. They both kept looking at each other.
“So you can’t guess?” he asked suddenly, with the sensation of throwing himself down from a bell tower.
“N-no,” Sonya whispered, barely audibly.
“Look carefully.”

And as soon as he said this, again a former, familiar sensation suddenly turned his soul to ice: he looked at her and suddenly, in her face, he seemed to see Lizaveta’s face. He vividly remembered the expression on Lizaveta’s face when he had approached her that time with the axe, and she had backed away from him to the wall, putting out her hand, with completely childlike fright in her face, exactly like small children when they suddenly begin to be frightened of something, look fixedly and uneasily at the thing that frightens them, shrink back and, holding out a little hand, get ready to cry. Almost the same thing happened now with Sonya: just as helplessly, with the same fright, she looked at him for some time and suddenly, putting out her left hand, she pressed her fingers slightly, just barely, against his chest and slowly began to rise from the bed, drawing further and further away from him, and her gaze at him grew more and more fixed. Her horror suddenly communicated itself to him too: exactly the same fright appeared in his face, he too began to look at her in exactly the same way, and almost even with the same childlike smile.
“Have you guessed?” he whispered at last.

“Lord!” a terrible wail broke from her breast. She fell helplessly on the bed, face down in the pillows. But a moment later she quickly raised herself, quickly moved close to him, seized him by both hands and, squeezing them tightly, as in a vice, with her thin fingers, again began looking into his face, motionless, as if glued to it. With this last, desperate look she wanted to search out and catch at least some last hope for herself. But there was no hope; no doubt remained at all; it was all so! Even later, afterwards, when she remembered that moment, it seemed strange and wonderful to her: why exactly had she seen at once then that there was no doubt any more? She could not say, for instance, that she had had some presentiment of the kind, could she? And yet now, as soon as he had told her this, it suddenly seemed to her that she really had had a presentiment of this very thing.
“Enough, Sonya, enough! Don’t torment me!” he begged in anguish.
He had meant to tell her quite, quite differently, but it had turned out like this.

As if not knowing what she was doing, she jumped up and, wringing her hands, went to the middle of the room; but she quickly came back and sat down beside him again, almost touching him, shoulder to shoulder. Suddenly, as if pierced, she shuddered, cried out, and threw herself on her knees before him, not knowing why herself.
“What have you done, what have you done to yourself!” she said in despair, and, jumping up from her knees, she threw her arms round his neck, embraced him and held him tight, tight in her arms.
Raskolnikov drew back and looked at her with a sad smile:
“How strange you are, Sonya: you embrace me and kiss me, when I have told you about that. You don’t know what you are doing.”
“No, there is no one more unhappy than you now in the whole world!” she exclaimed, as if in a frenzy, not hearing his remark, and suddenly burst into sobs, as if in hysterics.
A feeling long unfamiliar to him flooded into his soul like a wave and softened it all at once. He did not resist it: two tears rolled out of his eyes and hung on his lashes.
“So you won’t leave me, Sonya?” he said, looking at her almost with hope.
“No, no; never and nowhere!” cried Sonya. “I will follow you, I will go everywhere! Oh Lord!.. Oh, unhappy me!.. And why, why didn’t I know you before! Why didn’t you come before? Oh Lord!”
“Well, I have come.”

“Now! Oh, what is to be done now!.. Together, together!” she repeated as if in oblivion, and embraced him again. “I will go to penal servitude with you!” Something seemed to jerk through him suddenly; the former hateful and almost haughty smile forced itself onto his lips.
“Perhaps I don’t want to go to penal servitude yet, Sonya,” he said.
Sonya looked at him quickly.

After her first passionate and tormented sympathy for the unhappy man, the terrible idea of the murder struck her again. In the changed tone of his words she suddenly heard the murderer. She looked at him in amazement. She did not yet know anything: why, or how, or for what it had been. Now all these questions flared up at once in her mind. And again she did not believe it: “He, he a murderer! Is it possible?”
“But what is this! Where am I standing!” she said in deep bewilderment, as if not yet come to herself. “But how could you, you, such a... bring yourself to do it?.. But what is this!”
“Well, yes, to rob. Stop it, Sonya!” he answered somehow wearily and even as if with vexation.
Sonya stood as if stunned, but suddenly cried out:
“You were hungry! you... to help your mother? Yes?”
“No, Sonya, no,” he muttered, turning away and hanging his head. “I wasn’t so hungry... I really did want to help my mother, but... that is not quite true either... don’t torment me, Sonya!”
Sonya clasped her hands.

“But can it be, can it be that all this is real! Lord, what kind of truth is this! Who can believe it?.. And how, how is it that you give away your last money yourself, and yet you killed to rob! Ah!..” she cried suddenly. “That money you gave Katerina Ivanovna... that money... Lord, can it be that that money too...”

“No, Sonya,” he interrupted hastily, “that was not that money; calm yourself! That money my mother sent me, through a certain merchant, and I received it when I was ill, the same day I gave it away... Razumikhin saw... it was he who received it for me... that money is mine, my own, really mine.”
Sonya listened to him in bewilderment and tried with all her might to make sense of something.

“And that money... I don’t even know, by the way, whether there was any money there,” he added quietly and as if in thought. “I took a purse off her neck then, a chamois one... a full, tight sort of purse... but I didn’t look into it; I didn’t have time, I suppose... Well, and the things, some studs and little chains, I buried all those things and the purse under a stone in a strange courtyard on V— Prospect, the very next morning. It is all lying there now.”
Sonya listened with all her might.
“But then why... how could you say: to rob, when you didn’t take anything yourself?” she asked quickly, clutching at a straw.

“I don’t know... I haven’t decided yet whether I will take that money or not,” he said, again as if in thought, and suddenly, recollecting himself, he gave a quick, short laugh. “Eh, what a stupid thing I’ve just come out with, eh?”
The thought flashed through Sonya’s mind: “Is he mad?” But she dropped it at once: no, this was something else. She understood nothing, nothing here!

“You know, Sonya,” he said suddenly, with a kind of inspiration, “you know what I will tell you: if I had only killed because I was hungry,” he went on, stressing every word and looking at her enigmatically but sincerely, “then I would be... happy now! Know that!”

“And what is it to you, what is it to you,” he cried a moment later, even with a kind of despair, “well, what is it to you if I were to confess now that I did wrong? Well, what do you want with this stupid triumph over me? Ah, Sonya, is that what I came to you for now!”
Sonya was about to say something again, but stayed silent.
“That is why I called you to come with me yesterday, because you are all I have left.”
“Called me where?” Sonya asked timidly.

“Not to steal and not to kill, don’t worry, not for that,” he smiled caustically. “We are different people... And you know, Sonya, it is only now, only this moment, that I have understood: where was I calling you yesterday? And yesterday, when I called you, I didn’t understand myself where. I called you for one thing, I came for one thing: so that you would not leave me. You won’t leave me, Sonya?”
She pressed his hand.

“And why, why did I tell her, why did I reveal it to her!” he exclaimed in despair a minute later, looking at her with infinite torment. “Here you are waiting for explanations from me, Sonya, you sit and wait, I can see it; but what am I to tell you? You will understand nothing of it, and only suffer all over... because of me! Well, there, you are crying and embracing me again; well, why are you embracing me? Because I couldn’t bear it myself and came to unload it on someone else: ‘You suffer too, it will be easier for me!’ And can you love such a scoundrel?”
“But aren’t you suffering too?” cried Sonya.
Again the same feeling flooded into his soul like a wave, and again for an instant softened it.

“Sonya, I have a wicked heart, note that: much can be explained by that. That is why I came, because I am wicked. There are people who would not have come. But I am a coward and... a scoundrel! But... let it be! all this is not it... I must speak now, and I don’t know how to begin...”
He stopped and fell to thinking.
“E-eh, we are different people!” he cried again. “Not a pair. And why, why did I come! I will never forgive myself for it!”
“No, no, it is good that you came!” exclaimed Sonya. “It is better that I should know! Much better!” He looked at her with pain.

“And what if it really is so!” he said, as if he had thought of something. “Why, that is just how it was! Here is the thing: I wanted to become a Napoleon, that is why I killed... Well, do you understand now?”
“N-no,” Sonya whispered naively and timidly, “only... speak, speak! I will understand, I will understand everything for myself!” she begged him.
“You will understand? Well, very good, we shall see!”
He was silent and thought for a long time.

“The thing is this: I once asked myself this question: what if, for example, Napoleon had found himself in my place, and he had had, to begin his career, neither Toulon, nor Egypt, nor the crossing of Mont Blanc, but instead of all those fine and monumental things simply some ridiculous little old woman, a registrar’s widow, who had to be killed besides, in order to steal money from her trunk (for his career, you understand?), well, would he have brought himself to do it, if there had been no other way out? Would he not have been squeamish, because it is far too unmonumental and... and sinful? Well, I tell you that I tormented myself over this ‘question’ terribly long, so that I felt terribly ashamed when at last I guessed (suddenly, somehow) that not only would he not have been squeamish, it would not even have entered his head that it was unmonumental... and he would not even have understood at all: what is there to be squeamish about? And if only there had been no other road for him, he would have strangled her so that she didn’t even squeak, without any brooding!.. Well, and I... came out of my brooding... strangled her... following the example of authority... And that is exactly how it was! Do you find it funny? Yes, Sonya, what is funniest of all here is that perhaps that is exactly how it was...”
Sonya did not find it at all funny.
“You had better tell me plainly... without examples,” she begged, still more timidly and barely audibly.
He turned to her, looked at her sadly and took her hands.

“You are right again, Sonya. It is all nonsense, after all, almost mere chatter! You see: you know that my mother has almost nothing. My sister received an education, by chance, and is condemned to drag about as a governess. All their hopes were in me alone. I was studying, but I couldn’t keep myself at the university and was forced to leave for a time. Even if things had dragged on like that, in ten or twelve years (if circumstances had turned out well) I could still have hoped to become some kind of teacher or official, with a salary of a thousand roubles...” (He spoke as if reciting something learned by heart.) “And by that time my mother would have withered away from care and grief, and I would still not have managed to set her at rest, and my sister... well, something even worse might have happened to my sister!.. And what is the point of passing everything by all one’s life and turning away from everything, forgetting one’s mother, and respectfully enduring the insult to one’s sister, for instance? What for? So as to bury them and acquire new ones, a wife and children, and then leave them too without a penny and without a crust? Well... well, so I decided, having taken possession of the old woman’s money, to use it for my first years, without tormenting my mother, to keep myself at the university, for my first steps after the university, and to do all this broadly, radically, so as to set up a whole new career and set out on a new, independent road... Well... well, that’s all... Well, of course, killing the old woman, that was wrong of me... well, and enough!”
In a kind of helplessness he dragged himself to the end of his story and hung his head.
“Oh, that is not it, not it,” Sonya exclaimed in anguish. “And can one really... no, it is not like that, not like that!”
“You see for yourself that it is not like that!.. And yet I told it sincerely, the truth!”
“But what kind of truth is that! Oh Lord!”
“I only killed a louse, Sonya, a useless, nasty, harmful one.”
“A human being, a louse!”

“But I know myself that she is not a louse,” he answered, looking at her strangely. “But then, I am lying, Sonya,” he added, “I have been lying for a long time... All this is not it; you are right. There are quite, quite, quite other reasons here!.. I haven’t talked with anyone for a long time, Sonya... My head aches badly now.”

His eyes were burning with a feverish fire. He was almost beginning to rave; an uneasy smile wandered on his lips. A terrible helplessness was already showing through his excited state of mind. Sonya understood how he was suffering. Her head too was beginning to spin. And he spoke so strangely: as if something were understandable, but... “But how! How! Oh Lord!” And she wrung her hands in despair.

“No, Sonya, that is not it!” he began again, suddenly raising his head, as if a sudden turn of thought had struck and excited him again. “That is not it! Better... suppose (yes! that really is better!), suppose that I am vain, envious, wicked, vile, vindictive, well... and perhaps inclined to madness besides. (Let it all come at once! They talked about madness before, I noticed!) I told you just now that I couldn’t keep myself at the university. But do you know that perhaps I could have? My mother would have sent me money to pay what was needed, and for boots, clothes and bread I could have earned it myself; surely! There were lessons to be had; they offered half a rouble each. Razumikhin works, after all! But I turned spiteful and didn’t want to. That’s it, I turned spiteful (that is a good word!). Then, like a spider, I hid myself away in my corner. You have been in my kennel, you saw it... And do you know, Sonya, that low ceilings and cramped rooms cramp the soul and the mind! Oh, how I hated that kennel! And yet I didn’t want to leave it. I didn’t want to on purpose! I didn’t go out for days on end, and I didn’t want to work, and I didn’t even want to eat; I just lay there. If Nastasya brought something, I ate; if she didn’t, the day would pass like that; I didn’t ask on purpose, out of spite! At night there was no light; I lay in the dark, and I wouldn’t earn money for candles. I ought to have been studying; I sold my books; and on my table, on my notes and exercise books, there is a finger’s depth of dust even now. I preferred to lie and think. And I kept thinking... And I kept having such dreams, strange, various dreams; no need to say what! But only then I also began to imagine that... No, that isn’t it! I am telling it wrong again! You see, I kept asking myself then: why am I so stupid that, if others are stupid and I know for certain that they are stupid, I don’t want to be cleverer myself? Then I learned, Sonya, that if one waits until everyone becomes clever, it will take far too long... Then I learned besides that it will never happen, that people won’t change, and no one can remake them, and it is not worth wasting effort on it! Yes, that is so! That is their law... A law, Sonya! That is so!.. And I know now, Sonya, that whoever is strong and powerful in mind and spirit is master over them! Whoever dares much is right in their eyes. Whoever can spit on more is their lawgiver, and whoever can dare most of all is the most right of all! So it has been until now and so it will always be! Only a blind man would not see it!”

As he said this, Raskolnikov, though he was looking at Sonya, no longer cared whether she would understand or not. The fever had taken complete hold of him. He was in a kind of gloomy rapture. (Indeed, he had not talked with anyone for too long!) Sonya understood that this gloomy catechism had become his faith and law.

“I guessed then, Sonya,” he went on rapturously, “that power is given only to the one who dares to bend down and take it. There is only one thing here, one thing: one has only to dare! A thought came to me then, for the first time in my life, which no one had ever thought of before me! No one! It suddenly appeared to me, clear as the sun: how is it that not a single person until now has dared, or dares, walking past all this absurdity, simply to take the whole thing by the tail and shake it to the devil! I... I wanted to dare, and I killed... I only wanted to dare, Sonya; that is the whole reason!”
“Oh, be quiet, be quiet!” cried Sonya, clasping her hands. “You turned away from God, and God has struck you, given you over to the devil!..”
“By the way, Sonya, when I was lying there in the dark and kept imagining things, that was the devil tempting me, was it? eh?”
“Be quiet! Don’t laugh, you blasphemer; you don’t understand anything, anything! Oh Lord! He won’t understand anything, anything!”

“Be quiet, Sonya, I am not laughing at all; I know myself that the devil was dragging me. Be quiet, Sonya, be quiet!” he repeated gloomily and insistently. “I know everything. I thought all this over and whispered it over to myself when I was lying there in the dark... I argued it all out with myself, down to the last smallest detail, and I know everything, everything! And how sick, how sick I was then of all this chatter! I kept wanting to forget it all and begin again, Sonya, and stop chattering! And do you really think I went like a fool, headlong? I went as a clever man, and that is just what ruined me! And do you really think I didn’t know, for instance, at least this: that if I had begun to ask myself and question myself: have I the right to have power? then it follows that I have no right to have power. Or that if I ask the question: is a human being a louse? then it follows that a human being is not a louse for me, but a louse for the one to whom it never even occurs, and who goes straight ahead without questions... If I tormented myself for so many days over whether Napoleon would have gone or not, then I clearly felt already that I am not a Napoleon... All, all the torment of all this chatter I endured, Sonya, and I wanted to shake it all off my shoulders: I wanted, Sonya, to kill without casuistry, to kill for myself, for myself alone! I didn’t want to lie about it even to myself! It was not to help my mother that I killed: nonsense! I did not kill so that, having got means and power, I could become a benefactor of humanity. Nonsense! I simply killed; I killed for myself, for myself alone: and whether I would then become anyone’s benefactor, or spend my whole life like a spider catching everyone in my web and sucking the living juices out of them all, at that moment it was supposed to be all the same to me!.. And it was not money, above all, that I needed, Sonya, when I killed; it was not so much money I needed as something else... I know all this now... Understand me: perhaps, going along that same road, I would never have repeated the murder again. I needed to find out something else; something else was pushing me by the arms: I needed to find out then, and to find out quickly, whether I was a louse like everyone else, or a man? Whether I can step over or not! Whether I dare bend down and take, or not? Whether I am a trembling creature, or whether I have the right...”
“To kill? You have the right to kill?” Sonya clasped her hands.

“E-eh, Sonya!” he cried irritably; he was about to object to her, but fell silent contemptuously. “Don’t interrupt me, Sonya! I only wanted to prove one thing to you: that the devil dragged me there then, and only afterwards explained to me that I had no right to go there, because I am exactly the same louse as everyone else! He made a fool of me, and so I have come to you now! Receive your guest! If I were not a louse, would I have come to you? Listen: when I went to the old woman’s that time, I only went to try... Know that!”
“And you killed! You killed!”

“But how did I kill? Is that how people kill? Do people go to kill the way I went then? Some day I will tell you how I went... Did I kill the old woman? I killed myself, not the old woman! There, at one stroke, I did away with myself, for ever!.. And that old woman, the devil killed her, not I... Enough, enough, Sonya, enough! Leave me,” he cried suddenly in convulsive anguish, “leave me!”
He leaned his elbows on his knees and squeezed his head in his palms as in pincers.
“What suffering!” a tormented wail broke from Sonya.
“Well, what is to be done now, tell me!” he asked, suddenly raising his head and looking at her with a face hideously distorted by despair.

“What is to be done!” she exclaimed, suddenly jumping up from her place, and her eyes, until now full of tears, suddenly flashed. “Stand up!” (She seized him by the shoulder; he raised himself, looking at her almost in amazement.) “Go now, this very minute, stand at the crossroads, bow down, first kiss the earth which you have defiled, and then bow down to the whole world, on all four sides, and say to everyone, aloud: ‘I have killed!’ Then God will send you life again. Will you go? Will you go?” she asked him, trembling all over, as if in a fit, seizing him by both hands, squeezing them tightly in hers and looking at him with a fiery look.
He was amazed and even struck by her sudden rapture.
“Do you mean penal servitude, Sonya? I must inform on myself, must I?” he asked gloomily.
“Accept suffering and redeem yourself by it; that is what is needed.”
“No! I will not go to them, Sonya.”

“But how will you live, how will you live? What will you live with?” exclaimed Sonya. “Is it possible now? Well, how will you talk to your mother? (Oh, what will become of them, of them, now!) But what am I saying! You have already abandoned your mother and sister. You have already abandoned them, abandoned them. Oh Lord!” she cried. “He knows all this himself already! Well, how, how can one live without a single human being! What will become of you now!”

“Don’t be a child, Sonya,” he said quietly. “How am I guilty before them? Why should I go? What shall I tell them? All this is only a phantom... They destroy people by the million themselves, and count it a virtue besides. They are rogues and scoundrels, Sonya!.. I will not go. And what shall I say: that I killed, but didn’t dare take the money, and hid it under a stone?” he added with a caustic smile. “Why, they will laugh at me themselves; they will say: a fool, not to take it. A coward and a fool! They won’t understand anything, anything, Sonya, and they are not worthy to understand. Why should I go? I won’t go. Don’t be a child, Sonya...”
“You will be worn out with torment, worn out,” she repeated, stretching out her hands to him in desperate entreaty.
“Perhaps I have slandered myself,” he remarked gloomily, as if in thought. “Perhaps I am still a man and not a louse, and was in too much of a hurry to condemn myself... I will fight on yet.”
A haughty smile forced itself onto his lips.
“To carry such torment! And for a whole life, a whole life!..”

“I’ll get used to it...” he said sullenly and thoughtfully. “Listen,” he began a minute later, “stop crying, it’s time to talk business: I came to tell you that they are looking for me now, hunting me...”
“Ah!” cried Sonya in fright.

“Well, why did you cry out! You want me to go to penal servitude yourself, and now you are frightened? Only here is the thing: I won’t give myself up to them. I will fight them yet, and they will do nothing. They have no real evidence. Yesterday I was in great danger and thought I was already lost; but today things have improved. All their evidence cuts both ways; that is, I can turn their accusations to my own advantage, do you understand? and I will turn them; because I have learned now... But they will certainly put me in prison. If it hadn’t been for one incident, they might have put me there today, certainly; perhaps they will even put me there today yet... Only that is nothing, Sonya: I’ll sit there a while, and they will let me out... because they have not a single real proof and won’t have, I give you my word. And with what they have, you can’t lock a man away. Well, enough... I only wanted you to know... With my sister and mother I will try somehow to manage to reassure them and not frighten them... My sister, though, seems to be provided for now... and so my mother too... Well, that’s all. Be careful, though. Will you come to see me in prison, when I am inside?”
“Oh, I will! I will!”

They both sat side by side, sad and crushed, as if they had been thrown up alone on an empty shore after a storm. He looked at Sonya and felt how much of her love was upon him, and strangely, he suddenly felt it heavy and painful to be loved like that. Yes, it was a strange and terrible sensation! Coming to Sonya, he had felt that all his hope and all his way out lay in her; he had thought to lay down at least part of his torment, and suddenly, now, when her whole heart had turned to him, he suddenly felt and realised that he had become incomparably more unhappy than he had been before.
“Sonya,” he said, “better not come to see me when I am in prison.”
Sonya did not answer; she was crying. Several minutes passed.
“Are you wearing a cross?” she suddenly asked unexpectedly, as if she had just remembered.
At first he did not understand the question.

“No, you aren’t, are you? Here, take this one, of cypress wood. I have another left, a copper one, Lizaveta’s. Lizaveta and I exchanged crosses; she gave me her cross, and I gave her my little icon. I will wear Lizaveta’s now, and this one is for you. Take it... it’s mine! It’s mine!” she begged. “We shall go and suffer together, and we shall bear the cross together!..”
“Give it to me!” said Raskolnikov. He did not want to grieve her. But at once he drew back the hand he had held out for the cross.
“Not now, Sonya. Better later,” he added, to calm her.
“Yes, yes, better, better,” she took up eagerly. “When you go to your suffering, then you will put it on. You will come to me, I will put it on you, we will pray and go.”
At that moment someone knocked three times at the door.
“Sofya Semyonovna, may I come in?” came a very familiar, polite voice.
Sonya rushed to the door in fright. Mr Lebezyatnikov’s fair-haired face peeped into the room.
## CHAPTER II

“These cigarettes!” Porfiry Petrovich began at last, having finished lighting up and caught his breath. “Harm, pure harm, and I can’t give them up! I cough, sir, my throat has begun to tickle, and I get short of breath. I am a coward, you know, sir; I went the other day to B—n; he examines each patient for half an hour at least; he even laughed, looking at me: he tapped me and listened to me; ‘Tobacco,’ he says, ‘among other things, is not good for you; your lungs are enlarged.’ Well, and how am I to give it up? What am I to replace it with? I don’t drink, sir, that’s the whole trouble, he-he-he, that I don’t drink, that’s the trouble! Everything is relative, Rodion Romanych, everything is relative!”

“What, is he taking up his old official tricks again?” Raskolnikov thought with disgust. The whole recent scene of their last meeting suddenly came back to him, and the feeling of that time flooded back to his heart like a wave.

“And I came to see you two days ago, in the evening; didn’t you know?” Porfiry Petrovich went on, looking round the room. “I came into the room, this very one. Just like today, I was passing by: why not, I thought, return his visit. I came in, and the room was wide open; I looked round, waited, and didn’t even announce myself to your servant; I left. You don’t lock up?”
Raskolnikov’s face grew darker and darker. Porfiry seemed to have guessed his thoughts.

“I have come to explain myself, my dear Rodion Romanych, to explain myself, sir! I owe you an explanation, sir, I am bound to give one,” he went on with a little smile, and even gave Raskolnikov’s knee a light slap with his palm; but almost at the same instant his face suddenly took on a serious and concerned expression; it even seemed clouded with sadness, to Raskolnikov’s surprise. He had never yet seen or suspected such a face in him. “A strange scene took place between us last time, Rodion Romanych. Perhaps a strange scene took place between us at our first meeting too; but then... Well, now it all comes to the same thing! Here is the point, sir: I may have turned out very guilty before you; I feel it, sir. Remember how we parted: your nerves were singing and your knees were shaking, and my nerves were singing and my knees were shaking. And you know, somehow it even turned out improper between us then, not gentlemanly. And yet we are gentlemen, after all; that is, in any case, gentlemen first of all; that must be understood, sir. Remember what it came to... it was quite even indecent, sir.”
“What is he doing, what does he take me for?” Raskolnikov asked himself in amazement, raising his head and staring with all his eyes at Porfiry.

“I have decided that it will be better for us to act frankly now,” Porfiry Petrovich went on, tilting his head back a little and lowering his eyes, as if no longer wishing to embarrass his former victim with his look and as if disdaining his former methods and dodges. “Yes, sir, such suspicions and such scenes cannot go on for long. Mikolka resolved things for us then, or I don’t know what it would have come to between us. That damned little tradesman was sitting behind my partition then: can you imagine it? You know that already, of course; and I know myself that he came to see you afterwards; but what you supposed then did not happen: I had not sent for anyone, and I had not yet given any orders about anything. You will ask why I had not? Well, how shall I put it: it had all as it were stunned me myself then. I barely managed to give orders to send for the caretakers. (You noticed the caretakers as you passed, I dare say.) A thought flashed through me then, just one, quickly, like lightning; I was very firmly convinced then, you see, Rodion Romanych. Well, I thought, even if I let one thing slip for a while, I will catch the other by the tail; my own, my own at least, I won’t let slip. You are very irritable by nature, Rodion Romanych, sir; even too much so, sir, with all the other fundamental qualities of your character and heart, which I flatter myself I have partly grasped, sir. Well, of course, even then I could reason that it does not always happen that a man just gets up and blurts out the whole inside story to you. That does happen, especially when you drive a man past the last of his patience, but in any case rarely. That much I could reason too. No, I thought, if only I had one little feature! if only the tiniest little feature, only one, but only such that one could take hold of it with one’s hands, that it would be a thing, and not just this psychology. Because, I thought, if a man is guilty, then of course one can, in any case, wait for something substantial from him; one may even count on the most unexpected result. I was counting on your character then, Rodion Romanych, most of all on your character, sir! I had very great hopes of you then.”

“But you... but why are you talking like this now?” Raskolnikov muttered at last, without even taking in the question properly. “What is he talking about?” he wondered to himself. “Can it be that he really takes me for innocent?”

“Why am I talking like this? I have come to explain myself, sir; I consider it, so to speak, a sacred duty. I want to lay everything out for you to the very ground, how it all was, the whole story of all that, so to speak, darkening of that time. I have made you suffer a great deal, Rodion Romanych. I am not a monster, sir. Why, I understand too what it is for a man to drag all this on himself, a man who is downcast, but proud, masterful and impatient, especially impatient! I regard you, in any case, as a most noble man, sir, and even with the beginnings of magnanimity, sir, though I don’t agree with you in all your convictions, which I consider it my duty to declare beforehand, directly and with complete sincerity, for above all I don’t wish to deceive. Having come to know you, I felt an attachment to you. Perhaps you will laugh at such words of mine? You have the right, sir. I know that you didn’t like me from the first glance, because, essentially, there is nothing to like, sir. But think as you please; now I wish, for my part, by every means to smooth over the impression I produced and to prove that I too am a man with a heart and a conscience. I speak sincerely, sir.”
Porfiry Petrovich paused with dignity. Raskolnikov felt a rush of some new fear. The thought that Porfiry considered him innocent suddenly began to frighten him.

“To tell everything in order, how it suddenly began then, is hardly necessary,” Porfiry Petrovich went on; “I think it is even superfluous. And I could hardly do it, sir. Because how is one to explain it in detail? At first rumours started. What rumours they were, and from whom, and when... and on what occasion, properly speaking, it came to you, that too, I think, is superfluous. With me personally it began with a chance, a completely chance chance, which in the highest degree might have happened and might not have happened. What chance? Hm, I think there is no need to say that either. All this, the rumours and the chances, came together for me then into one thought. I confess frankly, because if one is going to confess, then confess everything: it was I who first fell upon you then. Those marks of the old woman’s on the things, let us say, and so on and so on, all that is nonsense, sir. One can count up a hundred such things. I also had occasion then to find out in detail about the scene in the police office, also by chance, sir, and not just in passing, but from a special narrator, a first-class one, who, without knowing it himself, had mastered that scene wonderfully. It all fits together, sir, it all fits together, Rodion Romanych, my dear! Well, how could I not turn in a certain direction? From a hundred rabbits you will never make a horse, from a hundred suspicions you will never make a proof, as a certain English proverb says, but that is only prudence, sir; but just try to cope with the passions, the passions, because an investigator is a man too, sir. Then I remembered your little article too, in that little journal; remember, we talked about it in detail at your very first visit. I scoffed at it then, but that was in order to draw you out further. I repeat, you are very impatient and very ill, Rodion Romanych. That you are bold, arrogant, serious and... that you have felt, felt a great deal, all that I have known for a long time, sir. I am familiar with all these sensations, and I read your little article as something familiar. It was conceived in sleepless nights and in frenzy, with the heart rising and pounding, with suppressed enthusiasm. And this suppressed, proud enthusiasm in young people is dangerous! I scoffed then, but now I will tell you that I terribly love in general, as an amateur, that is, this first, youthful, ardent trial of the pen. Smoke, mist, a string ringing in the mist. Your article is absurd and fantastic, but such sincerity flashes in it, there is youthful and incorruptible pride in it, the boldness of despair; it is a gloomy article, sir, but that is good, sir. I read your little article and put it aside, and... as I put it aside then, I thought: ‘Well, with this man it won’t pass off like that!’ Well, then, tell me now, after such antecedents, how could I not be carried away by what followed! Ah, Lord! But am I saying anything? Am I asserting anything now? I only noted it then. What is there in it, I thought? There is nothing in it, that is, absolutely nothing, and perhaps in the highest degree nothing. And for me, an investigator, to be carried away like that is not even proper at all: I have Mikolka on my hands, and with facts already; say what you like, but facts! And he too brings in his psychology; one must occupy oneself with them, because this is a matter of life and death. Why am I explaining all this to you now? So that you should know, and with your mind and heart not blame me for my spiteful conduct then. Not spiteful, sir, I speak sincerely, sir, he-he! What do you think: that I didn’t come to search your place then? I did, sir, I did, he-he, I did, sir, when you were lying ill here in your little bed. Not officially and not in my own person, but I did, sir. Everything in your lodging was examined down to the last hair, even while the traces were fresh; but, umsonst, in vain! I thought: now this man will come, he will come himself, and very soon; if he is guilty, he will certainly come. Another would not come, but this one will. And do you remember how Mr Razumikhin began letting things slip to you? We arranged that so as to excite you; that is why we deliberately started the rumour, so that he would let things slip to you, and Mr Razumikhin is the kind of man who cannot hold in his indignation. What struck Mr Zamyotov above all was your anger and your open boldness: well, think of it, in a tavern suddenly to blurt out: ‘I killed her!’ Too bold, sir, too insolent, sir, and if, I thought, he is guilty, then he is a terrible fighter! That is what I thought then, sir. I waited, sir! I waited for you with all my might, and as for Zamyotov, you simply crushed him then and... why, that is just the point, that all this damned psychology cuts both ways! Well, so I wait for you, I watch, and God sends you: here you come! My heart simply thumped. Eh! Well, why did you have to come then? Your laughter, your laughter, as you came in then, remember, why, I guessed everything then as if through glass, and if I had not been waiting for you in such a special way, I would have noticed nothing in your laughter either. That is what it means to be in the mood. And Mr Razumikhin then: ah! the stone, the stone, remember, the stone, the one under which the things are hidden? Why, it is as if I see it somewhere there, in a kitchen garden: it was a kitchen garden you spoke of, wasn’t it, to Zamyotov, and then at my place, the second time? And when we began going over that article of yours then, when you began to set it out, why, one took every word of yours twice over, as if something else were sitting under it! Well, Rodion Romanych, that is how I came to the last posts, and struck my forehead against them, and came to my senses. No, I said, what am I doing! Why, if one wants to, all this, I said, can be explained in the other direction down to the last detail, and it will come out even more naturally. Torment, sir! ‘No,’ I thought, ‘I had better have one little feature!..’ And when I heard about those bells then, I simply froze all over, a trembling even went through me. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘here is the little feature! This is it!’ And I didn’t even reason then; I simply didn’t want to. I would have given a thousand roubles at that moment, my own money, just to see you with my own eyes: how you walked a hundred paces beside that little tradesman, after he had said ‘murderer’ to your face, and didn’t dare ask him anything for a whole hundred paces!.. Well, and that chill in the spinal cord? Those bells, in your illness, in your half-delirium? And so, Rodion Romanych, why be surprised after that that I played such jokes with you then? And why did you come yourself at that very moment? Why, it was as if someone were pushing you too, by God, and if Mikolka had not separated us, then... and do you remember Mikolka then? Do you remember him well? Why, that was a thunderclap, sir! A thunderclap out of a cloud, a thunderbolt! Well, and how did I receive him? I didn’t believe the thunderbolt this much, you saw for yourself! Not a bit! Afterwards, after you had gone, when he began answering some points very, very coherently, so that I was surprised myself, even then I didn’t believe him a farthing’s worth! That is what it means to be fixed like adamant. No, I thought, morgen früh, not a chance! What Mikolka!”
“Razumikhin told me just now that you are still accusing Nikolai, and that you assured Razumikhin of it yourself...”

His breath caught and he did not finish. He was listening in inexpressible agitation as the man who had seen right through him was disowning himself. He was afraid to believe it and did not believe it. In the still ambiguous words he was greedily seeking and catching at something more precise and final.

“Mr Razumikhin!” cried Porfiry Petrovich, as if glad of a question from Raskolnikov, who had kept silent all this time. “He-he-he! Why, Mr Razumikhin had to be led off the scent: two’s company, three’s a crowd. Mr Razumikhin is not the man, sir, and an outsider besides; he came running to me all pale... Well, God be with him, why mix him up in this! And as for Mikolka, would you like to know what sort of subject he is, as I understand him, that is? First of all, he is still a child, a minor, and not exactly a coward, but rather like some sort of artist. Really, sir, don’t laugh at my describing him like that. Innocent, and receptive to everything. He has a heart; he is a dreamer. He sings, he dances, and they say he tells stories so that people come from other places to listen. He goes to school, and laughs till he drops if you show him your little finger, and drinks himself senseless, not from depravity, but in fits and starts, when they ply him with drink, still like a child. That time he stole, and he doesn’t know it himself; because ‘if I picked it up off the ground, how is that stealing?’ And do you know that he is one of the Old Believers, and not exactly an Old Believer, but simply a sectarian; there were Wanderers in his family, and he himself until recently, for two whole years, was under the spiritual guidance of a certain elder in his village. I found all this out from Mikolka and from his people from Zaraisk. Why, he simply wanted to run off into the wilderness! He had zeal, he prayed to God at night, read the old ‘true’ books and lost himself in them. Petersburg had a strong effect on him, especially the female sex, well, and wine. He is receptive, sir, and he forgot the elder and everything. I know that a certain artist here grew fond of him and began to visit him, and then this incident came along! Well, he lost his nerve: hang himself! Run away! What is to be done with the notion that has spread among the people about our legal system! To some the word ‘they’ll convict you’ is terrifying. Who is to blame! We shall see what the new courts will say. Oh, God grant it! Well, sir, in prison, evidently, he remembered the honest elder again; the Bible appeared again too. Do you know, Rodion Romanych, what ‘to suffer’ means to some of them? It is not for anyone in particular, but simply ‘one must suffer’; to accept suffering, that is, and if from the authorities, so much the better. In my time there was a most humble prisoner who sat in prison for a whole year, reading the Bible on the stove at night, and he read and read himself into it, you know, completely, so that out of the blue he grabbed a brick and threw it at the governor, without any offence on the governor’s part. And how he threw it: he deliberately aimed a yard wide, so as not to do any harm! Well, we know what end awaits a prisoner who attacks the authorities with a weapon: and so ‘he accepted suffering’. So I suspect now that Mikolka wants ‘to accept suffering’, or something of the kind. I know this for certain, even from facts, sir. Only he doesn’t know himself that I know. What, don’t you allow that fantastic people come out of such folk? Why, all the time! The elder has begun to act on him again, especially after the noose, he remembered him. But he will tell me everything himself; he will come. Do you think he will hold out? Wait, he will retract yet! I am expecting him at any hour to come and withdraw his statement. I have grown fond of this Mikolka and am studying him thoroughly. And what do you think! He-he! On some points he answered me very coherently; he has obviously got the necessary information and prepared himself cleverly; but on other points he simply knows not the least little thing, like a man stepping into a puddle, and doesn’t even suspect that he doesn’t know! No, my dear Rodion Romanych, Mikolka is not the one here! This is a fantastic, gloomy business, a modern business, a case of our time, sir, when the human heart has grown troubled; when the phrase is quoted that blood ‘refreshes’; when comfort is preached as the whole of life. Here there are bookish dreams, sir, here is a heart irritated by theory; here one sees resolve for the first step, but resolve of a special kind: he resolved, as if falling off a mountain or flying down from a bell tower, and came to the crime as if not on his own legs. He forgot to shut the door behind him, but he killed, killed two, by a theory. He killed, and he didn’t know how to take the money, and what he managed to snatch he carried off under a stone. It was not enough for him that he endured torment when he was sitting behind the door and they were breaking at the door and the bell was ringing; no, afterwards he goes to the empty flat, in half-delirium, to remember that bell, he needed to feel that spinal chill again... Well, let us say that was in illness; but here is something else: he killed, and yet considers himself an honest man, despises people, walks about like a pale angel; no, what Mikolka, my dear Rodion Romanych, Mikolka is not the one here!”
These last words, after everything said before, which had so resembled a renunciation, were too unexpected. Raskolnikov trembled all over, as if pierced.

“Then... who... killed them?..” he asked, unable to hold back, in a gasping voice. Porfiry Petrovich even recoiled against the back of his chair, as if he too were so unexpectedly amazed by the question.

“What do you mean, who killed them?..” he repeated, as if not believing his ears. “Why, you killed them, Rodion Romanych! It was you who killed them, sir...” he added, almost in a whisper, in a voice of complete conviction.
Raskolnikov jumped up from the sofa, stood for a few seconds and sat down again without saying a word. Small convulsions suddenly passed over his whole face.

“Your lip is trembling again, as it did then,” Porfiry Petrovich muttered, as if even with sympathy. “You have not understood me rightly, I think, Rodion Romanych,” he added after a short silence, “that is why you are so amazed. I have come precisely to say everything now and to bring the matter out into the open.”
“It wasn’t I who killed them,” Raskolnikov whispered, like frightened small children when they are caught in the act.
“No, it was you, sir, Rodion Romanych, you, sir, and no one else, sir,” Porfiry whispered sternly and with conviction.

They both fell silent, and the silence lasted even strangely long, about ten minutes. Raskolnikov leaned his elbows on the table and silently ruffled his hair with his fingers. Porfiry Petrovich sat quietly and waited. Suddenly Raskolnikov looked contemptuously at Porfiry.
“You are at your old tricks again, Porfiry Petrovich! Still the same methods of yours: don’t you get sick of it, really?”

“Eh, come now, what do I want with methods now! It would be another matter if there were witnesses here; but as it is we are whispering one to one. You see yourself that I have not come to chase you and catch you like a hare. Whether you confess or not is all the same to me at this moment. For my own part I am convinced without you.”
“And if so, why have you come?” Raskolnikov asked irritably. “I put my former question to you: if you consider me guilty, why don’t you take me to prison?”
“Well, there’s a question! I will answer you point by point: in the first place, it is not to my advantage to put you under arrest just like that.”
“How, not to your advantage! If you are convinced, then you must...”

“Eh, what if I am convinced? For the time being all this is my dreams, sir. And why should I put you away there to rest? You know yourself, if you are asking for it. Suppose I bring the little tradesman to confront you, and you say to him: ‘Are you drunk or not? Who saw me with you? I simply took you for a drunk, and you were drunk’; well, what shall I say to you then, all the more since your story is even more plausible than his, because in his statement there is nothing but psychology, which is not even proper for a mug like his, while you hit the very point, because he drinks like a fish, the scoundrel, and is far too well known for it. And I myself have frankly admitted to you, several times already, that this psychology cuts both ways and that the second end is the bigger and much more plausible one, and that apart from this I have nothing against you so far. And though I will still put you away, and have even come myself (quite unlike ordinary people) to announce everything to you beforehand, I tell you straight out (also unlike ordinary people) that it will not be to my advantage. Well, sir, in the second place, I have come to you because...”
“Well, yes, in the second place?” (Raskolnikov was still gasping.)

“Because, as I declared just now, I consider myself obliged to give you an explanation. I don’t want you to regard me as a monster, all the more since I am sincerely well disposed towards you, believe it or not. Consequently, in the third place, I have come to you with an open and direct proposal: to make a voluntary confession. It will be incalculably more advantageous for you, and more advantageous for me too, because it will be off my shoulders. Well, is that frank on my part or not?”
Raskolnikov thought for a minute.
“Listen, Porfiry Petrovich, you say yourself: nothing but psychology, and yet you have gone off into mathematics. Well, what if you yourself are mistaken now?”
“No, Rodion Romanych, I am not mistaken. I have a little feature. I found that little feature even then, sir; the Lord sent it!”
“What little feature?”

“I won’t say what, Rodion Romanych. And in any case I have no right to put it off any longer now; I shall put you away, sir. So consider: now it is all the same to me, and therefore I am doing this solely for you. By God, it will be better, Rodion Romanych!”
Raskolnikov smiled maliciously.

“Why, this is not only ridiculous, it is even shameless. Well, even if I were guilty (which I am not saying at all), why on earth should I come to you with a confession, when you yourself already say that I shall be sitting there with you at rest?”

“Eh, Rodion Romanych, don’t believe words entirely; perhaps it won’t be entirely at rest! That is only a theory, and mine at that, sir, and what sort of authority am I for you? Perhaps I am hiding something from you even now, sir. I can’t just take everything and lay it out for you, he-he! The second point: what advantage, you ask? But do you know what reduction of sentence will follow for you? When will you come, at what moment? Just consider that! When another man has already taken the crime on himself and muddled the whole case? And I swear to you by God himself that I will fix and arrange things ‘there’ so that your confession will come out as if quite unexpected. We will destroy all this psychology completely; I will turn all suspicions against you into nothing, so that your crime will appear as a kind of darkening of the mind, because, in conscience, that is what it is. I am an honest man, Rodion Romanych, and I will keep my word.”
Raskolnikov fell sadly silent and hung his head; he thought for a long time and at last smiled again, but his smile was gentle and sad now:
“Eh, I don’t want it!” he said, as if no longer hiding anything from Porfiry. “It isn’t worth it! I don’t want your reduction at all!”
“There, that is just what I was afraid of!” Porfiry exclaimed hotly and as if involuntarily. “That is just what I was afraid of, that you would not want our reduction.”
Raskolnikov looked at him sadly and impressively.
“Eh, don’t scorn life!” Porfiry went on. “There is a great deal of it still ahead. How can you not want a reduction, how can you not! You are an impatient man!”
“A great deal of what still ahead?”
“Of life! What sort of prophet are you, how much do you know? Seek and ye shall find. Perhaps this is just what God was waiting for you for. And it is not for ever, the chain...”
“There will be a reduction...” laughed Raskolnikov.

“What, are you afraid of bourgeois shame, perhaps? It may be that you are afraid, and don’t know it yourself, because you are young! But all the same, it is not for you to be afraid or ashamed of making a confession.”

“E-eh, I spit on it!” Raskolnikov whispered contemptuously and with disgust, as if not wishing even to speak. He half rose again, as if he wanted to go out somewhere, but sat down again in visible despair.

“That’s just it, you spit on it! You have lost your faith, and you think I am flattering you crudely; but how long have you lived yet? How much do you understand? You invented a theory, and you were ashamed that it failed, that it turned out very unoriginal! It turned out base, that is true, but all the same you are not a hopeless scoundrel. Not that kind of scoundrel at all! At least you didn’t fool yourself for long; you went all the way to the last posts at once. Do you know what I take you for? I take you for one of those men who, even if you cut out his guts, will stand and look at his torturers with a smile, if only he finds faith or God. Well, find them, and you will live. In the first place, you have needed a change of air for a long time. Well, suffering is a good thing too. Suffer. Mikolka perhaps is right to want suffering. I know that you don’t believe, but don’t be cunning and clever about it; give yourself to life directly, without reasoning; don’t worry: it will carry you straight to the shore and set you on your feet. What shore? How should I know? I only believe that you have a great deal of life still ahead. I know that you take my words now as a lecture learned by heart; but perhaps you will remember them later, they may be of use some day; that is why I say them. It is still a good thing that you killed only an old woman. If you had invented another theory, you might perhaps have done something a hundred million times more hideous! Perhaps you ought even to thank God; how do you know: perhaps God is keeping you for something. And you have a great heart, and fear less. Have you lost your nerve before the great fulfilment that lies ahead? No, it is shameful to lose your nerve here. If you have taken such a step, then brace yourself. This is justice now. Go and fulfil what justice demands. I know you don’t believe, but by God, life will carry you through. You will come to love it yourself later. All you need now is air, air, air!”
Raskolnikov even started.
“But who are you,” he cried, “what sort of prophet are you? From the height of what majestic calm do you deliver these wise prophecies to me?”

“Who am I? I am a finished man, nothing more. A man, perhaps, who feels and sympathises, who perhaps knows a thing or two, but a completely finished man. But you are another matter: God has prepared life for you (and who knows, perhaps with you too it will pass like smoke and nothing will come of it). Well, what if you pass into another category of people? You are not going to regret comfort, you, with your heart? What if perhaps no one sees you for too long? It is not a matter of time, but of you yourself. Become a sun, and everyone will see you. A sun must first of all be a sun. Why are you smiling again: because I am such a Schiller? And I bet you suppose that I am trying to flatter you now! Well, perhaps I really am, he-he-he! Perhaps you had better not take my word for it, Rodion Romanych, perhaps never believe me entirely; that is my nature, I agree; only I will add this: how low a man I am and how honest, you can judge for yourself, I think!”
“When do you intend to arrest me?”
“Why, I can still give you a day and a half or two to walk about. Think it over, my dear, pray to God. And it is more advantageous, by God, more advantageous.”
“And what if I run away?” Raskolnikov asked, smiling somehow strangely.

“No, you won’t run away. A peasant will run away, a fashionable sectarian will run away, the lackey of someone else’s thought, because you need only show him the tip of your little finger, like Midshipman Dyrka, and he will believe in anything you like for the rest of his life. But you no longer believe in your theory; what would you run away with? And what would you do as a fugitive? The life of a fugitive is nasty and hard, and what you need above all is life and a definite position, the air that suits you; well, is the air there yours? You will run away and come back of your own accord. You cannot do without us. And if I lock you up in the prison castle, well, you will sit there a month, two, three, and then suddenly, mark my words, you will come of your own accord, and how, perhaps, quite unexpectedly to yourself. Even an hour before you will not know that you are coming to confess. I am even sure that you will ‘think it over and decide to accept suffering’; you don’t take my word for it now, but you will settle on it yourself. Because suffering, Rodion Romanych, is a great thing; don’t look at the fact that I have grown fat; no matter, I know all the same; don’t laugh at it: there is an idea in suffering. Mikolka is right. No, you won’t run away, Rodion Romanych.”
Raskolnikov got up from his seat and took his cap. Porfiry Petrovich got up too.
“Going for a walk? It will be a fine evening, if only there isn’t a storm. Though it would be better if it freshened things up...”
He too reached for his cap.

“Please, Porfiry Petrovich, don’t take it into your head,” Raskolnikov said with stern insistence, “that I have confessed to you today. You are a strange man, and I listened to you out of mere curiosity. I have confessed nothing to you... Remember that.”

“Why, yes, I know, I will remember; look at that, he is even trembling. Don’t worry, my dear; your will be done. Walk about a little; only you mustn’t walk about too much. Just in case, I have one more little request for you,” he added, lowering his voice. “It is a ticklish little one, but important: if, that is, just in case (which, however, I don’t believe and consider you quite incapable of), if by chance, well, just in case, the wish should come to you during these forty or fifty hours to end the business somehow differently, in some fantastic way, to raise your hands against yourself like that (an absurd supposition, but you will forgive me for it), then leave a short but detailed little note. Just two lines, just two little lines, and mention the stone: it will be more noble, sir. Well, sir, goodbye... Good thoughts, good beginnings!”

Porfiry went out, somehow stooping and as if avoiding looking at Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov went to the window and waited with irritable impatience for the moment when, by his reckoning, the other would come out into the street and walk some distance away. Then he hurriedly left the room himself.
## CHAPTER III

He was hurrying to Svidrigailov’s. What he could hope for from this man he did not know himself. But in this man lay hidden some kind of power over him. Having once realised this, he could not rest, and now, besides, the time had come.
On the way one question especially tormented him: had Svidrigailov been to Porfiry’s?
As far as he could judge, and he would have sworn to it, no, he had not! He thought again and again, recalled Porfiry’s whole visit, considered: no, he had not, of course he had not!
But if he had not been yet, would he go to Porfiry or not?

For the time being it seemed to him that he would not. Why? He could not have explained that either, but even if he could have, he would not have racked his brains over it much just now. All this tormented him, and at the same time he somehow had no time for it. Strangely, perhaps no one would have believed it, but he cared somehow weakly and absently about his present, immediate fate. Something else tormented him, something far more important, extraordinary, about himself and no one else, but something different, something essential. Besides, he felt a boundless moral weariness, though his reason worked better this morning than in all these last days.

And was it worth it now, after all that had happened, to try to overcome all these new paltry difficulties? Was it worth it, for instance, to try to intrigue so that Svidrigailov would not go to Porfiry; to study, to find out, to waste time on some Svidrigailov!
Oh, how sick he was of all this!

And yet he was still hurrying to Svidrigailov’s; was he not expecting something new from him, some pointers, a way out? People clutch at straws, after all! Was it not fate, or some instinct, bringing them together? Perhaps it was only weariness, despair; perhaps what he needed was not Svidrigailov but someone else, and Svidrigailov had simply turned up. Sonya? But why would he go to Sonya now? To ask for her tears again? And besides, Sonya was frightening to him. Sonya stood for an inexorable sentence, a decision without change. Here it was either her road or his. Especially at this moment he was not able to see her. No, wouldn’t it be better to try Svidrigailov: what was he? And he could not help admitting inwardly that the man had indeed seemed for a long time to be somehow necessary to him for something.

Well, but what could there be in common between them? Even their villainy could not be the same. This man was very unpleasant besides, obviously extremely depraved, certainly cunning and deceitful, perhaps very wicked. Such stories went around about him. It was true that he had busied himself on behalf of Katerina Ivanovna’s children; but who knew for what purpose, and what it meant? This man always had some intentions and projects.

All these days one more thought had constantly flashed through Raskolnikov’s mind and terribly disturbed him, though he even tried to drive it away, so heavy was it for him! He sometimes thought: Svidrigailov had kept hovering round him, and was hovering round him now; Svidrigailov had learned his secret; Svidrigailov had had designs on Dunya. And what if he still had them? It could almost certainly be said that he had. And what if now, having learned his secret and so gained power over him, he wanted to use it as a weapon against Dunya?

This thought sometimes tormented him even in his sleep, but for the first time it came to him as consciously and vividly as now, when he was going to Svidrigailov’s. This thought alone drove him to gloomy fury. In the first place, everything would change then, even in his own position: he would have to reveal his secret to Dunechka at once. He would perhaps have to give himself up, to keep Dunechka from some incautious step. A letter? This morning Dunya had received some letter! From whom in Petersburg could she receive letters? (Luzhin, perhaps?) It was true that Razumikhin was keeping guard there; but Razumikhin knew nothing. Perhaps he ought to reveal himself to Razumikhin too? Raskolnikov thought of it with loathing.

“In any case I must see Svidrigailov as soon as possible,” he decided finally to himself. “Thank God, here it is not so much the details that are needed as the essence of the matter; but if, if only he is capable of it, if Svidrigailov is plotting anything against Dunya, then...”

Raskolnikov was so tired from all this time, from this whole month, that he could no longer resolve such questions except by one decision: “Then I will kill him,” he thought in cold despair. A heavy feeling gripped his heart; he stopped in the middle of the street and began to look round: what road was he taking, and where had he got to? He was on — Prospect, thirty or forty paces from the Haymarket, which he had passed. The whole second floor of the house on the left was taken up by a tavern. All the windows were wide open; the tavern, judging by the figures moving in the windows, was packed full. In the hall singers were pouring out their songs, a clarinet and a violin were ringing, and a Turkish drum was thundering. Women’s shrieks could be heard. He was about to go back, puzzled why he had turned onto — Prospect, when suddenly, at one of the end windows of the tavern, open like the rest, he saw Svidrigailov sitting right by the window at a tea table, with a pipe in his teeth. This struck him terribly, to the point of horror. Svidrigailov was watching and examining him in silence, and, which also struck Raskolnikov at once, seemed to have been about to get up, so as to slip away quietly before he was noticed. Raskolnikov at once pretended that he had not noticed him either and was looking aside, lost in thought, while he went on watching him out of the corner of his eye. His heart was beating anxiously. So it was: Svidrigailov obviously did not want to be seen. He took the pipe from his lips and was about to hide; but, having got up and pushed back his chair, he probably noticed suddenly that Raskolnikov saw him and was watching him. Something like the scene of their first meeting at Raskolnikov’s, during his sleep, took place between them. A roguish smile appeared on Svidrigailov’s face and grew broader and broader. Each knew that both saw and were watching each other. At last Svidrigailov burst out laughing loudly.
“Well, well! come in, then, if you want to; I’m here!” he shouted from the window.
Raskolnikov went up into the tavern.

He found him in a very small back room with one window, adjoining the big hall, where at twenty little tables, to the shouts of a desperate chorus of singers, merchants, officials and all sorts of people were drinking tea. From somewhere came the click of billiard balls. On the little table before Svidrigailov stood an opened bottle of champagne and a glass half full of wine. In the little room there were also an organ-grinder boy with a small hand organ and a healthy, red-cheeked girl in a tucked-up striped skirt and a Tyrolean hat with ribbons, a singer of about eighteen, who, in spite of the choral song in the other room, was singing to the organ-grinder’s accompaniment, in a rather husky contralto, some lackey’s song...
“Well, that’s enough!” Svidrigailov interrupted her as Raskolnikov came in.
The girl broke off at once and stopped in respectful expectation. She had been singing her rhymed lackey’s ditty with a kind of serious and respectful shade in her face too.
“Hey, Philip, a glass!” shouted Svidrigailov.
“I won’t drink any wine,” said Raskolnikov.

“As you like; it’s not for you. Drink, Katya! Nothing more will be needed today; off you go!” He poured her a whole glass of wine and put down a yellow banknote. Katya drank the glass at one go, as women drink wine, that is, without stopping, in twenty swallows, took the note, kissed Svidrigailov’s hand, which he very seriously allowed her to kiss, and went out of the room, and the boy with the organ trailed after her.
