They had both been brought in from the street. Svidrigailov had not been living in Petersburg even a week, and already everything around him was on a kind of patriarchal footing. The tavern waiter, Philip, was also already an “acquaintance” and was being obsequious. The door to the hall could be locked; Svidrigailov was at home in this room and perhaps spent whole days in it. The tavern was dirty, wretched, and not even middling.

“I was going to see you and looking for you,” Raskolnikov began, “but why did I suddenly turn onto — Prospect from the Haymarket just now! I never turn this way or come here. I turn right from the Haymarket. And this isn’t the way to your place either. I had only just turned, and here you are! That is strange!”
“Why don’t you say straight out: it’s a miracle!”
“Because perhaps it is only chance.”

“What a twist all these people have!” laughed Svidrigailov. “They won’t admit it, even if inside they believe in a miracle! You say yourself that it is ‘perhaps’ only chance. And what little cowards everyone here is about their own opinion, you can’t imagine, Rodion Romanych! I don’t mean you. You have an opinion of your own and were not afraid to have it. That is how you caught my curiosity.”
“Nothing else?”
“Why, that is enough.”
Svidrigailov was obviously in an excited state, but only a tiny bit; he had drunk only half a glass of wine.
“It seems to me that you came to see me before you knew that I was capable of having what you call an opinion of my own,” Raskolnikov remarked.

“Well, then it was a different matter. Everyone has his own steps. And as for the miracle, I will tell you that you seem to have slept through these last two or three days. I named this tavern to you myself, and there was no miracle in your coming straight here; I explained the whole way to you myself, told you the place where it stands and the hours when I can be found here. Do you remember?”
“I forgot,” answered Raskolnikov in surprise.

“I believe you. I told you twice. The address was stamped on your memory mechanically. And you turned here mechanically, and yet strictly according to the address, without knowing it yourself. Even as I told you, I didn’t expect that you had understood me. You give yourself away far too much, Rodion Romanych. And here is something else: I am convinced that in Petersburg many people talk to themselves as they walk. It is a city of half-mad people. If we had sciences, then doctors, lawyers and philosophers could make most precious studies of Petersburg, each in his own field. Rarely will you find so many gloomy, harsh and strange influences on the soul of man as in Petersburg. The climatic influences alone are worth something! And yet it is the administrative centre of all Russia, and its character must be reflected in everything. But that is not the point now; the point is that I have several times watched you from the side. You come out of the house holding your head up still. After twenty paces you are already lowering it, folding your hands behind your back. You look, and obviously see nothing either before you or at the sides any more. At last you begin moving your lips and talking to yourself, and sometimes you free a hand and declaim, and at last you stop in the middle of the road for a long time. That is very bad, sir. Perhaps someone besides me notices you, and that is not to your advantage. It is all the same to me, essentially, and I won’t cure you, but of course you understand me.”
“And do you know that I am being followed?” asked Raskolnikov, glancing at him searchingly.
“No, I know nothing,” Svidrigailov answered, as if surprised.
“Well, then let us leave me in peace,” Raskolnikov muttered, frowning.
“Very well, let us leave you in peace.”

“Tell me instead: if you come here to drink, and twice named this place yourself for me to come and see you here, why, when I looked up at the window from the street just now, were you hiding and wanting to leave? I noticed that very well.”

“He-he! And why, when I was standing on your threshold that time, were you lying on your sofa with your eyes closed, pretending to be asleep, when you were not asleep at all? I noticed that very well.”
“I may have had... reasons... you know them yourself.”
“And I may have had my reasons, though you won’t learn them.”

Raskolnikov rested his right elbow on the table, propped his chin from below with the fingers of his right hand and stared intently at Svidrigailov. For a minute he examined his face, which had always struck him before too. It was a strange face, as if like a mask: white, ruddy, with ruddy, scarlet lips, with a light fair beard and rather thick fair hair still. The eyes were somehow too blue, and their look somehow too heavy and fixed. There was something terribly unpleasant in this handsome face, which was extremely youthful for his years. Svidrigailov’s clothes were smart, summery, light; he was especially smart in his linen. On his finger was a huge ring with a precious stone.

“Must I really bother with you too?” Raskolnikov said suddenly, coming straight out into the open with convulsive impatience. “Though perhaps you are the most dangerous of men, if you wish to do harm, I don’t want to break myself any more. I will show you right now that I don’t value myself as much as you probably think. Know, then, that I have come to tell you straight out that if you keep your former intention regarding my sister, and if for that purpose you think of making use of anything that has been discovered lately, I will kill you before you get me put in prison. My word is sure: you know that I can keep it. Second, if you want to declare anything to me (because all this time it has seemed to me that you wanted to tell me something), then declare it quickly, because time is precious, and perhaps very soon it will be too late.”
“But where are you hurrying to like this?” asked Svidrigailov, examining him curiously.
“Everyone has his own steps,” Raskolnikov said gloomily and impatiently.

“You invited frankness yourself just now, and at the very first question you refuse to answer,” Svidrigailov remarked with a smile. “You keep thinking I have some purposes, and so you look at me suspiciously. Well, that is perfectly understandable in your position. But however much I wish to become close to you, I still won’t take the trouble to persuade you otherwise. By God, the game isn’t worth the candle, and I didn’t intend to talk to you about anything so very special.”
“Then why did you need me so much? You were hovering round me, weren’t you?”

“Why, simply as a curious subject for observation. I liked you for the fantastic nature of your position, that’s what! Besides, you are the brother of a person who interested me very much, and finally, from that very person, at one time, I heard a terrible lot about you, and often, from which I concluded that you have great influence over her; isn’t that enough? He-he-he! However, I admit that your question is very complex for me, and it is hard for me to answer it. Well, for example, you came to me now not only on business but for something new, didn’t you? Isn’t that so? Isn’t that so?” Svidrigailov insisted with a roguish smile. “Well, imagine after that that I myself, while still on my way here, in the train, was counting on you, that you too would tell me something new, and that I would manage to borrow something from you! That’s how rich we are!”
“Borrow what?”

“What shall I tell you? How do I know what? You see what a wretched little tavern I sit in all the time, and I enjoy it; that is, not exactly enjoy it, but one has to sit somewhere. Well, take that poor Katya; you saw her?.. Well, if I were, for example, at least a glutton, a club gourmet, but look what I can eat!” (He jabbed a finger at the corner, where on a little table, on a tin plate, stood the remains of a dreadful beefsteak with potatoes.) “By the way, have you dined? I had a snack and want no more. Wine, for example, I don’t drink at all. Nothing but champagne, and even of champagne only one glass a whole evening, and even that gives me a headache. I ordered it now to wind myself up, because I am going somewhere, and you see me in a special frame of mind. That is why I hid earlier like a schoolboy, because I thought you would hinder me; but it seems” (he took out his watch) “I can stay with you an hour; it is half past four now. Would you believe it, if only there were something; well, to be a landowner, well, a father, well, an uhlan, a photographer, a journalist... n-nothing, no speciality! Sometimes it’s even boring. Really, I thought you would tell me something new.”
“But who are you, and why have you come here?”
“Who am I? You know: a nobleman; I served two years in the cavalry, then just loafed about here in Petersburg, then married Marfa Petrovna and lived in the country. There is my biography!”
“You are a gambler, I believe?”
“No, what kind of gambler am I. A card sharper is not a gambler.”
“So you were a card sharper?”
“Yes, I was a card sharper.”
“Well, and did you get beaten?”
“It happened. Why?”
“Well, then you could have challenged someone to a duel... and in general it livens one up.”
“I won’t contradict you, and besides, I am no master at philosophising. I confess to you that I came here sooner mostly on account of women.”
“When you had only just buried Marfa Petrovna?”
“Well, yes,” Svidrigailov smiled with disarming frankness. “What of it? You seem to find something wrong in my talking about women like this?”
“That is, do I find anything wrong in depravity, or not?”

“In depravity! Well, so that’s where you’re going! But anyway, in order: first I will answer you about women in general; you know, I am inclined to chatter. Tell me, why should I restrain myself? Why give up women, if I am fond of them at least? At least it is an occupation.”
“So that is all you hope for here, depravity?”

“Well, what of it, depravity then! They’ve got so attached to depravity. But I do like a direct question, at least. In this depravity there is at least something constant, even founded in nature and not subject to fancy, something that stays in the blood like an ever-burning coal, always kindling, which you won’t put out for a long time yet, perhaps not so soon even with the years. You will agree yourself, isn’t it an occupation of its kind?”
“What is there to rejoice in? It is a disease, and a dangerous one.”

“Ah, so that’s where you’re going! I agree that it is a disease, like everything that goes beyond measure (and here one is bound to go beyond measure), but in the first place it is one way with one man and another way with another, and in the second, of course, keep measure in everything, calculation, even a base one, but what is to be done? If it weren’t for this, one would have to shoot oneself, perhaps. I agree that a decent man is obliged to be bored, but still...”
“And could you shoot yourself?”

“Come now!” Svidrigailov parried with disgust. “Do me the favour of not talking about that,” he added hastily, and even without any of the bravado that showed in all his previous words. Even his face seemed to change. “I confess to an unforgivable weakness, but what is to be done: I am afraid of death and don’t like it when people talk about it. Do you know that I am partly a mystic?”
“Ah! Marfa Petrovna’s ghosts! Well, do they keep coming?”

“Never mind them, don’t mention them; there haven’t been any yet in Petersburg; and the devil take them!” he cried with a kind of irritable look. “No, let us rather talk about... though, however... Hm! Eh, there is little time, I can’t stay with you long, and that’s a pity! There would be something to tell.”
“And what is it you have, a woman?”
“Yes, a woman, just one unexpected incident... no, that’s not what I mean.”
“Well, and the vileness of all these surroundings no longer affects you? You have already lost the strength to stop?”

“So you lay claim to strength too? He-he-he! You surprised me just now, Rodion Romanych, though I knew beforehand that it would be so. You talk to me about depravity and aesthetics! You are a Schiller, you are an idealist! All this, of course, is as it should be, and one would have to be surprised if it were otherwise, but still, somehow it is strange in reality... Ah, it’s a pity there is so little time, because you yourself are a most curious subject! And by the way, do you like Schiller? I am terribly fond of him.”
“But what a braggart you are, though!” said Raskolnikov with some disgust.

“Well, by God, no!” answered Svidrigailov, laughing. “But then, I won’t argue; let me be a braggart; but why not brag a little, when it is harmless? I lived seven years in the country at Marfa Petrovna’s, and so, falling now on an intelligent man like you, intelligent and in the highest degree curious, I am simply glad to chat; besides, I have drunk this half glass of wine and it has gone to my head a tiny bit. And above all, there is one circumstance which has wound me up very much, but about which I... will keep silent. Where are you going?” Svidrigailov asked suddenly, in alarm.

Raskolnikov had begun to get up. He felt heavy, and stifled, and somehow awkward at having come here. He had become convinced that Svidrigailov was the emptiest and most worthless villain in the world.

“E-eh! Sit down, stay,” Svidrigailov begged. “And order yourself some tea at least. Well, sit down; well, I won’t talk nonsense, about myself, that is. I’ll tell you something. Well, would you like me to tell you how a woman, to use your style, tried to ‘save’ me? It will even be an answer to your first question, because that person is your sister. May I tell it? And we’ll kill time.”
“Tell it, but I hope that you...”
“Oh, don’t worry! Besides, Avdotya Romanovna can inspire nothing but the deepest respect even in such a nasty and empty man as I am.”
## CHAPTER IV

“You know, perhaps (indeed I told you myself),” Svidrigailov began, “that I was in the debtors’ prison here, for an enormous sum, and without the slightest means in view for paying it. There is no need to go into detail about how Marfa Petrovna bought me out then; do you know to what a degree of stupefaction a woman can sometimes love? She was an honest woman, far from stupid (though completely uneducated). Imagine, then, that this very jealous and honest woman resolved to condescend, after many terrible frenzies and reproaches, to a kind of contract with me, which she kept all the time of our marriage. The point is that she was considerably older than I, and besides, she always kept a clove of some sort in her mouth. I had enough swinishness in my soul, and a kind of honesty of my own, to tell her straight out that I could not be completely faithful to her. This confession drove her to frenzy, but it seems that my coarse frankness pleased her in a way: ‘So he doesn’t want to deceive me himself, since he declares it beforehand’; well, and for a jealous woman that is the first thing. After long tears, a verbal contract of the following kind was made between us: first, I would never leave Marfa Petrovna and would always remain her husband; second, I would not go away anywhere without her permission; third, I would never take a permanent mistress; fourth, in return for this, Marfa Petrovna allowed me to cast an eye on the maidservants sometimes, but not otherwise than with her secret knowledge; fifth, God forbid that I should fall in love with a woman of our own class; sixth, if by chance, which God forbid, some passion should visit me, a great and serious one, then I must reveal it to Marfa Petrovna. As regards this last point, Marfa Petrovna was, however, fairly calm all the time; she was an intelligent woman, and therefore could not look on me otherwise than as a profligate and a rake, incapable of serious love. But an intelligent woman and a jealous woman are two different things, and there lies the trouble. However, to judge certain people impartially, one must give up beforehand certain preconceived views and the everyday habit of the people and things that usually surround us. I have the right to hope for this from your judgement more than from anyone’s. Perhaps you have already heard a great deal that is funny and absurd about Marfa Petrovna. She did indeed have some very funny habits; but I will tell you straight out that I sincerely regret the countless sorrows of which I was the cause. Well, and that is enough, I think, for a very decent oraison funèbre, a funeral oration, by the tenderest husband for the tenderest wife. When we quarrelled, I was silent for the most part and did not get irritated, and this playing the gentleman almost always achieved its aim; it had an effect on her, and she even liked it; there were times when she was even proud of me. But she could not stand your sister all the same. And how did it come about that she risked taking such a beauty into her house as a governess! I explain it by Marfa Petrovna’s being a passionate and impressionable woman, and that, quite simply, she herself fell in love, literally fell in love, with your sister. Well, and Avdotya Romanovna too! I understood very well at the first glance that things were bad here, and what do you think? I resolved not even to raise my eyes to her. But Avdotya Romanovna herself made the first step: would you believe it or not? Would you believe too that Marfa Petrovna went so far as to be angry with me at first for my constant silence about your sister, for my being so indifferent to her incessant, adoring remarks about Avdotya Romanovna? I don’t understand myself what she wanted! Well, of course, Marfa Petrovna told Avdotya Romanovna the whole inside story about me. She had an unfortunate trait of telling absolutely everyone all our family secrets and complaining about me to everyone incessantly; how could she pass by such a new and beautiful friend? I suppose they talked of nothing but me, and without doubt Avdotya Romanovna came to know all those gloomy, mysterious tales that are ascribed to me... I bet you have heard something of that kind too?”
“I have. Luzhin accused you of even being the cause of a child’s death. Is it true?”

“Do me the favour of leaving all these vulgarities alone,” Svidrigailov declined with disgust and peevishly. “If you absolutely must know about all that nonsense, I will tell you some time separately, but now...”
“There was talk too of some footman of yours in the country, and that you were the cause of something there too.”
“Do me the favour, enough!” Svidrigailov interrupted again with obvious impatience.
“Isn’t that the footman who came to fill your pipe after his death... you told me about it yourself?” Raskolnikov was growing more and more irritated.

Svidrigailov looked at Raskolnikov attentively, and it seemed to the latter that a malicious smile flashed for an instant in that look, like lightning; but Svidrigailov restrained himself and answered very politely:

“That is the very one. I see that all this interests you extremely too, and I shall consider it my duty, at the first convenient opportunity, to satisfy your curiosity on every point. The devil take it! I see that I really might seem a romantic figure to someone. Judge, then, how much I am obliged after that to thank the late Marfa Petrovna for having told your sister so many mysterious and curious things about me. I dare not judge the impression; but in any case it was to my advantage. With all Avdotya Romanovna’s natural aversion to me, and in spite of my constant gloomy and repellent air, she came at last to pity me, to pity a lost man. And when a girl’s heart comes to pity, that of course is most dangerous of all for her. Then she is sure to want to ‘save’, and bring to reason, and resurrect, and call to nobler aims, and revive to a new life and activity; well, we know what can be dreamed of in that line. I grasped at once that the little bird was flying into the net of its own accord, and for my part I got ready. You seem to be frowning, Rodion Romanych? Never mind, sir; the business, as you know, came to nothing. (The devil take it, how much wine I am drinking!) You know, I have always been sorry, from the very beginning, that fate did not let your sister be born in the second or third century of our era, somewhere as the daughter of a ruling princeling or some governor or proconsul in Asia Minor. She would undoubtedly have been one of those who suffered martyrdom, and of course she would have smiled when they burned her breast with red-hot pincers. She would have gone to it on purpose herself, and in the fourth and fifth centuries she would have gone off into the Egyptian desert and lived there thirty years, feeding on roots, raptures and visions. That is all she thirsts for herself, and she demands to take some torment for someone as soon as possible, and if you don’t give her this torment, she might jump out of a window. I have heard something about a certain Mr Razumikhin. He is a sensible fellow, they say (as his name shows; a seminarist, I suppose), so let him take care of your sister. In a word, I think I have understood her, and I count that an honour to myself. But then, that is, at the beginning of our acquaintance, you know yourself, one is always somehow more frivolous and more stupid, one looks wrongly, one sees the wrong thing. The devil take it, why is she so beautiful? It’s not my fault! In a word, with me it began with the most irresistible sensual impulse. Avdotya Romanovna is chaste, terribly, unheard-of and unseen chaste. (Note that I am telling you this about your sister as a fact. She is chaste, perhaps to the point of illness, in spite of all her broad mind, and it will harm her.) There was a girl with us then, Parasha, black-eyed Parasha, who had just been brought from another village, a maidservant, whom I had never seen before; very pretty, but incredibly stupid: she burst into tears, raised a howl through the whole yard, and there was a scandal. Once, after dinner, Avdotya Romanovna deliberately sought me out alone in an avenue in the garden and with flashing eyes demanded that I leave poor Parasha in peace. That was almost our first conversation alone together. Of course I considered it an honour to satisfy her wish, tried to pretend to be struck, embarrassed; well, in a word, I played the part not badly. Relations began, mysterious conversations, moral lessons, instructions, entreaties, supplications, even tears; would you believe it, even tears! That is how strong the passion for propaganda becomes in some girls! I, of course, laid everything on my fate, pretended to be hungering and thirsting for light, and at last brought into play the greatest and most unshakeable means of conquering a woman’s heart, a means that never deceives anyone and acts decisively on every one of them, without any exception. That means is well known: flattery. There is nothing in the world harder than straightforwardness, and nothing easier than flattery. If there is only a hundredth part of a false note in straightforwardness, a dissonance occurs at once, and after it a scandal. But if in flattery everything, down to the last note, is false, even then it is pleasant and is listened to not without pleasure; with a coarse pleasure, perhaps, but still with pleasure. And however coarse the flattery, at least half of it is sure to seem true. And this is so for all levels of development and all strata of society. Even a vestal virgin can be seduced by flattery. And about ordinary people there is nothing to say. I can’t remember without laughing how I once seduced a lady devoted to her husband, her children and her virtues. How merry it was, and how little work it took! And the lady really was virtuous, at least in her own way. My whole tactic consisted in simply being crushed every minute and falling prostrate before her chastity. I flattered shamelessly, and as soon as I managed to get a pressure of the hand, even a glance, I would reproach myself for having wrested it from her by force, that she had resisted, that she had resisted so much that I would certainly never have got anything if I had not been so depraved myself; that she, in her innocence, had not foreseen the treachery and had yielded unintentionally, without knowing it herself, without being aware, and so on and so on. In a word, I achieved everything, and my lady remained in the highest degree convinced that she was innocent and chaste and fulfilled all her duties and obligations, and had fallen quite by accident. And how angry she was with me when I told her in the end that, in my sincere conviction, she had been seeking pleasure exactly as much as I. Poor Marfa Petrovna too was terribly susceptible to flattery, and if only I had wanted, I could certainly have had her whole estate made over to me in her lifetime. (But I am drinking a terrible lot of wine and chattering.) I hope you won’t be angry if I mention now that the same effect began to come about with Avdotya Romanovna too. But I was stupid and impatient myself and spoiled the whole thing. Several times before (and once somehow especially) Avdotya Romanovna had terribly disliked the expression of my eyes; would you believe that? In a word, a certain fire flared up in them more and more strongly and incautiously, which frightened her and at last became hateful to her. There is no need to tell the details, but we parted. Then I acted stupidly again. I began jeering in the coarsest way at all these propagandas and conversions; Parasha came on the scene again, and not she alone; in a word, Sodom began. Oh, if you had seen, Rodion Romanych, even once in your life, your sister’s eyes as they sometimes know how to flash! It doesn’t matter that I am drunk now and have drunk a whole glass of wine already; I am telling the truth; I assure you that I dreamed of that look; at last I could not bear even the rustle of her dress. Really, I thought I would have a fit of the falling sickness; I never imagined I could come to such a frenzy. In a word, it was necessary to make peace; but that was already impossible. And imagine what I did then? To what a degree of stupidity fury can bring a man! Never undertake anything in fury, Rodion Romanych. Reckoning that Avdotya Romanovna was, after all, essentially a beggar (ah, forgive me, I didn’t mean that... but isn’t it all the same, if the same idea is expressed?), in a word, that she lived by the work of her hands, that she was supporting both her mother and you (ah, the devil, you are frowning again...), I resolved to offer her all my money (I could have raised up to thirty thousand even then) on condition that she run away with me, even here to Petersburg. Of course I would have sworn eternal love, bliss, and so on and so on. Would you believe it, I was so smitten then that if she had said to me: cut Marfa Petrovna’s throat or poison her and marry me, it would have been done at once! But everything ended in the catastrophe you already know of, and you can judge for yourself to what fury I could come on learning that Marfa Petrovna had got hold of that vilest of pettifoggers, Luzhin, and had almost put together a marriage, which essentially would have been the same thing as I had proposed. Isn’t that so? Isn’t that so? It is, isn’t it? I notice you have begun listening very attentively... an interesting young man...”

Svidrigailov struck the table with his fist in impatience. He had turned red. Raskolnikov saw clearly that the glass or glass and a half of champagne which he had drunk, sipping imperceptibly, had had a morbid effect on him, and he resolved to take advantage of the opportunity. Svidrigailov was very suspicious to him.
“Well, after this I am fully convinced that you came here too with my sister in view,” he said to Svidrigailov directly and without concealment, so as to irritate him still more.
“Eh, come now,” Svidrigailov seemed suddenly to check himself. “I told you... and besides, your sister can’t bear me.”
“Yes, I am convinced of that too, that she can’t; but that is not the point now.”

“And you are convinced that she can’t?” (Svidrigailov narrowed his eyes and smiled mockingly.) “You are right, she doesn’t love me; but never vouch for the things that have passed between husband and wife or lover and mistress. There is always one little corner there that remains unknown to the whole world and is known only to the two of them. Do you vouch that Avdotya Romanovna looked on me with aversion?”
“From certain words and little words of yours during your story I notice that you have your own designs even now, and the most urgent intentions, on Dunya; vile ones, of course.”
“What! Such words and little words slipped out of me?” Svidrigailov suddenly took fright most naively, not paying the slightest attention to the epithet applied to his intentions.
“They are slipping out even now. Well, what are you so afraid of, for instance? What have you suddenly taken fright at now?”

“I am afraid and take fright? Take fright at you? It is rather for you to be afraid of me, cher ami, my dear friend. And what nonsense this is, though... But then, I have got tipsy, I see it; I nearly let something slip again. To the devil with wine! Hey, water!”
He seized the bottle and without ceremony flung it out of the window. Philip brought water.

“All this is nonsense,” said Svidrigailov, wetting a towel and putting it to his head, “but I can check you with one word and reduce all your suspicions to dust. Do you know, for instance, that I am getting married?”
“You told me that before too.”

“Did I? I forgot. But then I couldn’t speak positively, because I hadn’t even seen the bride yet; I only intended it. Well, but now I have a bride, and the thing is done, and if it were not for business, urgent business, I would certainly take you and drive you to them now, because I want to ask your advice. Hey, the devil! Only ten minutes left. You see, look at the clock; but then, I will tell you, because it is an interesting little thing, my marriage, in its way, that is; where are you going? Leaving again?”
“No, I won’t leave now.”

“Won’t leave at all? We shall see! I will take you there, that is true, and show you the bride, but not now; now it will soon be time for you to go. You go right, I go left. Do you know this Resslich? This same Resslich in whose place I am living now, eh? Do you hear? No, what do you think, she is the very one about whom they say that the girl, in the water, in winter... well, do you hear? Do you hear? Well, she cooked all this up for me; ‘you are so bored,’ she says, ‘amuse yourself for a while.’ And I am a gloomy, boring man, you know. You think I am merry? No, gloomy: I do no harm, but sit in a corner; sometimes no one can get a word out of me for three days. And this Resslich, the hussy, I tell you, has this in mind: I shall get bored, abandon my wife and go away, and the wife will fall to her, and she will put her into circulation; in our class, that is, and higher. There is, she says, a certain paralysed father, a retired official; he sits in an armchair and hasn’t moved his legs for two years. There is a mother too, she says, a sensible lady, the mama. A son is serving somewhere in the provinces and doesn’t help. A daughter has married and doesn’t visit, and they have two little nephews on their hands (as if their own were not enough), and they have taken their youngest daughter out of the gymnasium before she finished the course; in a month she will just turn sixteen, so in a month she can be married off. To me, that is. We went; how funny it is with them; I introduce myself: a landowner, a widower, of a well-known family, with such and such connections, with capital; well, what of it that I am fifty and she isn’t even sixteen? Who looks at that? Well, but it is tempting, isn’t it? It is tempting, ha-ha! You should have seen how I got talking with papa and mama! It would be worth paying just to see me at that moment. She comes out, curtseys; well, you can imagine, still in a short little dress, an unopened little bud, she blushes, flushes like the dawn (they had told her, of course). I don’t know what you think about women’s faces, but in my opinion those sixteen years, those still childish little eyes, that timidity and those little tears of bashfulness, in my opinion that is better than beauty, and she is pretty as a picture besides. Fair little hairs, fluffed up in little curls like a lamb’s, plump little scarlet lips, little feet, a delight!.. Well, we were introduced; I announced that I was in a hurry on account of family circumstances, and the very next day, that is, the day before yesterday, we were given their blessing. Since then, as soon as I arrive, I take her on my knees at once and don’t let her down... Well, she flushes like the dawn, and I kiss her every minute; mama, of course, impresses on her that this is your husband and this is how it must be; in a word, raspberries! And this present state of being a bridegroom is perhaps even better than being a husband. Here is what they call la nature et la vérité, nature and truth! Ha-ha! I have talked with her a couple of times; the girl is far from stupid; sometimes she gives me such a stealthy glance that it simply burns. And you know, her little face is like Raphael’s Madonna. The Sistine Madonna has a fantastic face, the face of a sorrowing holy fool; hasn’t that struck you? Well, something in that style. As soon as we had been blessed, the next day I brought fifteen hundred roubles’ worth: a set of diamonds, another of pearls, and a lady’s silver dressing case, this big, with all sorts of things, so that even she, the Madonna, flushed in her little face. I took her on my knees yesterday, and rather too unceremoniously, I suppose: she flushed all over and little tears spurted out, but she doesn’t want to show it, and she is all aflame herself. Everyone went out for a minute, we were left quite alone, and suddenly she throws herself on my neck (for the first time herself), embraces me with both little arms, kisses me and swears that she will be an obedient, faithful and good wife to me, that she will make me happy, that she will devote her whole life, every minute of her life, she will sacrifice everything, everything, and for all this she wishes to have from me only my respect, and ‘I need nothing more,’ she says, ‘nothing, nothing, no presents!’ You will agree yourself that to hear such a confession alone from such a sixteen-year-old little angel, in a tulle dress, with fluffed-up little curls, with the blush of girlish shame and little tears of enthusiasm in her eyes, you will agree yourself, it is rather tempting. It is tempting, isn’t it? It is worth something, eh? Well, it is worth it, isn’t it? Well... well, listen... well, let’s go to my bride... only not now!”
“In a word, it is this monstrous difference in age and development that arouses your lust! And are you really going to marry like this?”

“Why not? Certainly. Everyone looks after himself, and he lives merriest of all who knows best how to deceive himself. Ha-ha! But why have you driven into virtue with the whole shaft like that? Spare me, my dear fellow, I am a sinful man. He-he-he!”
“You did, however, provide for Katerina Ivanovna’s children. But then... but then you had your reasons for that... I understand everything now.”

“I love children in general; I am very fond of children,” Svidrigailov laughed loudly. “On that score I can even tell you a most curious episode, which is still going on. On the very first day after my arrival I went round to various of these sewers; well, after seven years I simply flung myself on them. You probably notice that I am in no hurry to get together with my own company, with my former friends and acquaintances. Well, and I shall hold out without them as long as possible. You know: in the country at Marfa Petrovna’s I was tormented to death by memories of all these mysterious places and little places, in which, if you know, you can find a lot. The devil take it! The people drink, the educated young burn out from inaction in impossible dreams and fancies, they deform themselves in theories; Jews have come from somewhere and hide money, and all the rest are debauched. From the first hours this city breathed on me with a familiar smell. I happened on a so-called dancing evening, a terrible sewer (and I love sewers with a little dirt in them, precisely), well, of course, a cancan such as doesn’t exist anywhere and never existed in my time. Yes, sir, there is progress in that. Suddenly I look, a girl of about thirteen, very prettily dressed, is dancing with a certain virtuoso; another is facing her, vis-à-vis. Her mother is sitting on a chair against the wall. Well, you can imagine what a cancan it was! The girl is embarrassed, blushes, at last takes offence and begins to cry. The virtuoso picks her up and begins to whirl her round and perform in front of her; everyone around laughs, and (I love our public at such moments, even a cancan public) they laugh and shout: ‘Serves her right, that’s how it should be! Don’t bring children!’ Well, I don’t care a straw, and it’s none of my business whether they console themselves logically or not! I at once marked out my place, sat down by the mother and began saying that I too was new to the place, what boors they all were here, that they didn’t know how to distinguish true merit and to show due respect; I let it be known that I had a lot of money; I invited her to let me drive them home in my carriage; drove them home, got acquainted (they were living in some little closet, sublet from lodgers; they had only just arrived). I was told that she and her daughter could only regard my acquaintance as an honour; I learn that they have neither stick nor stone, and have come to petition about something in some government office; I offer my services, money; I learn that they went to the evening by mistake, thinking that dancing really was taught there; I offer for my part to help with the education of the young lady, in French and dancing. They accept with rapture, consider it an honour, and I still know them... If you like, we’ll go, only not now.”
“Stop it, stop your vile, low anecdotes, you depraved, low, lustful man!”
“Our Schiller, our Schiller, our Schiller! Où va-t-elle la vertu se nicher? Where will virtue make its nest next? And you know, I will tell you such things on purpose, to hear your cries. A delight!”
“I should think so; am I not ridiculous to myself at this moment?” Raskolnikov muttered angrily.
Svidrigailov laughed at the top of his voice; at last he called Philip, paid and began to get up.
“Well, how drunk I am, assez causé, enough talk!” he said. “A delight!”

“Of course you feel delight,” cried Raskolnikov, getting up too. “Isn’t it a delight for a worn-out profligate to tell of such adventures, with some monstrous intention of the same kind in view, and in such circumstances, and to such a man as I... It inflames you.”

“Well, if so,” Svidrigailov answered even with some surprise, examining Raskolnikov, “if so, then you are a decent cynic yourself. At least you contain an enormous amount of material. You can be aware of much, much... and you can do much too. Well, but that’s enough. I sincerely regret that I have talked with you so little, but you won’t get away from me... Just wait...”

Svidrigailov went out of the tavern. Raskolnikov followed him. Svidrigailov, however, was not very drunk; it had gone to his head only for a moment, and the tipsiness was passing with every minute. He was very preoccupied with something, something extremely important, and he was frowning. Some expectation was evidently agitating and troubling him. Towards Raskolnikov he had somehow suddenly changed in the last few minutes, and with every minute he was becoming coarser and more mocking. Raskolnikov noticed all this and was alarmed too. Svidrigailov had become very suspicious to him; he resolved to follow him.
They came out onto the pavement.
“You go right and I go left, or perhaps the other way round, only... adieu, mon plaisir, farewell, my joy, until our happy next meeting!”
And he went to the right, towards the Haymarket.
## CHAPTER V
Raskolnikov followed him.
“What’s this!” cried Svidrigailov, turning round. “I think I said...”
“It means that I won’t leave you alone now.”
“Wha-a-at?”
Both stopped, and for a minute both looked at each other, as if taking each other’s measure.

“From all your half-drunken stories,” Raskolnikov cut him short sharply, “I have concluded positively that not only have you not given up your vilest designs on my sister, but you are even more taken up with them than ever. I know that my sister received some letter this morning. You couldn’t sit still the whole time... Suppose you have dug up some wife on the way; that means nothing. I wish to make sure personally...”
Raskolnikov could hardly have defined himself what exactly he wanted now and what exactly he wished to make sure of personally.
“So that’s it! Would you like me to call the police right now?”
“Call them!”

Again they stood facing each other for a minute. At last Svidrigailov’s face changed. Having made sure that Raskolnikov was not frightened by the threat, he suddenly took on the merriest and friendliest air.

“What a fellow! I deliberately didn’t speak to you about your affair, though of course curiosity torments me. It is a fantastic affair. I had put it off till another time, but really, you could provoke a dead man... Well, come along, only I’ll tell you in advance: I am going home now only for a minute, to get some money; then I lock up the flat, take a cab and go to the Islands for the whole evening. Well, why should you come after me?”
“For the time being I am going to the house, and not to you, but to Sofya Semyonovna, to apologise for not being at the funeral.”

“As you please, but Sofya Semyonovna is not at home. She has taken all the children to a certain lady, a certain distinguished old lady, an old acquaintance of mine from long ago and a manager of some orphan institutions. I charmed this lady by paying her the money for all three of Katerina Ivanovna’s nestlings; besides, I donated more money to the institutions; finally, I told her Sofya Semyonovna’s story, with all the honours, hiding nothing. It produced an indescribable effect. That is why Sofya Semyonovna was told to come today, straight to the — Hotel, where my lady is staying for the time being, down from her summer place.”
“No matter, I’ll call all the same.”

“As you like, only I am no companion for you there; but what is it to me! Here we are at home now. Tell me, I am convinced you look at me suspiciously because I myself was delicate enough not to trouble you with questions until now... you understand? It seemed to you something extraordinary; I bet it did! Well, after that, be delicate.”
“And listen at doors!”

“Ah, you mean that!” laughed Svidrigailov. “Yes, I would have been surprised if, after everything, you had let it pass without a remark. Ha-ha! Though I did understand something of what you got up to that time... there... and told Sofya Semyonovna yourself, still, what is it all? Perhaps I am quite a backward man and can understand nothing any more. Explain, for God’s sake, my dear! Enlighten me with the newest principles.”
“You couldn’t have heard anything; you are lying about it all!”

“But I don’t mean that, I don’t mean that (though I did hear a thing or two, by the way); no, I mean that you keep groaning and groaning! The Schiller in you is troubled every minute. And now, it seems, one mustn’t listen at doors. If so, go and declare to the authorities that, well, it was like this and like this, such an accident happened to me: a small mistake came out in my theory. But if you are convinced that one mustn’t listen at doors, but that one may crack old women with whatever comes to hand, for one’s own pleasure, then go away somewhere quickly, to America! Run, young man! Perhaps there is still time. I speak sincerely. Have you no money? I will give you some for the journey.”
“I am not thinking of that at all,” Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust.

“I understand (don’t trouble yourself, though: if you like, don’t say much); I understand what questions are going round in you: moral ones, are they? questions of citizen and man? But you push them aside; what do you want with them now? He-he! Because you are still a citizen and a man? But if so, you shouldn’t have poked your nose in; no use taking on what isn’t your business. Well, shoot yourself; what, don’t you feel like it?”
“You seem to want to irritate me on purpose, just so that I’ll leave you alone now...”

“What a strange fellow, but we have arrived; welcome to the stairs. You see, here is the entrance to Sofya Semyonovna’s; look, there is no one! You don’t believe me? Ask Kapernaumov; she gives them her key. Here is madame de Kapernaumov herself, eh? What? (she is a little deaf) gone out? Where? Well, there, did you hear now? She isn’t in and won’t be until late in the evening, perhaps. Well, now come to my place. You wanted to come to me too, didn’t you? Well, here we are at my place. Madame Resslich isn’t at home. That woman is always busy, but she is a good woman, I assure you... perhaps she might be of use to you, if you were somewhat more sensible. Well, kindly look: I take this five-per-cent bond out of the bureau (see how many more I have!), and this one will go to the money-changer today. Well, did you see? I have no more time to lose. The bureau is locked, the flat is locked, and we are on the stairs again. Well, shall we take a cab? I am going to the Islands, you know. Would you care for a drive? Here, I take this carriage to Yelagin; what? You refuse? You couldn’t hold out? Let’s go for a drive, never mind. It seems rain is coming on; never mind, we’ll put the hood up...”

Svidrigailov was already sitting in the carriage. Raskolnikov decided that his suspicions were unjust, at least at this moment. Without answering a word, he turned and walked back in the direction of the Haymarket. If he had turned round even once on the way, he would have had time to see how Svidrigailov, having driven no more than a hundred paces, paid off the carriage and found himself on the pavement. But he could see nothing any more and had already gone round the corner. Deep disgust drew him away from Svidrigailov. “And I could expect anything, even for a moment, from that coarse villain, that lustful profligate and scoundrel!” he exclaimed involuntarily. It is true that Raskolnikov pronounced his judgement too hastily and lightly. There was something in Svidrigailov’s whole situation that at least gave him a certain originality, if not mystery. As for his sister in all this, Raskolnikov remained convinced, all the same, that Svidrigailov would not leave her in peace. But it was becoming too heavy and unbearable to think and think again about all this!

As was his habit, when he was left alone, after twenty paces he fell into deep thought. Going up onto the bridge, he stopped at the railing and began looking at the water. And meanwhile Avdotya Romanovna was standing over him.

He had met her at the entrance to the bridge, but had walked past without making her out. Dunechka had never yet met him like this in the street and was struck to the point of fright. She stopped and did not know whether to call out to him or not. Suddenly she noticed Svidrigailov hurrying towards her from the direction of the Haymarket.

But he seemed to be approaching mysteriously and carefully. He did not go up onto the bridge, but stopped to one side, on the pavement, trying with all his might not to let Raskolnikov see him. He had long since noticed Dunya and began making signs to her. It seemed to her that with his signs he was begging her not to call out to her brother and to leave him alone, and was calling her to him.
And Dunya did so. She quietly went round her brother and came up to Svidrigailov.

“Let us go quickly,” Svidrigailov whispered to her. “I don’t wish Rodion Romanych to know of our meeting. I warn you that I was sitting with him not far from here, in a tavern, where he sought me out himself, and I barely got rid of him. For some reason he knows of my letter to you and suspects something. Surely it wasn’t you who revealed it to him? And if not you, then who?”

“Now we have turned the corner,” Dunya interrupted, “now my brother won’t see us. I declare to you that I will not go any further with you. Tell me everything here; all this can be said in the street too.”

“In the first place, it cannot possibly be said in the street; in the second, you must hear Sofya Semyonovna too; in the third, I will show you certain documents... Well, and finally, if you don’t agree to come into my place, I refuse all explanations and leave at once. At the same time I will ask you not to forget that a very curious secret of your beloved brother’s is entirely in my hands.”
Dunya stopped in indecision and looked at Svidrigailov with a piercing look.
“What are you afraid of!” he remarked calmly. “The city is not the country. And even in the country you did more harm to me than I to you, and here...”
“Has Sofya Semyonovna been told?”

“No, I haven’t said a word to her, and I am not even quite sure whether she is at home now. But probably she is. She buried her relative today: it’s not a day for paying visits. For the time being I don’t want to tell anyone about this, and I even partly regret having told you. The slightest carelessness here amounts to informing. I live right here, in this house; here we are coming to it. This is our house’s caretaker; the caretaker knows me very well; see, he is bowing; he sees that I am walking with a lady, and of course he has had time to notice your face, and that will be of use to you if you are very afraid and suspect me. Forgive me for speaking so crudely. I myself rent a room from tenants. Sofya Semyonovna lives wall to wall with me, also renting from tenants. The whole floor is let to lodgers. Why should you be afraid, like a child? Or am I really so very terrible?”

Svidrigailov’s face twisted into a condescending smile; but he was in no mood for smiling now. His heart was pounding and his breath was catching in his chest. He was deliberately speaking more loudly, so as to hide his growing agitation; but Dunya did not manage to notice this special agitation; she was far too irritated by the remark that she was afraid of him like a child and that he was so terrible for her.
“Though I know that you are a man... without honour, I am not in the least afraid of you. Go ahead,” she said, apparently calmly, but her face was very pale.
Svidrigailov stopped at Sonya’s door.

“Allow me to find out whether she is in. No. Bad luck! But I know that she may come very soon. If she has gone out, it can only be to a certain lady, about her orphans. Their mother has died. I have got mixed up in this too and made arrangements. If Sofya Semyonovna doesn’t come back within ten minutes, I will send her to you myself, today if you like; well, and here is my room. Here are my two rooms. Behind the door lives my landlady, Madame Resslich. Now look here; I will show you my main documents: from my bedroom this door leads into two completely empty rooms, which are to let. Here they are... you need to look at this a little more attentively...”

Svidrigailov occupied two furnished, fairly spacious rooms. Dunechka looked round mistrustfully, but noticed nothing special either in the furnishings or in the arrangement of the rooms, though one might have noticed something, for instance, that Svidrigailov’s lodging was somehow placed between two almost uninhabited flats. The entrance to his rooms was not directly from the corridor, but through two of the landlady’s rooms, almost empty. And from the bedroom Svidrigailov, unlocking a door that was locked with a key, showed Dunechka another empty flat that was to let. Dunechka stopped on the threshold, not understanding why she was being invited to look, but Svidrigailov hastened to explain:

“Here, look here, into this second large room. Note this door; it is locked with a key. By the door stands a chair, the only chair in both rooms. I brought it from my lodging, so as to listen more comfortably. Right there behind the door stands Sofya Semyonovna’s table; she sat there and talked with Rodion Romanych. And I listened here, sitting on the chair, two evenings running, both times for two hours or so, and of course I could have learned something; what do you think?”
“You listened?”
“Yes, I listened; now let’s go to my room; there is nowhere even to sit here.”

He led Avdotya Romanovna back into his first room, which served him as a sitting room, and invited her to sit down on a chair. He sat down himself at the other end of the table, at least seven feet from her, but probably the same flame was already shining in his eyes that had once so frightened Dunechka. She shuddered and looked round mistrustfully once more. Her gesture was involuntary; she evidently did not want to show mistrust. But the isolated position of Svidrigailov’s lodging struck her at last. She wanted to ask whether at least his landlady was at home, but she did not ask... out of pride. Besides, there was another suffering in her heart, incomparably greater than fear for herself. She was in unbearable torment.

“Here is your letter,” she began, laying it on the table. “Is what you write possible? You hint at a crime supposedly committed by my brother. You hint too clearly; you dare not back out of it now. Know, then, that I had heard this stupid tale even before you, and I don’t believe a single word of it. It is a vile and ridiculous suspicion. I know the story, and how and why it was invented. You cannot have any proofs. You promised to prove it: speak, then! But know beforehand that I don’t believe you! I don’t believe you!..”
Dunechka said this in a rapid patter, hurrying, and for an instant colour rushed into her face.
“If you didn’t believe it, could it have happened that you would risk coming to me alone? Why did you come, then? Out of mere curiosity?”
“Don’t torment me; speak, speak!”

“There is no need to say that you are a brave girl. By God, I thought you would ask Mr Razumikhin to accompany you here. But he was neither with you nor anywhere around you; I did look; that was daring; so you wanted to spare Rodion Romanych. But then, everything in you is divine... As for your brother, what shall I tell you? You saw him yourself just now. What was he like?”
“Surely you don’t base it on that alone?”

“No, not on that, but on his own words. Here, two evenings running, he came to Sofya Semyonovna. I showed you where they sat. He made her his full confession. He is a murderer. He killed the old woman, an official’s widow, a moneylender, with whom he himself had pawned things; he also killed her sister, a dealer named Lizaveta, who came in by chance during the murder of her sister. He killed them both with an axe which he had brought with him. He killed them to rob them, and he did rob them; he took money and some things... He told all this himself, word for word, to Sofya Semyonovna, who alone knows the secret, but took no part in the murder either by word or deed; on the contrary, she was as horrified as you are now. Rest assured, she will not give him away.”
“It cannot be!” Dunechka muttered with pale, deadened lips; she was gasping. “It cannot be; there is no reason, not the slightest reason, no occasion... It is a lie! A lie!”

“He robbed them; that is the whole reason. He took money and things. It is true that, by his own admission, he made no use of either the money or the things, but carried them off somewhere under a stone, where they are lying now. But that is because he did not dare make use of them.”
“But is it likely that he could steal, rob? That he could even think of it?” cried Dunya, and jumped up from her chair. “Why, you know him, you have seen him? Could he be a thief?”
She was as if beseeching Svidrigailov; she had forgotten all her fear.

“Here, Avdotya Romanovna, there are thousands and millions of combinations and sortings. A thief steals, but then he knows in himself that he is a scoundrel; but I have heard of a certain noble man who broke open the mail; so who knows, perhaps he really thought he had done a decent thing! Of course I would not have believed it myself, any more than you, if it had been passed on to me from outside. But I believed my own ears. He explained all his reasons to Sofya Semyonovna as well; but at first she didn’t believe her ears either, but at last she believed her eyes, her own eyes. He told her personally himself, after all.”
“What... reasons!”

“It is a long story, Avdotya Romanovna. Here, how shall I put it to you, there is a theory of a kind, the same sort of thing by which I find, for example, that a single villainy is permissible if the main aim is good. A single evil and a hundred good deeds! It is also, of course, galling for a young man of merit and boundless vanity to know that if there were, for instance, only three thousand, his whole career, his whole future in his aim in life, would take shape differently, and yet there are not those three thousand. Add to this the irritation of hunger, of a cramped lodging, of rags, of a vivid awareness of the beauty of his social position, and at the same time the position of his sister and mother. Most of all, though, vanity, pride and vanity; but then, God knows, perhaps even with good inclinations... I don’t blame him, please don’t think so; and it’s none of my business. There was also a little theory of his own here, a so-so sort of theory, according to which people are divided, you see, into material and special people, that is, people for whom, because of their high position, the law is not written; on the contrary, they themselves compose laws for the rest of people, the material, the rubbish. Never mind, a so-so little theory; une théorie comme une autre, a theory like any other. Napoleon carried him away terribly; that is, properly speaking, what carried him away was that very many men of genius did not look at a single evil, but stepped over it without thinking. He seems to have imagined that he too was a man of genius; that is, he was sure of it for a certain time. He has suffered very much and suffers even now from the thought that he knew how to compose the theory, but is not able to step over without thinking, and so is not a man of genius. Well, and that is humiliating for a young man with vanity, especially in our age...”
“And the pangs of conscience? So you deny him any moral feeling? Is he really like that?”

“Ah, Avdotya Romanovna, everything has become muddled now; that is, it was never in any particular order anyway. Russian people in general are broad people, Avdotya Romanovna, broad as their land, and extremely inclined to the fantastic, to the disorderly; but it is a misfortune to be broad without special genius. And do you remember how much we talked together in this vein and on this same subject, sitting in the evenings on the terrace in the garden, every time after supper? You reproached me for this very breadth. Who knows, perhaps we were talking at the very time when he was lying here thinking over his own thing. In our educated society, you know, there are no especially sacred traditions, Avdotya Romanovna: unless someone puts something together for himself from books... or derives something from the chronicles. But those are mostly scholars and, you know, all fools in their way, so that it is not even proper for a man of the world. However, you know my opinions in general; I accuse absolutely no one. I myself am a man who keeps his hands clean, and I stick to that. But we have talked about this more than once. I even had the happiness of interesting you with my opinions... You are very pale, Avdotya Romanovna!”
“I know this theory of his. I read his article in a journal about people to whom everything is permitted... Razumikhin brought it to me...”
“Mr Razumikhin? Your brother’s article? In a journal? Is there such an article? I didn’t know. That must be curious! But where are you going, Avdotya Romanovna?”
“I want to see Sofya Semyonovna,” Dunechka said in a weak voice. “How does one get to her? Perhaps she has come back; I absolutely want to see her now. Let her...”
Avdotya Romanovna could not finish; her breath literally failed her.
“Sofya Semyonovna will not come back until night. That is what I suppose. She should have come very soon, but if not, then very late...”
“Ah, so you are lying! I see... you lied... you lied about everything!.. I don’t believe you! I don’t believe you! I don’t believe you!” Dunechka shouted in a real frenzy, losing her head completely.
Almost fainting, she fell onto a chair which Svidrigailov hastened to place for her.
“Avdotya Romanovna, what is the matter, come to yourself! Here is water. Drink one sip...”
He sprinkled water on her. Dunechka shuddered and came to herself.

“It has had a strong effect!” Svidrigailov muttered to himself, frowning. “Avdotya Romanovna, calm yourself! Know that he has friends. We will save him, rescue him. Would you like me to take him abroad? I have money; I can get a ticket in three days. And as for his having killed, he will still do many good deeds, so that all this will be smoothed over; calm yourself. He may still be a great man. Well, what is the matter with you? How do you feel?”
“Wicked man! He is still mocking. Let me go...”
“Where are you going? Where are you going?”
“To him. Where is he? Do you know? Why is this door locked? We came in through this door, and now it is locked with a key. When did you manage to lock it?”

“One could hardly shout through all the rooms what we were talking about here. I am not mocking at all; I am only tired of talking in this language. Well, where are you going in such a state? Or do you want to betray him? You will drive him to frenzy, and he will give himself up. Know that they are already watching him; they are already on his track. You will only give him away. Wait: I saw him and spoke with him just now; he can still be saved. Wait, sit down, let us think it over together. That is why I called you, to talk about this alone and think it over properly. Do sit down!”
“How can you save him? Can he be saved?”
Dunya sat down. Svidrigailov sat down beside her.
“All this depends on you, on you, on you alone,” he began, with flashing eyes, almost in a whisper, losing the thread and not even getting some words out from agitation.
Dunya drew further away from him in fright. He too was trembling all over.

“You... one word from you, and he is saved! I... I will save him. I have money and friends. I will send him off at once, and I will take a passport myself, two passports. One his, the other mine. I have friends; I have men of business... Do you want it? I will get a passport for you too... for your mother... what do you want with Razumikhin? I love you too... I love you infinitely. Let me kiss the hem of your dress, let me! let me! I can’t bear hearing it rustle. Tell me: do this, and I will do it! I will do everything. I will do the impossible. What you believe, I will believe too. I will do everything, everything! Don’t look, don’t look at me like that! Do you know that you are killing me...”
He was even beginning to rave. Something had suddenly happened to him, as if it had suddenly gone to his head. Dunya jumped up and rushed to the door.
“Open! open!” she shouted through the door, calling for someone and shaking the door with her hands. “Open, then! Is there really no one?”
Svidrigailov stood up and came to himself. A malicious and mocking smile was slowly forcing itself onto his still trembling lips.
“There is no one at home there,” he said quietly and deliberately. “The landlady has gone out, and it is wasted effort shouting like that: you only agitate yourself for nothing.”
“Where is the key? Open the door at once, at once, you low man!”
“I have lost the key and cannot find it.”

“Ah! So this is violence!” cried Dunya; she turned pale as death and rushed into the corner, where she quickly shielded herself with a little table that happened to be at hand. She did not scream; but she fixed her eyes on her tormentor and watched his every movement keenly. Svidrigailov did not move from his place either, and stood facing her at the other end of the room. He had even mastered himself, at least outwardly. But his face was as pale as before. The mocking smile did not leave him.

“You said ‘violence’ just now, Avdotya Romanovna. If it is violence, you can judge for yourself that I have taken measures. Sofya Semyonovna is not at home; it is very far to the Kapernaumovs’, five locked rooms. Finally, I am at least twice as strong as you, and besides, I have nothing to fear, because you cannot complain afterwards either: you won’t really want to betray your brother, will you? And no one will believe you anyway: why on earth would a girl go alone to a single man’s lodging? So that even if you sacrifice your brother, you will prove nothing even then: violence is very hard to prove, Avdotya Romanovna.”
“Scoundrel!” Dunya whispered in indignation.

“As you like, but note that I was speaking only by way of supposition. In my own personal conviction you are perfectly right: violence is a vileness. I said it only to show that absolutely nothing would remain on your conscience, even if... even if you wanted to save your brother voluntarily, in the way I propose to you. You would simply have submitted to circumstances, well, to force, finally, if one can’t do without that word. Think about it; the fate of your brother and your mother is in your hands. And I will be your slave... all my life... I will wait here...”
Svidrigailov sat down on the sofa, about eight paces from Dunya. For her there was no longer the slightest doubt of his unshakeable resolve. Besides, she knew him...
Suddenly she took a revolver out of her pocket, cocked it and lowered her hand with the revolver onto the little table. Svidrigailov jumped up from his place.

“Aha! So that’s how it is!” he cried in surprise, but smiling maliciously. “Well, that changes the course of things completely! You are making things extremely easy for me yourself, Avdotya Romanovna! But where did you get a revolver? Surely not from Mr Razumikhin? Ba! But the revolver is mine! An old acquaintance! And how I searched for it then!.. Our country shooting lessons, which I had the honour of giving you, were not wasted after all.”

“It is not your revolver, but Marfa Petrovna’s, whom you killed, you villain! You had nothing of your own in her house. I took it when I began to suspect what you were capable of. Dare to take even one step, and I swear I will kill you!”
Dunya was in a frenzy. She held the revolver ready.
“Well, and your brother? I ask out of curiosity,” said Svidrigailov, still standing in his place.
“Inform on him if you like! Don’t move! Don’t come near! I’ll shoot! You poisoned your wife, I know it; you are a murderer yourself!..”
“And are you firmly convinced that I poisoned Marfa Petrovna?”
“You! You hinted at it yourself; you talked to me about poison... I know you went to fetch it... you had it ready... It was certainly you... scoundrel!”
“Even if it were true, it would be because of you... all the same you would have been the cause.”
“You’re lying! I always hated you, always...”

“Ehe, Avdotya Romanovna! You seem to have forgotten how in the heat of propaganda you were already inclining and melting... I saw it in your little eyes; remember, in the evening, in the moonlight, and the nightingale was singing too?”
“You’re lying!” (fury flashed in Dunya’s eyes) “You’re lying, you slanderer!”
“Lying? Well, perhaps I am lying. I lied. One shouldn’t mention these little things to women.” (He smiled.) “I know you will shoot, you pretty little wild thing. Well, shoot!”

Dunya raised the revolver and, deathly pale, her lower lip gone white and trembling, her big black eyes flashing like fire, she looked at him, resolved, measuring and waiting for the first movement on his part. Never had he seen her so beautiful. The fire that flashed from her eyes at the moment she raised the revolver seemed to scorch him, and his heart contracted with pain. He took a step, and the shot rang out. The bullet grazed his hair and struck the wall behind. He stopped and laughed quietly:

“The wasp has stung! Aims straight at the head... What is this? Blood!” He took out a handkerchief to wipe off the blood that was running in a thin trickle down his right temple; the bullet had probably just grazed the skin of his skull. Dunya lowered the revolver and looked at Svidrigailov not so much in fear as in a kind of wild bewilderment. It was as if she herself no longer understood what she had done and what was happening!
“Well, a miss! Shoot again, I am waiting,” Svidrigailov said quietly, still smiling, but somehow gloomily. “At this rate I shall have time to seize you before you cock it!”
Dunechka shuddered, quickly cocked the revolver and raised it again.
“Leave me alone!” she said in despair. “I swear I will shoot again... I... will kill you!..”
“Well, what of it... at three paces you can’t help killing. Well, but if you don’t kill me... then...” His eyes flashed, and he took two more steps.
Dunechka fired: a misfire!
“You loaded it carelessly. Never mind! You have another cap there. Put it right; I’ll wait.”

He stood two steps away from her, waiting and looking at her with wild resolve, with an inflamed, passionate, heavy look. Dunya understood that he would sooner die than let her go. “And... and of course she will kill him now, at two paces!..”
Suddenly she threw the revolver away.

“She has thrown it away!” Svidrigailov said in surprise, and drew a deep breath. Something seemed to have lifted from his heart all at once, and perhaps not only the weight of mortal fear; indeed, he hardly felt it at that moment. It was a deliverance from another, more sorrowful and gloomy feeling, which he could not have defined in all its force himself.

He went up to Dunya and quietly put his arm round her waist. She did not resist, but, trembling all over like a leaf, looked at him with imploring eyes. He wanted to say something, but his lips only twisted, and he could not get it out.
“Let me go!” Dunya said imploringly. Svidrigailov shuddered: this “you”, the familiar “you”, was spoken somehow not as it had been before.
“So you don’t love me?” he asked quietly.
Dunya shook her head.
“And... you can’t?.. Never?” he whispered in despair.
“Never!” whispered Dunya.

There passed an instant of terrible, mute struggle in Svidrigailov’s soul. He looked at her with an inexpressible look. Suddenly he took away his arm, turned away, walked quickly to the window and stood before it.
Another instant passed.
“Here is the key!” (He took it out of the left pocket of his coat and put it on the table behind him, without looking or turning to Dunya.) “Take it; go quickly!..”
He was looking stubbornly out of the window.
Dunya went to the table to take the key.
“Quickly! Quickly!” repeated Svidrigailov, still not moving and not turning round. But in this “quickly”, evidently, some terrible note had sounded.

Dunya understood it, seized the key, rushed to the door, quickly unlocked it and broke out of the room. A minute later, like a madwoman, not knowing what she was doing, she ran out onto the canal and ran in the direction of the — Bridge.

Svidrigailov stood at the window about three minutes more; at last he slowly turned round, looked about him and quietly passed his palm over his forehead. A strange smile twisted his face, a pitiful, sad, weak smile, a smile of despair. The blood, already drying, had stained his palm; he looked at the blood angrily; then he wetted a towel and washed his temple. The revolver, which Dunya had thrown away and which had flown to the door, suddenly caught his eye. He picked it up and examined it. It was a small, pocket, three-shot revolver of an old make; there were still two charges in it and one cap. It could be fired once. He thought, thrust the revolver into his pocket, took his hat and went out.
## CHAPTER VI

All that evening until ten o’clock he spent in various taverns and sewers, going from one to another. Katya turned up somewhere too, and sang another lackey’s song, about how someone, “a scoundrel and a tyrant”,
> Began to kiss Katya.

Svidrigailov stood drinks for Katya, and the organ-grinder, and the singers, and the waiters, and two little clerks of some sort. He had taken up with these little clerks, properly speaking, because both of them had crooked noses: one nose went crookedly to the right and the other to the left. This struck Svidrigailov. At last they lured him into some pleasure garden, where he paid for them and for their admission. In this garden there was one thin, three-year-old fir tree and three little bushes. Besides that, a “Vauxhall” had been built, in essence a drinking house, but one could get tea there too, and in addition there stood a few green tables and chairs. A chorus of wretched singers and some drunken German from Munich, a sort of clown with a red nose but for some reason extremely melancholy, entertained the public. The little clerks quarrelled with some other little clerks and started a fight. Svidrigailov was chosen by them as judge. He had been judging them for a quarter of an hour, but they shouted so much that there was not the slightest possibility of making anything out. The likeliest thing was that one of them had stolen something and had even managed to sell it on the spot to a Jew who happened to be there; but, having sold it, did not want to share with his comrade. It turned out in the end that the object sold was a teaspoon belonging to the Vauxhall. They missed it in the Vauxhall, and the matter began to take on troublesome proportions. Svidrigailov paid for the spoon, got up and left the garden. It was about ten o’clock. He himself had not drunk a single drop of wine all this time and had only ordered tea for himself in the Vauxhall, and that more for form’s sake. Meanwhile the evening was stifling and gloomy. By ten o’clock terrible clouds had come up from all sides; thunder struck, and the rain poured down like a waterfall. The water did not fall in drops but lashed the earth in whole streams. Lightning flashed every minute, and one could count to five during each glare. Soaked to the skin, he reached home, locked himself in, opened his bureau, took out all his money and tore up two or three papers. Then, thrusting the money into his pocket, he was about to change his clothes, but, looking out of the window and listening to the storm and the rain, he waved his hand, took his hat and went out without locking his lodging. He went straight to Sonya’s. She was at home.

She was not alone; around her were four of Kapernaumov’s little children. Sofya Semyonovna was giving them tea. She received Svidrigailov silently and respectfully, looked with surprise at his soaked clothes, but did not say a word. The children all ran away at once in indescribable terror.
Svidrigailov sat down at the table and asked Sonya to sit beside him. She timidly prepared to listen.

“I may go to America, Sofya Semyonovna,” said Svidrigailov, “and since we are probably seeing each other for the last time, I have come to make certain arrangements. Well, did you see that lady today? I know what she said to you; there is no need to repeat it.” (Sonya made a movement and blushed.) “Those people have a well-known turn. As for your little sisters and your little brother, they really are provided for, and the money due to them I have paid out for each of them, against receipts, where it ought to go, into safe hands. You had better take these receipts yourself, though, just in case. Here, take them! Well, sir, that is done now. Here are three five-per-cent bonds, three thousand in all. Take this for yourself, for yourself alone, and let it stay between us, so that no one knows, whatever you may hear. You will need it, because, Sofya Semyonovna, to live as before is vile, and you have no need to any more.”
“I have received so much kindness from you, sir, and the orphans, sir, and the late one,” Sonya hurried, “that if I have thanked you so little until now, then... don’t think...”
“Eh, enough, enough.”
“And this money, Arkady Ivanovich, I am very grateful to you, but I don’t need it now. I can always feed myself alone; don’t think it ingratitude: if you are so charitable, then this money, sir...”

“It is for you, for you, Sofya Semyonovna, and please, without any special talk, because I have no time even. And you will need it. Rodion Romanovich has two roads: either a bullet through the head, or down the Vladimirka road to Siberia.” (Sonya looked at him wildly and trembled.) “Don’t worry, I know everything, from him himself, and I am not a chatterer; I won’t tell anyone. You taught him well that time, to go and give himself up and tell. It will be much better for him. Well, if it turns out to be the Vladimirka, he will go down it, and you will follow him, won’t you? Won’t you? Won’t you? Well, and if so, then the money will be needed. It will be needed for him, you understand? Giving it to you is the same as giving it to him. Besides, you promised to pay Amalia Ivanovna’s debt too; I heard. Why do you take on such contracts and obligations so thoughtlessly, Sofya Semyonovna? It was Katerina Ivanovna who owed money to that German woman, not you, so you might well spit on the German woman. One can’t live in the world like that. Well, sir, if anyone ever asks you, well, tomorrow or the day after, about me or concerning me (and you will be asked), don’t mention that I came to see you now, and on no account show the money or tell anyone that I gave it to you. Well, goodbye now.” (He got up from his chair.) “My regards to Rodion Romanych. By the way: keep the money for the time being with Mr Razumikhin, say. Do you know Mr Razumikhin? Of course you do. He’s not a bad fellow. Take it to him tomorrow or... when the time comes. And until then hide it well away.”
Sonya also jumped up from her chair and looked at him in fright. She very much wanted to say something, to ask something, but in the first minutes she did not dare, and did not know how to begin.
“But how will you... how will you go out now, sir, in such rain?”

“Well, to be getting ready for America and afraid of rain, he-he! Goodbye, my dear Sofya Semyonovna! Live, and live long; you will be of use to others. By the way... tell Mr Razumikhin that I sent my regards. Pass it on just like that: Arkady Ivanovich Svidrigailov sends his regards. Without fail, now.”
He went out, leaving Sonya in amazement, in fright, and with a kind of vague and heavy suspicion.

It turned out later that on that same evening, after eleven o’clock, he paid yet another very eccentric and unexpected visit. The rain still had not stopped. Soaked all over, at twenty past eleven he entered the cramped little flat of his bride’s parents, on Vasilyevsky Island, on the Third Line, on Maly Prospect. He had difficulty getting them to open, and at first caused great confusion; but Arkady Ivanovich, when he wished, was a man of most charming manners, so that the first guess of the bride’s sensible parents (a very witty one, though) that Arkady Ivanovich had probably got so drunk somewhere that he no longer knew what he was doing at once fell of its own accord. The paralysed parent was wheeled out in his chair to Arkady Ivanovich by the bride’s tender-hearted and sensible mother, who, as was her custom, at once began on certain remote questions.
