(This woman never asked direct questions, but always first brought into play smiles and the rubbing of hands, and then, if something had to be found out without fail and for certain, for instance when Arkady Ivanovich would be pleased to fix the wedding, she would begin with the most curious and almost greedy questions about Paris and court life there, and only afterwards come by degrees to the Third Line of Vasilyevsky Island.) At another time all this would of course have inspired great respect, but this time Arkady Ivanovich proved somehow especially impatient and flatly wished to see the bride, though he had been told at the very beginning that the bride had already gone to bed. Of course the bride appeared. Arkady Ivanovich told her straight out that he had to leave Petersburg for a while on account of a very important circumstance, and so had brought her fifteen thousand silver roubles in various notes, asking her to accept them from him as a present, since he had long meant to give her this trifle before the wedding. No particular logical connection between the present and his immediate departure, and the absolute necessity of coming for that purpose in the rain and at midnight, was of course shown by these explanations, but the affair nevertheless went off very smoothly. Even the necessary oohs and aahs, questions and surprises became somehow suddenly extraordinarily moderate and restrained; on the other hand the most ardent gratitude was expressed and even reinforced by the tears of the most sensible mother. Arkady Ivanovich got up, laughed, kissed the bride, patted her on the cheek, confirmed that he would come soon, and, noticing in her little eyes a childish curiosity, but together with it a very serious, mute question, thought for a moment, kissed her a second time, and at once sincerely regretted in his soul that the present would go immediately under lock and key in the keeping of the most sensible of mothers. He went out, leaving everyone in an extraordinarily excited state. But the tender-hearted mama at once, in a half-whisper and a rapid patter, resolved certain most important perplexities, namely, that Arkady Ivanovich was a great man, a man of affairs and connections, a rich man; God knows what goes on in his head; he took it into his head and went, he took it into his head and gave the money, and so there was nothing to wonder at. Of course it was strange that he was soaked through, but the English, for instance, are even more eccentric, and all these people of high tone pay no attention to what is said about them and don’t stand on ceremony. Perhaps he even goes about like that on purpose, to show that he is afraid of no one. And above all, not a word to anyone about this, because God knows what may come of it yet, and the money under lock and key as quickly as possible, and of course the best thing in all this was that Fedosya had stayed in the kitchen, and above all on no account, on no account, on no account must anything be told to that sly Resslich woman, and so on and so on. They sat whispering until two o’clock. The bride, however, went to bed much earlier, surprised and a little sad.

And Svidrigailov meanwhile, at midnight exactly, was crossing — Bridge in the direction of the Petersburg Side. The rain had stopped, but the wind was roaring. He was beginning to shiver, and for a minute he looked with a kind of special curiosity, and even questioningly, at the black water of the Little Neva. But soon it seemed to him very cold to stand over the water; he turned and went along — Prospect. He walked along the endless — Prospect for a very long time, almost half an hour, more than once stumbling in the dark on the wooden paving, but did not stop searching with curiosity for something on the right side of the prospect. Somewhere here, already at the end of the prospect, he had noticed, driving past not long ago, a hotel, a wooden one but large, and its name, as far as he remembered, was something like the Adrianople. He was not mistaken in his reckoning: this hotel, in such a wilderness, was so conspicuous a point that it was impossible not to find it, even in the dark. It was a long, wooden, blackened building, in which, in spite of the late hour, lights were still burning and some animation could be noticed. He went in and asked a ragged fellow who met him in the corridor for a room. The ragged fellow, looking Svidrigailov over, roused himself and at once led him to a remote room, stuffy and cramped, somewhere at the very end of the corridor, in a corner, under the stairs. But there was no other; all were taken. The ragged fellow looked at him questioningly.
“Is there tea?” asked Svidrigailov.
“That can be done, sir.”
“What else is there?”
“Veal, sir, vodka, sir, snacks, sir.”
“Bring veal and tea.”
“And nothing else will be wanted?” the ragged fellow asked, even in some perplexity.
“Nothing, nothing!”
The ragged fellow withdrew, completely disappointed.

“It must be a fine place,” thought Svidrigailov. “How is it I didn’t know it. I too probably look like a man coming back from some café-chantant who has already had some adventure on the way. But it is curious, though, who stays and spends the night here?”

He lit a candle and examined the room in more detail. It was a little cage, so small that it was hardly high enough for Svidrigailov, with one window; a very dirty bed, a plain painted table and a chair took up almost all the space. The walls looked as if they were nailed together from boards, with scuffed wallpaper so dusty and torn that its colour (yellow) could still be guessed, but no pattern could be made out any more. One part of the wall and ceiling was cut away at a slant, as usual in attics, but here the staircase ran over this slope. Svidrigailov put down the candle, sat on the bed and fell to thinking. But a strange and incessant whispering in the next little cage, sometimes rising almost to a shout, drew his attention at last. This whispering had not stopped since he came in. He listened: someone was abusing another and reproaching him almost in tears, but only one voice could be heard. Svidrigailov stood up, shaded the candle with his hand, and at once a little crack gleamed in the wall; he went up to it and began to look. In a room somewhat larger than his own there were two guests. One of them, without his frock coat, with an extremely curly head and a red, inflamed face, stood in an orator’s pose, his legs apart to keep his balance, and, striking his breast with his hand, was pathetically reproaching the other for being a beggar and not even having any rank, for his having dragged him out of the mud and being able to throw him out whenever he liked, and that all this was seen only by the finger of the Most High. The reproached friend sat on a chair and looked like a man who extremely wants to sneeze but cannot manage it. Now and then he looked at the orator with a sheepish and bleary look, but obviously had no idea what it was about and was hardly even hearing anything. On the table a candle was burning down, and there stood an almost empty carafe of vodka, wine glasses, bread, tumblers, cucumbers and the cups of tea drunk long ago. Having examined this picture attentively, Svidrigailov indifferently moved away from the crack and sat down on the bed.

The ragged fellow, coming back with the tea and the veal, could not help asking once more: “isn’t anything else needed?”, and, hearing again the answer no, withdrew for good. Svidrigailov fell on the tea to warm himself and drank a glass, but could not eat a morsel, having completely lost his appetite. A fever was evidently beginning in him. He took off his coat and his jacket, wrapped himself in the blanket and lay down on the bed. He was vexed: “It would have been better to be well this time, at least,” he thought, and smiled. The room was stuffy, the candle burned dimly, the wind was roaring outside, somewhere in a corner a mouse was scratching, and the whole room seemed to smell of mice and of something leathery. He lay as if dreaming: thought followed thought; it seemed he would very much have liked to fasten his imagination on something in particular. “There must be some garden under the window,” he thought, “the trees are rustling; how I dislike the rustle of trees at night, in a storm and in the dark; a nasty sensation!” And he remembered how, passing Petrovsky Park earlier, he had thought of it even with disgust. Then he remembered — Bridge too, and the Little Neva, and again he seemed to grow cold, as he had earlier when he stood over the water. “Never in my life have I liked water, even in landscapes,” he thought again, and suddenly smiled again at a strange thought: “Why, it seems that now I ought not to care about all this aesthetics and comfort, and yet just here I have become choosy, like an animal that must choose a place for itself... in a similar case. I ought to have turned into the Petrovsky earlier! It seemed dark, I suppose, cold, he-he! Practically needed pleasant sensations!.. By the way, why don’t I put out the candle?” (He blew it out.) “The neighbours have gone to bed,” he thought, seeing no light in the crack of before. “Well, Marfa Petrovna, now would be the time for you to come: it is dark, and the place is suitable, and the moment original. And just now you won’t come...”

For some reason he suddenly remembered how earlier, an hour before carrying out his design on Dunechka, he had recommended Raskolnikov to entrust her to Razumikhin’s protection. “Really, I said it mostly to provoke myself then, as Raskolnikov guessed. A rogue, though, that Raskolnikov! He has carried a great deal on himself. He may become a great rogue in time, when the nonsense has jumped out of him, but now he wants to live far too much! On that point those people are scoundrels. Well, the devil take him, let him do as he likes; what is it to me.”

He still could not sleep. Little by little the image of Dunechka from earlier began to rise before him, and suddenly a trembling passed through his body. “No, I must give that up now,” he thought, coming to himself, “I must think of something else. Strange and funny: I never had any great hatred for anyone, never even especially wished for revenge, and that is a bad sign, a bad sign! I didn’t like arguing either, and never got heated; also a bad sign! And how much I promised her earlier: pah, the devil! And yet perhaps she would have ground me down somehow...” He fell silent again and clenched his teeth: again the image of Dunechka appeared before him exactly as she had been when, having fired the first time, she took terrible fright, lowered the revolver and, gone numb, looked at him, so that he would have had time to seize her twice, and she would not have raised a hand in defence if he had not reminded her himself. He remembered how at that moment he had felt as if sorry for her, as if his heart had been squeezed... “Eh! To the devil! These thoughts again; all this must be dropped, dropped!..”

He was already dozing off; the feverish trembling was subsiding, when suddenly something seemed to run under the blanket over his arm and his leg. He started: “Pah, the devil, I believe it’s a mouse!” he thought. “I left the veal on the table...” He terribly did not want to uncover himself, get up and freeze, but suddenly again something brushed unpleasantly against his leg; he tore off the blanket and lit the candle. Trembling with feverish cold, he bent down to examine the bed: there was nothing; he shook the blanket, and suddenly a mouse jumped out onto the sheet. He rushed to catch it; but the mouse did not run off the bed, but flashed in zigzags in all directions, slipped out from under his fingers, ran over his arm and suddenly darted under the pillow; he threw off the pillow, but in an instant felt something jump inside his shirt, brushing over his body, and already behind, on his back, under the shirt. He trembled nervously and woke up. The room was dark; he was lying on the bed, wrapped as before in the blanket; the wind was howling under the window. “What vileness!” he thought with vexation.

He got up and sat on the edge of the bed with his back to the window. “Better not to sleep at all,” he decided. It was cold and damp from the window, however; without getting up, he pulled the blanket over himself and wrapped himself in it. He did not light the candle. He was not thinking of anything and did not want to think; but dreams rose one after another, scraps of thoughts flashed by, without beginning or end and without connection. It was as if he were falling into a half-doze. Whether it was the cold, or the darkness, or the damp, or the wind howling under the window and shaking the trees that called up in him some persistent fantastic inclination and desire, he kept seeing flowers. He imagined a lovely landscape; a bright, almost hot day, a holiday, Trinity Sunday. A rich, luxurious country cottage in the English taste, all overgrown with fragrant beds of flowers, planted round with borders running all round the house; a porch twined with climbing plants and lined with beds of roses; a light, cool staircase laid with a sumptuous carpet and set about with rare flowers in Chinese jars. He particularly noticed in the jars of water on the windowsills bunches of white, delicate narcissi, bending on their bright green, fleshy, long stalks, with a strong aromatic scent. He did not even want to move away from them, but he went up the stairs and entered a large, high hall, and again here too, everywhere, by the windows, by the open doors to the terrace, on the terrace itself, everywhere there were flowers. The floors were strewn with freshly mown fragrant grass, the windows were open, fresh, light, cool air came into the room, little birds were chirping under the windows, and in the middle of the hall, on tables covered with white satin cloths, stood a coffin. This coffin was covered with white gros de Naples and edged with a thick white ruche. Garlands of flowers wound round it on all sides. All in flowers there lay in it a girl, in a white tulle dress, her hands folded and pressed to her breast, as if carved out of marble. But her loose hair, the hair of a light blonde, was wet; a wreath of roses was twined round her head. The stern and already rigid profile of her face was also as if carved out of marble, but the smile on her pale lips was full of a kind of unchildlike, boundless grief and great complaint. Svidrigailov knew this girl; there was no icon or lighted candles at this coffin, and no prayers could be heard. This girl was a suicide, drowned. She was only fourteen, but hers was already a broken heart, and it had destroyed itself, wounded by an outrage that had horrified and amazed this young, childish consciousness, flooded her angelically pure soul with undeserved shame and torn from her a last cry of despair, unheard, but insolently trampled on, in a dark night, in the gloom, in the cold, in a damp thaw, when the wind was howling...

Svidrigailov came to himself, got up from the bed and stepped to the window. He felt for the latch and opened the window. The wind rushed furiously into his cramped little room and as if with frost plastered his face and his chest, covered only by a shirt. Under the window there really must have been something like a garden, and it seems a pleasure garden too; probably in the daytime singers sang here as well and tea was brought out to the little tables. But now spray was flying from the trees and bushes into the window; it was dark as a cellar, so that only some dark patches could barely be made out, marking objects. Svidrigailov, bending down and leaning his elbows on the windowsill, had been looking for five minutes now, without tearing himself away, into this murk. Amid the darkness and the night a cannon shot rang out, and after it another.

“Ah, the signal! The water is rising,” he thought. “By morning it will pour into the streets, where the ground is lower, flood the basements and cellars, the basement rats will float up, and amid the rain and wind people will begin, cursing, wet, to drag their rubbish up to the upper floors... And what time is it now?” And just as he thought this, somewhere close by, ticking and as if hurrying with all its might, a wall clock struck three. “Ehe, in an hour it will be getting light! Why wait? I’ll go out now, go straight to the Petrovsky: somewhere there I’ll choose a big bush, all drenched with rain, so that you have only to brush it with your shoulder and millions of drops will shower your whole head...” He moved away from the window, shut it, lit the candle, pulled on his waistcoat and coat, put on his hat and went out with the candle into the corridor, to find the ragged fellow asleep somewhere in a little closet among all sorts of junk and candle ends, pay him for the room and leave the hotel. “The very best moment; one couldn’t choose a better!”

He walked a long time along the whole long, narrow corridor without finding anyone, and was about to call out loudly, when suddenly, in a dark corner between an old cupboard and a door, he made out some strange object, something seemingly alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a child, a girl of five, no more, in a little dress soaked like a floor cloth, trembling and crying. She did not seem frightened of Svidrigailov, but looked at him with dull surprise with her big black eyes, and now and then sobbed, like children who have cried for a long time but have already stopped and are even comforted, and yet every so often suddenly sob again. The little girl’s face was pale and worn out; she was stiff with cold, but “how did she get here? So she must have hidden here and not slept all night.” He began to question her. The little girl suddenly brightened up and began to babble something to him very, very quickly in her child’s language. There was something about “mummy”, and that “mummy will beat me”, about some cup that she had “bwoken”. The little girl talked without stopping; from all these stories one could somehow guess that this was an unloved child, whom her mother, some always drunken cook, probably from this very hotel, had beaten and terrified; that the little girl had broken her mother’s cup and was so frightened that she had run away in the evening; she had probably hidden for a long time somewhere in the yard, in the rain, at last got in here, hidden behind the cupboard and sat here in the corner all night, crying, trembling from the damp, from the dark and from fear that she would now be beaten hard for all this. He took her in his arms, went to his room, sat her on the bed and began to undress her. Her little shoes, full of holes, on her bare feet, were as wet as if they had lain all night in a puddle. Having undressed her, he laid her on the bed, covered her and wrapped her completely, head and all, in the blanket. She fell asleep at once. Having finished all this, he again fell gloomily to thinking.

“And now I have taken it into my head to get mixed up with this!” he decided suddenly, with a heavy and malicious feeling. “What nonsense!” In vexation he took the candle, to go and find the ragged fellow at all costs and leave here quickly. “Eh, the girl!” he thought with a curse, already opening the door, but he came back once more to look at the girl, whether she was asleep and how she was sleeping. He carefully lifted the blanket. The little girl was sleeping a sound and blissful sleep. She had grown warm under the blanket, and colour had already spread over her pale little cheeks. But strangely: this colour showed as if brighter and stronger than an ordinary child’s flush could be. “It is a feverish flush,” thought Svidrigailov; it was exactly like a flush from wine, exactly as if she had been given a whole glass to drink. Her scarlet little lips were as if burning, glowing; but what is this? It suddenly seemed to him that her long black lashes were quivering and blinking, as if lifting, and from under them a sly, sharp, somehow unchildlike winking little eye was peeping out, as if the little girl were not asleep but pretending. Yes, so it is: her little lips are parting in a smile; the corners of her lips are quivering, as if still holding back. But now she has quite stopped holding back; this is laughter now, open laughter; something insolent, provoking shines in this face that is not at all a child’s; it is depravity, it is the face of a camellia, the insolent face of a French courtesan for sale. Now, no longer hiding at all, both eyes open: they run over him with a fiery and shameless look, they call him, they laugh... There was something infinitely hideous and outrageous in that laughter, in those eyes, in all this vileness in a child’s face. “What! five years old!” Svidrigailov whispered in real horror. “This... what is this?” But now she is turning her whole burning little face to him, holding out her arms... “Ah, cursed thing!” cried Svidrigailov in horror, raising his hand over her... But at that very moment he woke up.
He is on the same bed, wrapped in the blanket just the same; the candle is not lit, and full daylight is already whitening in the windows.

“Nightmare all night long!” He raised himself angrily, feeling that he was all broken; his bones ached. Outside there was a completely thick fog and nothing could be made out. It was getting on for five; he had overslept! He got up and put on his jacket and coat, still damp. Feeling the revolver in his pocket, he took it out and adjusted the cap; then he sat down, took a notebook out of his pocket and on the title page, the most noticeable one, wrote a few lines in a large hand. Having reread them, he fell to thinking, his elbows on the table. The revolver and the notebook lay right there, by his elbow. Flies that had woken up were clinging to the untouched portion of veal that stood right there on the table. He looked at them for a long time, and at last began trying to catch one fly with his free right hand. He exhausted himself for a long time in the effort but could not catch it. At last, catching himself at this interesting occupation, he came to himself, started, got up and walked resolutely out of the room. A minute later he was in the street.

A thick, milky fog lay over the city. Svidrigailov walked along the slippery, dirty wooden paving towards the Little Neva. He imagined the water of the Little Neva risen high during the night, Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the wet grass, the wet trees and bushes, and at last that very bush... In vexation he began examining the houses, so as to think of something else. He met neither a passer-by nor a cab along the prospect. The bright yellow wooden houses with their shutters closed looked dismal and dirty. The cold and damp went through his whole body, and he began to shiver. Now and then he came upon shop and greengrocers’ signs and read each one carefully. Now the wooden paving had ended. He was already level with a large stone house. A dirty, chilled little dog with its tail between its legs ran across his path. Some dead-drunk man in a greatcoat lay face down across the pavement. He looked at him and went on. A tall watchtower flashed on his left. “Ba!” he thought. “Why, here is the place; why go to the Petrovsky? At least with an official witness...” He almost smiled at this new thought and turned into — Street. Here stood the large building with the watchtower. At the large closed gates of the building, leaning his shoulder against them, stood a small man wrapped in a grey soldier’s greatcoat and wearing a brass Achilles helmet. With a drowsy look he glanced coldly sideways at Svidrigailov as he came up. On his face could be seen that age-old peevish grief which is imprinted so sourly on every face, without exception, of the Jewish tribe. The two of them, Svidrigailov and Achilles, examined each other silently for some time. At last it seemed to Achilles out of order that a man who was not drunk should stand before him three paces away, staring point-blank and saying nothing.
“And vat, vat do you vant here?” he said, still not stirring or changing his position.
“Why, nothing, brother; good morning!” answered Svidrigailov.
“Zis is not ze place.”
“I am going to foreign parts, brother.”
“To foreign parts?”
“To America.”
“To America?”
Svidrigailov took out the revolver and cocked it. Achilles raised his eyebrows.
“And vat, vat, zese jokes are not for here!”
“But why isn’t this the place?”
“Because it is not ze place.”
“Well, brother, it makes no difference. The place is a good one; if they ask you, just answer that he went, so to speak, to America.”
He put the revolver to his right temple.
“But here you can’t, zis is not ze place!” Achilles started up, his pupils growing wider and wider.
Svidrigailov pulled the trigger.
## CHAPTER VII

That same day, but in the evening, at about seven o’clock, Raskolnikov was approaching his mother’s and sister’s lodging, the same lodging in Bakaleev’s house where Razumikhin had settled them. The entrance to the stairs was from the street. Raskolnikov came up, still holding back his step and as if hesitating: should he go in or not? But he would not have turned back for anything; his decision was made. “Besides, it makes no difference; they don’t know anything yet,” he thought, “and they are already used to thinking me an eccentric...” His clothes were dreadful: everything dirty, having been out all night in the rain, torn, frayed. His face was almost disfigured by tiredness, bad weather, physical exhaustion and an almost day-long struggle with himself. He had spent the whole of that night alone, God knows where. But at least he had made up his mind.

He knocked at the door; his mother opened it to him. Dunechka was not at home. Even the servant was not there at that moment. At first Pulkheria Alexandrovna was struck dumb with joyful amazement; then she seized his hand and pulled him into the room.

“Well, here you are!” she began, stammering with joy. “Don’t be angry with me, Rodya, for meeting you so foolishly, with tears: I am laughing, not crying. You think I am crying? No, I am rejoicing, but I have such a silly habit: the tears flow. I have had it since your father’s death; I cry at everything. Sit down, my dear; you are tired, I can see. Ah, how dirty you have got.”
“I was out in the rain yesterday, Mama...” Raskolnikov began.

“No, no, don’t!” Pulkheria Alexandrovna started up, interrupting him. “You thought I would start questioning you at once, in my old womanish way; don’t worry. I understand, I understand everything; I have learned the ways here now, and really, I see myself that it is wiser here. I have decided once and for all: how am I to understand your ideas and demand accounts from you? Perhaps you have God knows what affairs and plans in your head, or some thoughts are being born there; so am I to nudge your elbow: what are you thinking about? Here I... Ah, Lord! What am I doing, rushing here and there like a madwoman... Here, Rodya, I am reading your article in the journal for the third time already; Dmitry Prokofich brought it to me. I simply gasped when I saw it: what a fool I am, I thought to myself, so this is what he is busy with, here is the answer to everything! Perhaps he has new thoughts in his head just now; he is thinking them over, and I torment him and trouble him. I read it, my dear, and of course there is a lot I don’t understand; but then, that is how it should be: how could I?”
“Show it to me, Mama.”

Raskolnikov took the paper and glanced at his article in passing. However much it contradicted his situation and his state, he felt that strange and caustically sweet feeling which an author experiences on seeing himself in print for the first time; besides, his twenty-three years told. This lasted only an instant. Having read a few lines, he frowned, and a terrible anguish gripped his heart. All his inner struggle of the last months came back to him at once. With disgust and vexation he threw the article on the table.

“But only, Rodya, however stupid I am, I can still judge that you will very soon be one of the first men, if not the very first, in our learned world. And they dared to think that you had gone mad. Ha-ha-ha! You don’t know, but they did think it! Ah, low worms, how could they understand what intelligence is! And Dunechka too almost believed it; just think! Your late father twice sent things to the journals: first poems (I still keep the exercise book; I will show it to you some day), and then a whole story (I begged him myself to let me copy it out), and how we both prayed that they would accept it; they didn’t! Six or seven days ago, Rodya, I was breaking my heart, looking at your clothes, how you live, what you eat and what you go about in. And now I see that I was stupid again, because if you want to, you will get everything for yourself at once now, by your intelligence and talent. It is just that for the time being you don’t want to, and are busy with much more important things...”
“Isn’t Dunya at home, Mama?”

“No, Rodya. Very often I don’t see her at home; she leaves me alone. Dmitry Prokofich, thanks to him, comes in to sit with me and keeps talking about you. He loves you and respects you, my dear. I am not saying that your sister is so very disrespectful to me. I am not complaining. She has her character and I have mine; she has some secrets of her own now; well, I have no secrets from you two. Of course I am firmly sure that Dunya is too intelligent, and besides, she loves both me and you... but I don’t know what all this will lead to. Here you have made me happy now, Rodya, by coming in, and she has gone out; she will come back, and I will say: your brother was here while you were out, and where were you pleased to spend your time? Don’t spoil me too much, Rodya: if you can, come in; if you can’t, there is nothing to be done, I will wait anyway. After all, I shall know all the same that you love me, and that is enough for me. I will read your writings, I will hear about you from everyone, and now and then you will come yourself to see me; what could be better? Here you have come now to comfort your mother, I can see...”
Here Pulkheria Alexandrovna suddenly began to cry.

“Me again! Don’t look at me, fool that I am! Ah, Lord, why am I sitting here,” she cried, jumping up from her place, “there is coffee, and I haven’t offered you any! That is what an old woman’s egoism means. At once, at once!”
“Mama, leave that; I am going in a moment. I didn’t come for that. Please, listen to me.”
Pulkheria Alexandrovna came up to him timidly.

“Mama, whatever happens, whatever you hear about me, whatever you are told about me, will you love me as you do now?” he asked suddenly, from the fullness of his heart, as if not thinking about his words and not weighing them.
“Rodya, Rodya, what is the matter with you? How can you ask such a thing! Who would tell me anything about you? I wouldn’t believe anyone, whoever came to me; I would simply drive them away.”

“I came to assure you that I have always loved you, and now I am glad that we are alone, glad even that Dunechka is not here,” he went on with the same impulse. “I came to tell you straight out that though you will be unhappy, still you should know that your son loves you now more than himself, and that everything you thought about me, that I am cruel and don’t love you, all that was untrue. I shall never stop loving you... Well, and that is enough; it seemed to me that I had to do this and begin with this...”
Pulkheria Alexandrovna silently embraced him, pressed him to her breast and wept quietly.

“What is the matter with you, Rodya, I don’t know,” she said at last. “All this time I thought that we were simply boring you, but now I see from everything that a great sorrow is in store for you; that is why you are so miserable. I have foreseen it for a long time, Rodya. Forgive me for speaking of it; I keep thinking about it and don’t sleep at night. Last night your sister too lay delirious the whole night through, and kept talking about you. I caught something, but understood nothing. All morning I went about as if before an execution, expecting something, foreseeing something, and now it has come! Rodya, Rodya, where are you going? Are you going away somewhere?”
“I am.”

“So I thought! But I can go with you, if you need me. And Dunya; she loves you, she loves you very much; and Sofya Semyonovna, perhaps, let her come with us, if need be; you see, I will gladly take her even as a daughter. Dmitry Prokofich will help us get ready together... but... where are you... going?”
“Goodbye, Mama.”
“What! Today!” she cried, as if losing him for ever.
“I can’t stay, it is time, I very much need to...”
“And I can’t come with you?”
“No, but kneel down and pray to God for me. Your prayer, perhaps, will reach him.”
“Let me make the sign of the cross over you, let me bless you! There, there. Oh God, what are we doing!”

Yes, he was glad, he was very glad that no one was there, that he and his mother were alone. It was as if his heart had softened all at once for all that terrible time. He fell down before her, he kissed her feet, and both, embracing, wept. And this time she did not wonder or ask questions. She had long understood that something terrible was happening to her son, and that now some dreadful moment had come for him.

“Rodya, my dear, my first-born,” she said, sobbing, “now you are just as you were when you were little; you used to come to me just like this, and hug me and kiss me just like this; back when your father and I lived together and were poor, you comforted us just by being with us, and when I buried your father, how many times did we weep, hugging each other just like now, on his grave. And if I have been crying for a long time, it is because a mother’s heart foresaw trouble. As soon as I saw you the first time then, in the evening, remember, when we had just arrived here, I guessed everything from your look alone; my heart simply trembled then, and today, when I opened the door to you and looked, well, I thought, the fatal hour has come. Rodya, Rodya, you aren’t going right now?”
“No.”
“You will come again?”
“Yes... I will come.”
“Rodya, don’t be angry, I don’t even dare ask. I know I don’t dare, but just tell me two little words: are you going far?”
“Very far.”
“What is there, some position, a career for you?”
“Whatever God sends... only pray for me...”
Raskolnikov went to the door, but she clung to him and looked into his eyes with a desperate look. Her face was distorted with horror.
“Enough, Mama,” said Raskolnikov, deeply regretting that he had taken it into his head to come.
“Not for ever? It isn’t for ever yet, is it? You will come, you will come tomorrow?”
“I will, I will; goodbye.”
He tore himself away at last.

The evening was fresh, warm and clear; the weather had cleared up since the morning. Raskolnikov was walking to his lodging; he was hurrying. He wanted to finish everything before sunset. Until then he would rather not meet anyone. Going up to his lodging, he noticed that Nastasya, tearing herself away from the samovar, was watching him intently and following him with her eyes. “Can there be someone in my room?” he thought. He imagined Porfiry, with disgust. But when he reached his room and opened it, he saw Dunechka. She was sitting all alone, in deep thought, and had evidently been waiting for him a long time. He stopped on the threshold. She rose from the sofa in fright and stood up straight before him. Her look, fixed motionlessly on him, expressed horror and inconsolable grief. And from that look alone he understood at once that she knew everything.
“Well, shall I come in to you, or go away?” he asked mistrustfully.
“I sat at Sofya Semyonovna’s all day; we were both waiting for you. We thought you would certainly go there.”
Raskolnikov came into the room and sat down on a chair in exhaustion.
“I am somehow weak, Dunya; I am very tired; and I would like to be in full control of myself at least at this moment.”
He glanced up at her mistrustfully.
“Where were you all night?”

“I don’t remember well; you see, sister, I wanted to make up my mind finally, and many times I walked near the Neva; that I remember. I wanted to end it there, but... I couldn’t bring myself to...” he whispered, again glancing mistrustfully at Dunya.
“Thank God! And how we were afraid of exactly that, Sofya Semyonovna and I! So you still believe in life: thank God, thank God!”
Raskolnikov smiled bitterly.

“I didn’t believe, but just now my mother and I were weeping in each other’s arms; I don’t believe, but I asked her to pray for me. God knows how this happens, Dunechka, and I understand nothing of it.”
“You were at Mother’s? And you told her?” Dunya exclaimed in horror. “Can it be that you brought yourself to tell her?”

“No, I didn’t tell her... in words; but she understood a great deal. She heard you raving in the night. I am sure she understands half already. Perhaps I did wrong to go. I don’t even know why I went. I am a low man, Dunya.”
“A low man, and yet you are ready to go to suffering! You are going, aren’t you?”

“I am. Right now. Yes, it was to escape this shame that I wanted to drown myself, Dunya, but I thought, standing over the water, that if I have considered myself strong until now, then let me not be afraid of shame now either,” he said, running ahead. “Is that pride, Dunya?”
“It is pride, Rodya.”
It was as if a fire flashed in his dulled eyes; it seemed to please him that he was still proud.
“And don’t you think, sister, that I was simply afraid of the water?” he asked with a hideous smile, looking into her face.
“Oh, Rodya, stop it!” Dunya exclaimed bitterly.
The silence lasted about two minutes. He sat with his eyes lowered, looking at the ground; Dunechka stood at the other end of the table and looked at him in torment. Suddenly he stood up:
“It is late, it is time. I am going now to give myself up. But I don’t know why I am going to give myself up.”
Big tears were running down her cheeks.
“You are crying, sister, but can you give me your hand?”
“And did you doubt it?”
She hugged him tightly.
“Aren’t you, by going to suffering, already washing away half your crime?” she cried, pressing him in her arms and kissing him.

“Crime? What crime?” he cried suddenly, in a kind of sudden fury. “That I killed a vile, harmful louse, an old moneylender, of no use to anyone, for whose killing forty sins would be forgiven, who sucked the juice out of the poor, and that is a crime? I don’t think about it and I don’t think of washing it away. And why does everyone keep jabbing at me from all sides: ‘crime, crime!’ Only now do I see clearly the whole absurdity of my faint-heartedness, now that I have decided to go to this unnecessary shame! I am deciding simply out of my baseness and lack of talent, or perhaps out of advantage, as that... Porfiry proposed!..”
“Brother, brother, what are you saying! But you have shed blood!” Dunya cried in despair.

“Which everyone sheds,” he took up, almost in a frenzy, “which flows and has always flowed in the world like a waterfall, which people pour out like champagne, and for which men are crowned in the Capitol and called afterwards benefactors of humanity. Just look more closely and see! I myself wanted good for people, and would have done hundreds, thousands of good deeds instead of this one piece of stupidity, not even stupidity but simply clumsiness, since the whole idea was not at all as stupid as it seems now, after the failure... (After failure everything seems stupid!) By this stupidity I only wanted to put myself in an independent position, to take the first step, to obtain means, and then everything would have been smoothed over by an immeasurable, comparatively, benefit... But I, I couldn’t even stand the first step, because I am a scoundrel! That is the whole point! And still I won’t look at it your way: if I had succeeded, they would have crowned me, and now it’s the trap!”
“But that is not it, not it at all! Brother, what are you saying!”

“Ah! Not the right form, not an aesthetically nice form! Well, I decidedly don’t understand: why is pelting people with bombs, in a regular siege, a more respectable form? Fear of aesthetics is the first sign of impotence!.. Never, never have I realised this more clearly than now, and more than ever I don’t understand my crime! Never, never have I been stronger and more convinced than now!..”

Colour even rushed into his pale, exhausted face. But as he uttered this last exclamation, his eyes happened to meet Dunya’s, and he met so much, so much torment for him in that look that he involuntarily came to himself. He felt that all the same he had made these two poor women unhappy. All the same, he was the cause...

“Dunya, dear! If I am guilty, forgive me (though I cannot be forgiven, if I am guilty). Goodbye! Let us not argue! It is time, it is very much time. Don’t follow me, I beg you; I still have to call somewhere... But go now and sit beside Mother at once. I beg you! It is my last and greatest request to you. Don’t leave her all the time; I left her in an anxiety which she will hardly bear: she will either die or go out of her mind. Be with her! Razumikhin will be with you; I have spoken to him... Don’t cry for me: I will try to be both brave and honest, all my life, though I am a murderer. Perhaps some day you will hear my name. I won’t disgrace you, you’ll see; I will still prove... now, for the time being, goodbye,” he hastened to conclude, again noticing a strange expression in Dunya’s eyes at his last words and promises. “Why are you crying so? Don’t cry, don’t cry; we are not parting for good!.. Ah, yes! Wait, I forgot!..”

He went to the table, took a thick, dusty book, opened it and took out a small portrait in watercolour on ivory, which had been put between the pages. It was a portrait of his landlady’s daughter, his former bride, who had died of a fever, that same strange girl who had wanted to go into a convent. For a minute he gazed at that expressive and sickly little face, kissed the portrait and handed it to Dunechka.

“I talked a great deal with her about this too, with her alone,” he said thoughtfully. “I told her heart much of what was afterwards fulfilled so hideously. Don’t worry,” he turned to Dunya, “she did not agree, any more than you, and I am glad that she is gone. The main thing, the main thing is that everything will now go a new way, will break in two,” he cried suddenly, returning again to his anguish, “everything, everything, but am I prepared for it? Do I want it myself? They say it is necessary for my trial! What for, what for, all these senseless trials? What for; will I be more aware then, crushed by torments, by idiocy, in an old man’s impotence after twenty years of penal servitude, than I am aware now? And what will I live for then? Why do I agree to live like that now? Oh, I knew I was a scoundrel when I stood over the Neva at dawn today!”

At last they both went out. It was hard for Dunya, but she loved him! She walked off, but after about fifty paces she turned round to look at him once more. He could still be seen. But on reaching the corner, he too turned round; for the last time their eyes met; but, noticing that she was looking at him, he waved his hand impatiently and even with vexation for her to go on, and turned sharply round the corner himself.

“I am wicked, I see it,” he thought to himself, ashamed a minute later of his vexed gesture to Dunya. “But why do they love me so much themselves, if I am not worth it! Oh, if only I were alone and no one loved me, and I had never loved anyone myself! None of this would have happened! And it is curious: can it be that in these coming fifteen or twenty years my soul will be so humbled that I shall whimper reverently before people, calling myself a robber at every word? Yes, just so, just so! That is what they are exiling me for now; that is what they need... Here they all are, scurrying up and down the street, and every one of them is a scoundrel and a robber by his very nature; worse than that, an idiot! But just try to let me off exile, and they will all go wild with noble indignation! Oh, how I hate them all!”

He fell deep into thought about this: “By what process can it happen that at last, before all of them, he will be humbled without reasoning, humbled by conviction! And why not? Of course, that is how it must be. Will not twenty years of unbroken oppression finish one off completely? Water wears away stone. And why, why live after that, why am I going now, when I know myself that it will all be exactly so, as in a book, and not otherwise!”
He had asked himself this question for perhaps the hundredth time since the evening before, but still he went.
## CHAPTER VIII

When he came to Sonya’s, dusk was already beginning. All day Sonya had been waiting for him in terrible agitation. She and Dunya had waited together. Dunya had come to her in the morning, remembering Svidrigailov’s words of the day before, that Sonya “knew about it”. We will not give the details of the conversation and the tears of the two women, and how close they became to each other. Dunya carried away from this meeting at least one consolation: that her brother would not be alone: it was to her, Sonya, that he had come first with his confession; in her he had sought a human being when he needed a human being; and she would follow him wherever fate sent him. Dunya did not even ask, but she knew that it would be so. She looked at Sonya even with a kind of reverence, and at first almost embarrassed her by this reverent feeling with which she treated her. Sonya was even ready almost to cry: she, on the contrary, considered herself unworthy even to look at Dunya. Dunya’s beautiful image, when she had bowed to her with such attention and respect at their first meeting in Raskolnikov’s room, had remained in her soul ever since as one of the most beautiful and unattainable visions of her life.

At last Dunechka could not bear it and left Sonya, to wait for her brother in his lodging; she kept thinking he would go there first. Left alone, Sonya at once began to be tormented by fear at the thought that perhaps he really would end it by suicide. Dunya feared the same. But all day they had vied with each other in persuading each other by every argument that this could not be, and they had been calmer while they were together. Now, as soon as they had parted, each of them began to think of this alone. Sonya remembered how yesterday Svidrigailov had told her that Raskolnikov had two roads: the Vladimirka or... She knew besides his vanity, his arrogance, his pride and his unbelief. “Can it be that only faint-heartedness and fear of death can make him live?” she thought at last in despair. The sun meanwhile was already setting. She stood sadly before the window and looked out of it intently, but from this window only the blank unwhitewashed wall of the neighbouring house could be seen. At last, when she had come to complete conviction that the unhappy man was dead, he came into her room.
A joyful cry broke from her breast. But looking intently into his face, she suddenly turned pale.
“Well, yes!” said Raskolnikov, smiling. “I have come for your crosses, Sonya. It was you who sent me to the crossroads; what, now that it has come to the point, have you lost your nerve?”

Sonya looked at him in amazement. His tone seemed strange to her; a cold shiver passed over her body, but a minute later she guessed that both the tone and the words were all put on. And he was talking to her looking somehow into a corner, as if avoiding looking her straight in the face.

“You see, Sonya, I have decided that this way will perhaps be more advantageous. There is a circumstance here... Well, it would take long to tell, and there is no point. Do you know what alone makes me angry? I am vexed that all those stupid, bestial mugs will surround me in a moment, will goggle at me with their eyes, ask me their stupid questions, which one has to answer; they will point their fingers... Pah! You know, I am not going to Porfiry; I am sick of him. I would rather go to my friend Gunpowder; how I’ll surprise him, what an effect of a kind I shall produce. But I ought to be cooler; I have become far too bilious lately. Would you believe it: just now I almost shook my fist at my sister only because she turned round to look at me for the last time. Swinishness, such a state! Eh, what I have come to! Well, then, where are the crosses?”

He was as if not himself. He could not even stand still in one place for a minute, could not fix his attention on a single object; his thoughts leapt over one another, he was rambling; his hands were trembling slightly.
Sonya silently took two crosses out of a drawer, one of cypress wood and one of copper, crossed herself, made the sign of the cross over him and put the little cypress cross round his neck.

“So this is a symbol that I am taking up the cross, he-he! And really, I have suffered little so far! Cypress, that is, the common people’s; the copper one is Lizaveta’s; you are taking it for yourself; let me see? So she was wearing it... at that moment? I know two similar crosses too, a silver one and a little icon. I threw them down on the old woman’s breast that time. Those would be just right now, really; those are the ones I ought to put on... But then, I am talking nonsense, I’ll forget the business; I am somehow absent-minded!.. You see, Sonya, I came properly speaking to forewarn you, so that you would know... Well, that’s all... That is all I came for. (Hm, I thought, though, that I would say more.) Why, you wanted me to go yourself; well, so I shall sit in prison, and your wish will come true; well, why are you crying? You too? Stop it, enough; oh, how hard all this is for me!”

A feeling, however, was born in him; his heart contracted as he looked at her. “This one, what about this one?” he thought to himself. “What am I to her? Why is she crying, why is she getting me ready like a mother or Dunya? She will be my nurse!”
“Cross yourself, pray at least once,” Sonya asked in a trembling, timid voice.
“Oh, by all means, as much as you like! And with a pure heart, Sonya, with a pure heart...”
He wanted, however, to say something else.

He crossed himself several times. Sonya seized her shawl and threw it over her head. It was the green drap-de-dames shawl, probably the same one that Marmeladov had mentioned that time, “the family one”. The thought flashed through Raskolnikov’s mind, but he did not ask. Indeed, he had begun to feel himself that he was terribly absent-minded and somehow hideously agitated. He was frightened by this. He was struck too by the fact that Sonya meant to go out with him.

“What are you doing! Where are you going? Stay, stay! I go alone,” he cried in faint-hearted vexation and, almost angrily, went to the door. “And what is the need of a whole retinue!” he muttered as he went out.
Sonya stayed in the middle of the room. He had not even said goodbye to her; he had already forgotten her; one caustic and rebellious doubt was boiling up in his soul.
“But is it right, is it right, all this?” he thought again, going down the stairs. “Is it really impossible to stop even now and put everything right again... and not go?”

But still he went. He suddenly felt, finally, that there was no point in asking himself questions. Coming out into the street, he remembered that he had not said goodbye to Sonya, that she had stayed in the middle of the room, in her green shawl, not daring to move after his shout, and he stopped for a moment. At that same instant a thought suddenly lit him up brightly, as if it had been waiting to strike him finally.

“Well, what for, why did I go to her now? I told her: on business; on what business? There was no business at all! To announce that I am going; what of it? What a need! Do I love her, then? No, surely not? Why, I drove her away just now like a dog. Did I really need crosses from her? Oh, how low I have fallen! No: I needed her tears, I needed to see her fright, to watch her heart ache and be torn! I had to catch hold of something at least, to delay, to look at a human being! And I dared to hope so much in myself, to dream so about myself, beggar that I am, nothing that I am, scoundrel, scoundrel!”
He walked along the embankment of the canal, and he did not have far to go now. But on reaching the bridge he stopped, and suddenly turned onto the bridge, aside, and crossed to the Haymarket.

He looked round greedily to the right and the left, peered intently at every object and could fix his attention on nothing; everything slipped away. “In a week, in a month, I shall be driven somewhere in one of these prison carriages across this bridge; how shall I look at this canal then? Should I remember this?” flashed through his head. “Here is this signboard; how shall I read these very letters then? Here it says ‘Company’; well, remember this a, the letter a, and look at it in a month, at this very a: how shall I look at it then? What shall I feel and think then?.. God, how base all this must be, all these present... concerns of mine! Of course, all this must be curious... in its way... (ha-ha-ha! what am I thinking about!) I am becoming a child, I am showing off before myself; well, why am I shaming myself? Pah, how they push! That fat man, a German, I suppose, who pushed me: well, does he know whom he pushed? A peasant woman with a child is begging; it is curious that she thinks me happier than herself. Why not give her something, for the oddity of it? Ba, a five-kopeck piece has survived in my pocket; where from? Here, here... take it, mother!”
“God keep you!” came the beggar woman’s plaintive voice.

He came into the Haymarket. It was unpleasant, very unpleasant for him to rub shoulders with people, but he went precisely where more people could be seen. He would have given anything in the world to be left alone; but he felt himself that he would not stay alone for a single minute. In the crowd a drunk man was making a nuisance of himself: he kept wanting to dance, but kept falling to one side. People had gathered round him. Raskolnikov squeezed through the crowd, looked at the drunk man for a few minutes and suddenly laughed shortly and abruptly. A minute later he had already forgotten him, did not even see him, though he was looking at him. At last he moved away, not even remembering where he was; but when he reached the middle of the square, a movement suddenly took place in him, a single sensation took hold of him all at once, seized him entirely, body and mind.

He suddenly remembered Sonya’s words: “Go to the crossroads, bow down to the people, kiss the earth, because you have sinned against it too, and say aloud to the whole world: ‘I am a murderer!’” He trembled all over, remembering it. And the hopeless anguish and anxiety of all this time, but especially of the last hours, had so crushed him that he simply flung himself into the possibility of this whole, new, full sensation. It came over him suddenly like a kind of fit: it caught fire in his soul as a single spark, and suddenly, like a fire, seized him entirely. Everything in him softened at once, and the tears gushed out. Just as he stood, he fell to the ground...
He knelt in the middle of the square, bowed to the ground and kissed that dirty earth with delight and happiness. He stood up and bowed a second time.
“Look how sozzled he is!” a lad beside him remarked.
There was laughter.

“He’s going to Jerusalem, brothers, saying goodbye to his children, to his homeland, bowing to the whole world, kissing the capital city of St Petersburg and its soil,” added some tipsy little tradesman.
“Still a young lad!” put in a third.
“One of the gentry!” someone remarked in a solid voice.
“Nowadays you can’t tell who’s gentry and who isn’t.”

All these responses and remarks held Raskolnikov back, and the words “I killed”, which were perhaps ready to fly from his tongue, died away in him. He bore all these shouts calmly, however, and, without looking round, walked straight through a lane in the direction of the police office. One vision flashed before him on the way, but he was not surprised at it; he had already had a presentiment that it must be so. At the moment when, in the Haymarket, he had bowed to the ground the second time, turning to the left, about fifty paces from him he had seen Sonya. She was hiding from him behind one of the wooden booths that stood in the square; so she had accompanied his whole sorrowful procession! Raskolnikov felt and understood at that moment, once and for all, that Sonya was with him now for ever and would follow him even to the end of the world, wherever fate might send him. His whole heart turned over... but here he was already at the fatal place...

He went into the courtyard fairly briskly. He had to climb to the third floor. “I will climb up yet, for the time being,” he thought. In general it seemed to him that the fatal moment was still far off, that a lot of time still remained, that much could still be thought over.

Again the same rubbish, the same eggshells on the spiral staircase, again the doors of the flats wide open, again the same kitchens, from which fumes and stench poured out. Raskolnikov had not been here since that time. His legs were growing numb and giving way, but they went. He stopped for a moment to catch his breath, to collect himself, to go in like a man. “But what for? why?” he thought suddenly, grasping the meaning of his movement. “If I must drink this cup, isn’t it all the same? The nastier the better.” At that moment the figure of Ilya Petrovich Gunpowder flashed into his imagination. “Am I really going to him? Couldn’t I go to another? Couldn’t I go to Nikodim Fomich? Turn round now and go to the superintendent himself at his lodging? At least it would go off in a homely way... No, no! To Gunpowder, to Gunpowder! If I must drink, then drink it all at once...”

Gone cold and hardly aware of himself, he opened the door into the office. This time there were very few people in it; some caretaker was standing there and some other common man. The porter did not even look out from behind his partition. Raskolnikov went into the next room. “Perhaps I won’t have to speak after all,” flashed through him. Here some individual from among the clerks, in a civilian frock coat, was settling down to write something at a desk. In the corner another clerk was taking his seat. Zamyotov was not there. Nikodim Fomich, of course, was not there either.
“Is there no one here?” Raskolnikov asked, turning to the individual at the desk.
“Whom do you want?”
“A-a-ah! Not a sound to be heard, not a sight to be seen, but I smell a Russian smell... how does it go in the fairy tale... I forget! My r-respects to you!” a familiar voice cried suddenly.
Raskolnikov trembled. Gunpowder was standing before him; he had suddenly come out of the third room. “This is fate itself,” thought Raskolnikov. “Why is he here?”

“Come to us? On what business?” exclaimed Ilya Petrovich. (He was evidently in the most excellent and even slightly excited state of spirits.) “If it is on business, you have come too early. I am here myself by chance... But anyway, whatever I can do. I confess to you... what? what? Forgive me...”
“Raskolnikov.”
“Well, of course: Raskolnikov! And could you really suppose that I had forgotten! Please don’t take me for that kind of... Rodion Ro... Ro... Rodionych, I believe?”
“Rodion Romanych.”

“Yes, yes, yes! Rodion Romanych, Rodion Romanych! That is just what I was trying to get at. I even inquired many times. I confess to you that I have sincerely grieved since then that we were so, that time... it was explained to me afterwards; I learned that you were a young writer and even a scholar... and, so to speak, first steps... Oh Lord! Why, which of the writers and scholars did not take original steps at first! My wife and I both respect literature, and my wife to the point of passion!.. Literature and the arts! If only a man is noble; the rest can all be acquired by talents, knowledge, reason, genius! A hat: well, what does a hat mean, for instance? A hat is a pancake; I can buy one at Zimmermann’s; but what is kept under the hat and covered by the hat, that I cannot buy, sir!.. I confess I even wanted to come to you and explain myself, but I thought, perhaps you... But I won’t even ask: do you really need something? They say your family has come?”
“Yes, my mother and sister.”

“I even had the honour and happiness of meeting your sister; a cultivated and charming person. I confess I regretted that we got so heated with each other that time. A curious case! And as for my casting a certain look at you that time, about your fainting, it was afterwards explained in the most brilliant way! Bigotry and fanaticism! I understand your indignation. Perhaps you are changing lodgings, on account of the family’s arrival?”
“N-no, I just... I came in to ask... I thought I would find Zamyotov here.”

“Ah, yes! You have become friends, I heard, sir. Well, Zamyotov is not with us; you have missed him. Yes, sir, we have lost Alexander Grigorievich! Since yesterday he is no longer present; he has transferred... and in transferring he even quarrelled with everyone... so impolitely even... A flighty boy, nothing more; he might even have shown promise; but there you are, with our brilliant youth! He wants to take some examination or other, but with us it is only a matter of talking and showing off, and that will be the end of the examination. It is not as with you, for instance, or Mr Razumikhin there, your friend! Your career is in learning, and failures won’t throw you off any more! For you all these beauties of life, one may say, nihil est, are nothing; an ascetic, a monk, a hermit!.. For you, a book, a pen behind the ear, learned research: that is where your spirit soars! I myself, partly... have you been pleased to read Livingstone’s journals?”
“No.”

“But I have. Nowadays, by the way, a great many nihilists have spread about; well, but that is understandable; what times are these, I ask you? But then, with you... why, of course you are not a nihilist! Answer frankly, frankly!”

“No, you know, be frank with me, don’t be shy, as if you were alone with yourself! Service is one thing, and... you thought I was going to say friendship; no, sir, you didn’t guess! Not friendship, but the feeling of a citizen and a man, the feeling of humaneness and of love for the Most High. I may be an official person and on duty, but I am always bound to feel the citizen and the man in myself and to give an account... You were pleased to mention Zamyotov. Zamyotov will make some scandal in the French manner in an improper establishment, over a glass of champagne or Don wine; that is what your Zamyotov is! But I, perhaps, so to speak, am consumed with devotion and lofty feelings, and besides have importance, rank, hold a position! I am married and have children. I fulfil the duty of a citizen and a man, and who is he, allow me to ask? I treat you as a man ennobled by education. Here too, these midwives are spreading excessively.”

Raskolnikov raised his eyebrows questioningly. The words of Ilya Petrovich, who had obviously only just risen from the dinner table, rattled and poured out before him mostly as empty sounds. But part of them he did somehow understand; he looked questioningly and did not know how all this would end.

“I mean these cropped-haired girls,” the talkative Ilya Petrovich went on. “I have named them midwives myself, on my own account, and I find the name entirely satisfactory. He-he! They push into the academy, they study anatomy; well, tell me, if I fall ill, am I going to call in a young lady to treat me? He-he!”
Ilya Petrovich guffawed, entirely pleased with his witticisms.

“Granted, it is an immoderate thirst for enlightenment; but once one is enlightened, that is enough. Why abuse it? Why insult noble persons, as that scoundrel Zamyotov does? Why did he insult me, I ask you? And here too, how many of these suicides have spread, you cannot imagine. They all spend their last money and kill themselves. Girls, boys, old men... Here, only this morning there was a report about some gentleman who had recently arrived. Nil Pavlych, hey, Nil Pavlych! What was his name, the gentleman they reported earlier, who shot himself on the Petersburg Side?”
“Svidrigailov,” someone answered hoarsely and indifferently from the other room.
Raskolnikov started.
“Svidrigailov! Svidrigailov has shot himself!” he cried.
“What! You know Svidrigailov?”
“Yes... I know him... He came here recently...”

“Well, yes, he came recently, lost his wife, a man of dissolute conduct, and suddenly he shot himself, and so scandalously that you can’t imagine it... he left a few words in his notebook that he was dying in his right mind and asked that no one be blamed for his death. He had money, they say. How do you come to know him?”
“I... am acquainted... my sister lived in their house as a governess...”
“Ba, ba, ba... Then you can tell us about him. And you had no suspicion?”
“I saw him yesterday... he... was drinking wine... I knew nothing.”
Raskolnikov felt as if something had fallen on him and crushed him.
“You seem to have turned pale again. The air is so stale here...”
“Yes, it is time for me to go, sir,” muttered Raskolnikov. “Forgive me for troubling you...”
“Oh, not at all, as much as you like! You have given me pleasure, and I am glad to declare...”
Ilya Petrovich even held out his hand.
“I only wanted... I came to see Zamyotov...”
“I understand, I understand, and you have given me pleasure.”
“I... am very glad... goodbye, sir...” Raskolnikov smiled.

He went out; he was swaying. His head was spinning. He did not feel whether he was standing on his feet. He began to go down the stairs, leaning his right hand against the wall. It seemed to him that some caretaker with a book in his hand pushed him, climbing up towards him to the office; that some little dog was barking its head off somewhere on the lower floor and that some woman threw a rolling pin at it and shouted. He went down and came out into the courtyard. There in the courtyard, not far from the way out, stood Sonya, pale, numb all over, and she looked at him wildly, wildly. He stopped before her. Something sick and tormented showed in her face, something desperate. She clasped her hands. A hideous, lost smile forced itself onto his lips. He stood there, smiled, and turned back upstairs, to the office again.
Ilya Petrovich had sat down and was rummaging in some papers. Before him stood the same peasant who had just pushed Raskolnikov as he climbed the stairs.
“A-a-ah? You again! Have you left something?.. But what is the matter with you?”

Raskolnikov, with whitened lips and a fixed look, quietly came up to him, went right up to the table, leaned his hand on it, wanted to say something, but could not; only some incoherent sounds could be heard.
“You are unwell; a chair! Here, sit on the chair, sit down! Water!”
Raskolnikov sank onto the chair, but did not take his eyes off the face of Ilya Petrovich, who was very unpleasantly surprised. For a minute both looked at each other and waited. Water was brought.
“It was I...” Raskolnikov began.
“Drink some water.”
Raskolnikov pushed the water away with his hand and said quietly, deliberately, but distinctly:
“It was I who killed the old official’s widow and her sister Lizaveta with an axe that time, and robbed them.”
Ilya Petrovich’s mouth fell open. People came running from all sides.
Raskolnikov repeated his statement.
## EPILOGUE · I

Siberia. On the bank of a broad, desolate river stands a town, one of the administrative centres of Russia; in the town is a fortress, in the fortress a prison. In the prison, for nine months now, the convict of the second category Rodion Raskolnikov has been confined. Almost a year and a half has passed since the day of his crime.

The legal proceedings in his case went off without great difficulties. The criminal maintained his statement firmly, precisely and clearly, not confusing the circumstances, not softening them in his own favour, not distorting the facts, not forgetting the slightest detail. He told the whole process of the murder down to the last feature: he explained the secret of the pledge (the little wooden board with a metal strip) which had been found in the murdered old woman’s hands; he told in detail how he had taken the keys from the murdered woman, described those keys, described the trunk and what it was filled with; he even listed some of the separate objects that lay in it; he explained the riddle of Lizaveta’s murder; he told how Koch had come and knocked, and after him the student, repeating everything they had said to each other; how he, the criminal, had afterwards run down the stairs and heard Mikolka and Mitka shrieking; how he had hidden in the empty flat and come home; and in conclusion he pointed out the stone in the courtyard, on Voznesensky Prospect, under the gateway, under which the things and the purse were found. In a word, the case came out clear. The investigators and judges were very surprised, among other things, that he had hidden the purse and the things under the stone without making use of them, and most of all that he not only did not remember in detail all the things he had actually stolen, but was even mistaken about their number. The very circumstance that he had not once opened the purse and did not even know exactly how much money lay in it seemed incredible (in the purse there turned out to be three hundred and seventeen silver roubles and three twenty-kopeck pieces; from lying a long time under the stone some of the top notes, the largest ones, had been extremely damaged). They tried for a long time to find out why precisely the accused was lying in this one circumstance, when in everything else he confessed voluntarily and truthfully. At last some (especially among the psychologists) even admitted the possibility that he really had not looked into the purse, and so did not know what was in it, and, not knowing, had carried it straight under the stone; but from this very thing they at once concluded that the crime itself could not have happened otherwise than in a state of a certain temporary insanity, so to speak, of a morbid monomania of murder and robbery, without further aims or calculations of gain. Here, by the way, the newest fashionable theory of temporary insanity came in handy, which in our time people so often try to apply to certain criminals. Besides, Raskolnikov’s long-standing hypochondriac state was precisely attested by many witnesses: Doctor Zosimov, his former comrades, his landlady, the servant. All this greatly contributed to the conclusion that Raskolnikov was not quite like an ordinary murderer, bandit and robber, but that there was something else here. To the greatest vexation of those who defended this opinion, the criminal himself hardly tried to defend himself; to the final questions, what exactly could have inclined him to murder and what had induced him to commit robbery, he answered very clearly, with the coarsest exactness, that the cause of everything had been his wretched position, his poverty and helplessness, his wish to secure the first steps of his career in life with the help of at least three thousand roubles which he had counted on finding at the murdered woman’s. And he had resolved on the murder as a result of his frivolous and faint-hearted character, irritated, moreover, by privations and failures. To the questions what exactly had induced him to come and confess, he answered directly that it was sincere repentance. All this was almost coarse...

The sentence, however, turned out more merciful than might have been expected, judging by the crime committed, and perhaps precisely because the criminal not only did not wish to justify himself, but even seemed to express a desire to accuse himself still more. All the strange and peculiar circumstances of the case were taken into account. The sick and wretched state of the criminal before committing the crime was not subjected to the slightest doubt. The fact that he had not made use of what he had stolen was counted partly as the action of an awakened repentance, partly as a not entirely sound state of his mental faculties at the time of committing the crime. The circumstance of the unpremeditated murder of Lizaveta even served as an example supporting the latter supposition: a man commits two murders and at the same time forgets that the door is standing unlocked! Finally, the confession, made at the very time when the case had become extraordinarily muddled through the false self-accusation of a dispirited fanatic (Nikolai), and besides, when there was not only no clear evidence against the real criminal but almost not even any suspicion (Porfiry Petrovich had fully kept his word): all this finally contributed to softening the accused’s fate.

Other circumstances also came to light, quite unexpectedly, which were strongly in the accused’s favour. The former student Razumikhin dug up information from somewhere and presented proof that the criminal Raskolnikov, while he was at the university, had helped a poor, consumptive fellow student of his out of his last means and had almost kept him for half a year. And when that student died, he had looked after the surviving old and paralysed father of his dead comrade (who had kept and fed his father by his own labour almost from the age of thirteen), had at last placed the old man in a hospital, and when he too died, had buried him. All this information had a certain favourable influence on the decision of Raskolnikov’s fate. His former landlady herself, the mother of Raskolnikov’s dead bride, the widow Zarnitsyna, also testified that when they were still living in another house, at Five Corners, Raskolnikov, during a fire, at night, had carried two small children out of a flat that was already burning, and had been burned in doing so. This fact was carefully investigated and fairly well attested by many witnesses. In a word, it ended with the criminal being sentenced to penal servitude of the second category, for a term of only eight years, in consideration of his confession and of certain extenuating circumstances.

At the very beginning of the trial Raskolnikov’s mother fell ill. Dunya and Razumikhin found it possible to take her away from Petersburg for the whole time of the trial. Razumikhin chose a town on the railway, at a short distance from Petersburg, so as to be able to follow all the circumstances of the trial regularly and at the same time to see Avdotya Romanovna as often as possible. Pulkheria Alexandrovna’s illness was a strange one, a nervous one, and was accompanied by something like insanity, if not completely, then at least partly. Dunya, returning from her last meeting with her brother, found her mother already quite ill, in a fever and delirious. That same evening she agreed with Razumikhin on what exactly to answer her mother’s questions about her brother, and even invented with him, for her mother, a whole story about Raskolnikov’s departure somewhere far away, to the frontier of Russia, on a private commission which would at last bring him both money and fame. But they were struck by the fact that Pulkheria Alexandrovna herself asked nothing about any of this, either then or afterwards. On the contrary, she turned out to have a whole story of her own about her son’s sudden departure; she told with tears how he had come to say goodbye to her; she let it be understood by hints that only she alone knew many very important and mysterious circumstances, and that Rodya had many very powerful enemies, so that he even had to go into hiding. As for his future career, that too seemed to her certain and brilliant, once certain hostile circumstances had passed; she assured Razumikhin that her son would in time even become a statesman, as his article and his brilliant literary talent proved. She read that article incessantly, sometimes even aloud, almost slept with it, and yet she hardly asked where exactly Rodya was now, even though they were obviously avoiding talking to her about it, which alone might have aroused her suspicion. At last they began to fear this strange silence of Pulkheria Alexandrovna on certain points. She did not even complain, for example, that there were no letters from him, whereas before, living in her little town, she had lived only on the hope and expectation of getting a letter soon from her beloved Rodya. This last circumstance was far too inexplicable and greatly worried Dunya; the thought came to her that her mother perhaps had a presentiment of something terrible in her son’s fate and was afraid to ask, so as not to find out something still more terrible. In any case Dunya saw clearly that Pulkheria Alexandrovna was not in a sound state of mind.

Once or twice, however, it happened that she herself steered the conversation so that it was impossible, in answering her, not to mention where exactly Rodya was now; and when the answers inevitably turned out unsatisfactory and suspicious, she suddenly became extremely sad, gloomy and silent, which lasted a very long time. Dunya saw at last that it was hard to lie and invent, and came to the final conclusion that it was better to keep completely silent on certain points; but it became more and more obviously clear that the poor mother suspected something terrible. Dunya remembered, among other things, her brother’s words that their mother had been listening to her delirium, on the night before that last fatal day, after her scene with Svidrigailov: had she not overheard something then? Often, sometimes after several days and even weeks of sullen, gloomy silence and mute tears, the sick woman would come to life somehow hysterically and suddenly begin to talk aloud, almost without stopping, about her son, about her hopes, about the future... Her fancies were sometimes very strange. They humoured her, they agreed with her (perhaps she herself saw clearly that they were agreeing with her and only humouring her), but she went on talking all the same...

Five months after the criminal’s confession his sentence followed. Razumikhin saw him in prison whenever it was possible. So did Sonya. At last the parting came; Dunya swore to her brother that this parting was not for ever; so did Razumikhin. In Razumikhin’s young and ardent head a plan had firmly taken root: during the next three or four years to lay, as far as possible, at least the beginning of a future fortune, to save at least some money and move to Siberia, where the soil is rich in every respect and workers, people and capital are few; to settle there in the very town where Rodya would be and... all together to begin a new life. As they said goodbye, everyone wept. In the very last days Raskolnikov was very thoughtful, asked a great deal about his mother, and was constantly worried about her. He even tormented himself about her too much, which alarmed Dunya. On learning in detail of his mother’s morbid state of mind, he became very gloomy. With Sonya he was for some reason especially taciturn all the time. Sonya, with the help of the money Svidrigailov had left her, had long since got herself ready to follow the party of convicts in which he would be sent. Not a word had ever been said about this between her and Raskolnikov; but both knew that it would be so.
